stories.Headline: Casap, whose AI tools automate dispute and anti-fraud operations for banks, raised a $56M Series B led by Base10 Partners, bringing its total funding to $90M (Jeff John Roberts/Fortune)
stories.Summary:
Casap, a financial AI startup, announced on Wednesday a $56 million Series B funding round led by Base10 Partners, according to Fortune. The round brings the company's total funding to $90 million since it launched in 2023. Synchrony and Experian joined the round as strategic investors, and Casap declined to disclose a valuation. The company was founded by CEO Shanthi Shanmugam and Saisi Peter, a Chime veteran.

Casap's AI tools are built to handle disputes and chargebacks for banks and card companies, and the company says customers have cut first party fraud losses by as much as 51%. It also says its customers have raised their chargeback win rate to 96%, compared with a 60% industry average. Shanmugam says the tools cut the average time to resolve a dispute to 8 days, down from as long as 90 days under traditional methods. A human still reviews each case, but that review often takes only 1 to 2 minutes.

Shanmugam said the shift toward cardholders themselves committing fraud comes down to people thinking it is a victimless crime and telling what they see as white lies. She said the rules governing disputes are written in a way that almost assumes no one lies. She said banks often resolve disputes in a customer's favor below a threshold of around $30, and sometimes much higher, because investigations are costly. Casap does not disclose all the indicators it uses, but Shanmugam said they include the physical location of a card and spending patterns.

The startup says the rise in first party fraud has been driven by AI tools that make disputing charges easier and by social media groups that share fraud tips under the guise of getting free stuff. Casap, whose name is meant to convey getting a case done ASAP, plans to use the new funding to move into adjacent back office work, including customer complaints and collections. Its other investors include Lightspeed Venture Partners, Emergence and Primary. Before Casap, Shanmugam was a product manager at Robinhood, Meta and Salesforce.

Articles.Title: Casap, whose AI tools automate dispute and anti-fraud operations for banks, raised a $56M Series B led by Base10 Partners, bringing its total funding to $90M (Jeff John Roberts/Fortune)

stories.Headline: James Gallagher's Bill Targets AI-Driven Trafficking
stories.Summary:
James Gallagher introduced the Countering Online Trafficking Act in Washington, D.C., according to a report published on October 31, 2026. Gallagher has served as California Assembly Republican leader. The bill targets traffickers who use artificial intelligence to find and groom children online. It would require the State Department to evaluate whether its Office to Monitor and Combat Trafficking in Persons has the expertise to identify and respond to these evolving threats.

Under the bill, the office's ambassador-at-large would assess whether existing personnel have the technical background to address AI-facilitated trafficking. If the assessment finds gaps, the ambassador-at-large would then have to develop a plan to close them. The articles cite a State Department warning that AI can automate and expand grooming, letting traffickers reach far more targets than human recruiters could alone. The department's 2025 Trafficking in Persons Report said AI systems can automate and scale grooming through chatbots that optimize manipulation tactics using natural language processing and sentiment analysis.

Gallagher framed the legislation around the concern that criminals are moving faster than the institutions meant to stop them. He said human traffickers use new technology to prey on children and that the federal government must keep pace. He added that human trafficking is a horrific crime demanding action, and that the responsibility to protect the innocent remains constant even as technology changes. The articles also note that Gallagher previously helped secure passage of California's SB 14, which made qualifying child sex-trafficking offenses serious felonies under the state's three-strikes law.

The articles cite United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime figures showing detected trafficking victims worldwide rose 25% in 2022 compared with pre-pandemic 2019. Detected child victims rose 31% over the same period, girls accounted for a 38% rise among child victims, and children made up 38% of all detected victims by 2022. Victims trafficked for forced labor rose 47% between 2019 and 2022, while trafficking for forced criminality, including online scams, went from 1% of detected victims in 2016 to 8% by 2022. Women and girls made up 61% of detected victims in 2022, drawn from the 2024 Global Report on Trafficking in Persons covering 156 countries. The articles say the bill is framed as a diagnostic step rather than a sweeping overhaul, and whether the assessment finds serious gaps, and what any resulting plan would look like, remains to be seen.

Articles.Title: James Gallagher's Bill Targets AI-Driven Trafficking

stories.Headline: Oracle Announces Fusion Agentic Applications for Supply Chain Featuring Fusion Claw
stories.Summary:
Oracle announced new agentic applications for supply chain work that feature Fusion Claw, in a release dated October 26, 2026 in the United States and published in Japan on November 2, 2026. The announcement came at Oracle AI World in Las Vegas. Oracle described Fusion Claw as a governed agentic execution platform that lets Fusion Agentic Applications reason, calculate, adapt and act on specialized work such as detailed research, calculations, simulations, modeling and continuous replanning. The new Claw-powered applications are built into Oracle Fusion Cloud Applications.

The applications are available in Oracle Fusion Cloud Supply Chain & Manufacturing and include three named ones. Supply planning allocation weighs production lines, work centers, finished goods, components and business tradeoffs to decide how limited materials and capacity go to competing demand. Shipment load planning evaluates consolidation opportunities across timing, transport capacity, service commitments, cost and other constraints to cut transport costs and meet service levels. Procurement spend analyzes spend, supplier contracts and purchasing data to detect off-contract spending and deviations, explain root causes, quantify savings and recommend corrective actions for review and approval.

S.Y. Shenoy, Oracle's senior vice president of application development, said supply chain leaders need a connected view across products, plans, procurement, logistics and costs to decide faster and with better information. Shenoy said the Claw-powered applications let supply chain teams move to acting under governance across key processes and rethink how work is done. The applications reason across Oracle Fusion Applications data, weigh options and tradeoffs, coordinate the work needed to meet business goals and put approved actions into effect, Shenoy said. That helps leaders drive stronger business outcomes faster and with consistency and confidence, according to Shenoy.

The applications run on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and use industry-leading LLMs, and they extend the Fusion Applications suite from assistance toward governed execution of work. They are part of a wider Fusion AI ecosystem centered on Oracle AI Agent Studio for Fusion Applications, whose no-code and pro-code features let organizations build and manage agentic applications using reusable Oracle, partner and external agents. Built-in observability, ROI measurement and security management are designed to help organizations monitor agent activity, apply safeguards and run agents responsibly at scale. Oracle's release did not say when the applications would become generally available or how they would be priced.

Articles.Title: Oracle Announces Fusion Agentic Applications for Supply Chain Featuring Fusion Claw

stories.Headline: The responsible AI bank: Combining trust, technology and talent at Banreservas
stories.Summary:
Banreservas, the largest financial institution in the Dominican Republic, is expanding its use of artificial intelligence with an emphasis on responsible implementation, Euromoney reported on November 2, 2026. The bank has decades of experience financing key sectors, helping small and medium-sized enterprises expand, and bringing more Dominicans into the financial system. Its virtual assistant Alma incorporated AI capabilities in 2024, after starting as a menu-based system. Alma has been upgraded to a conversational assistant using natural language that can guide users to the information and services they need.

The changes have contributed to a 215% rise in customer interactions through Alma over the past two years. Alma is now used by 7% of customers who transact through the bank's channels, leaving scope for wider adoption as the system improves. The bank has continued to add features to the Banreservas app since its launch in 2020. SMEs make up approximately 98% of the country's businesses and over half of its jobs, and the bank aims to use AI to analyse cash flows, anticipate financing needs, streamline credit applications and tailor banking solutions to each business.

Dr. Leonardo Aguilera, chief executive officer of Banreservas, said the goal is to harness the efficiency and potential of AI without automating exclusion. He said the bank does not want to automate its relationship with SMEs but to understand them better, expand their opportunities and support them at every stage of growth. He also said important decisions must remain subject to human oversight, taking into account the broader context and individual characteristics of each business. Aguilera said that when a customer opens a deposit entirely through the app, that means one less branch visit, one less form printed and one less process that needs duplicating.

The bank's approach is that AI deployment should complement personalised customer service instead of replacing it. Automated systems can inadvertently exclude customers from financial services, endanger data privacy, outpace regulatory frameworks or expose banks to new cybersecurity threats. Staff and management will need to work alongside AI agents, which requires training, most of which is currently being done at Academia Banreservas, the bank's human resources development unit. After being named the Caribbean's best bank for SMEs in Euromoney's Awards for Excellence 2026, Banreservas aims to leverage AI to further strengthen its relationships with Dominican businesses.

Articles.Title: The responsible AI bank: Combining trust, technology and talent at Banreservas

stories.Headline: Fujitsu and partners launch AI pilot to standardize packaging damage assessment and cut returns
stories.Summary:
Fujitsu, the Home Appliance Supply Chain Council, the Distribution Economics Institute of Japan and SoftBank Robotics announced on November 2, 2026 that they have started a joint pilot project. The project aims to clarify and standardize criteria for judging packaging damage across the home appliance industry and to use AI to assess such damage. The goal is to cut unnecessary product returns during delivery. The work is run by the Council for Sustainable Home Appliance Logistics, made up of the Council and the Institute, and has been adopted under a Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism subsidy for promoting behavioral change in shippers and logistics operators using digital technology.

The pilot runs from November 2, 2026 to January 15, 2027. The Council and the Institute will plan the project, develop industry-wide packaging damage criteria based on existing criteria from manufacturers, mass retailers and logistics providers, and supply packaging image data and operational expertise. Fujitsu and SoftBank Robotics will provide AI technologies and data analysis. Fujitsu will contribute its Kozuchi platform and Amalgamation AI for Vision, which recognizes images with little data and can give reasons for its assessments, while SoftBank Robotics will provide a solution that analyzes smartphone photos of cardboard packaging and records the results for later review.

The partners will evaluate the accuracy of the AI damage assessment model and ways to standardize the assessment criteria. They will also check how feasible the system is in real logistics settings and analyze how well it reduces returns and redeliveries. They will assess whether it could be applied to optimize the whole supply chain. The project intends to publish the packaging damage criteria and explore use beyond the home appliance industry.

The background is that the logistics industry faces labor shortages and rising delivery costs. In home appliances, products are often returned or redelivered over minor abrasions or dents in cardboard even when the appliance itself is undamaged. Criteria vary by company and often depend on the subjective experience of onsite staff, so the same damage may be judged differently by location or staff. This can cause inefficiency, higher transport costs, more CO2 emissions and excess resource use.

Articles.Title: Fujitsu, Home Appliance Supply Chain Council, Distribution Economics Institute of Japan, and SoftBank Robotics launch pilot project to standardize packaging damage assessment and reduce product returns using AI

stories.Headline: A Senate draft could let Medicare test paying for AI that performs clinical tasks without real-time physician review
stories.Summary:
Sen. Bill Cassidy, a Louisiana Republican who chairs the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, released a discussion draft on Oct. 29 called the PATIENT AI Act. The draft would direct the CMS Innovation Center to run a five-year payment model for artificial intelligence applications that can perform a clinical function on their own. The proposal has not been introduced or voted on, and Cassidy is asking for public comments by Dec. 1. The draft does not define “autonomously,” set payment rates, list covered conditions or tasks, or say how much patients would pay out of pocket.

Under the draft, the model would start no later than 24 months after the law is enacted and run for five years. Medicare would choose which AI applications and providers take part using published criteria, including clinical promise, patient safety, evidence gaps, and potential benefit to Medicare patients. Participants would need to give patients informed beneficiary notice when an AI tool is part of their care, and participation could not reduce existing Medicare appeal rights. The evaluation would measure effects on patient outcomes, safety, access, and patient experience, not only cost.

Cassidy's office said the goal is to create regulatory predictability while prioritizing patient safety, and Cassidy said AI in health care must be done responsibly and to the benefit of patients, innovators, and consumers. Dr. John Whyte, CEO of the American Medical Association, told the Times that models built to independently provide patient care are not ready for widespread use. HHS spokesperson Grace Davis Jamison said the department was taking a responsible, evidence-based approach to AI and expanding its use as evidence demonstrates value. The draft also says it does not alter liability under federal or state law, and it sends the question of who is liable when autonomous AI causes harm to further study through a nonprofit review.

In September, the administration was weighing how Medicare could pay for AI tools that provide care or diagnoses, and officials discussed paying AI “physicians” 60% to 80% of what human doctors earn for the same service, according to a person involved who spoke to The New York Times, Becker's reported. That was described as a discussion, not a decision. The FDA has authorized more than 1,500 medical devices that include AI for narrow tasks, such as flagging tumors on scans, but has no rules designed for chatbots or AI agents that could prescribe medications, according to Becker's. Nothing changes for Medicare patients today, and Cassidy lost his Republican primary in May, with his term ending in early January, so any formal bill would likely need a new sponsor or reintroduction in the next Congress.

Articles.Title: A Senate draft could let Medicare test paying for AI that performs clinical tasks without real-time physician review - Medical Daily

stories.Headline: Argentina’s Milei pitches a regulation-free AI haven at the end of the world
stories.Summary:
Argentina's President Javier Milei pitched Patagonia as a haven for artificial intelligence data centers on November 2, 2026, according to the AP report. The article says he made the pitch as backlash against such centers grows in the United States and Europe. The report does not name any companies or give the size of any investment. It also does not say where in Patagonia the centers would go.

The article describes the proposal as regulation-free, meaning the data centers would face few or no rules. It does not list specific laws that would be changed or dropped. It gives no dates for when construction might start or when rules might be lifted. No figures on jobs, money or energy use appear in the article.

The article attributes the pitch to Milei and does not quote him directly beyond a few words. It does not say what other Argentine officials said about the plan. It also does not say how local governments in Patagonia responded. No reaction from US or European officials appears in the report.

The article ties the pitch to growing backlash in the US and Europe but gives no details on that backlash. It does not say what happens next, such as whether a bill, decree or formal proposal will follow. It does not say whether any company has signed on. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Security Flaws Found in Five Popular AI Coding Tools, Including OpenAI Codex
stories.Summary:
Security vulnerabilities have been found in five popular AI development tools, according to a report by The Register on Oct. 29 local time. The cybersecurity startup Forever Security identified the flaws in SpaceXAI's Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Anthropic's Claude Desktop, Microsoft's Visual Studio Code and OpenAI's Codex. The tools give their embedded browsers capabilities and system access that ordinary web browsers do not allow. Forever Security called this class of vulnerabilities Embrace, short for EMbedded BRowser.

The flaws could allow remote code execution in Cursor, data theft in Claude Desktop, Codex and VS Code, and address bar spoofing in GitHub Copilot. Forever Security reported the Cursor flaw on Sept. 10, and Cursor applied a patch on Oct. 1. GitHub fixed its Copilot flaw on its own through the v1.1.29 patch released on Oct. 13. The Codex and VS Code flaws remained unpatched at the time of publication.

Anthropic first rejected the Claude Desktop report submitted on July 23, saying the issue did not involve a security boundary protected by Workspace Trust. The next day another company, Noma Security, reported the same flaw, and Anthropic then recognized it as valid. OpenAI received the Codex report on July 27 but did not respond to the researchers, though it told The Register it was aware of the issue and working on a fix. Microsoft classified the VS Code report from Sept. 10 as invalid, citing the same Workspace Trust argument.

Workspace Trust is a VS Code feature that decides whether an opened project or folder can be trusted and limits what functions and permissions are available inside it. Forever Security found that restrictions on local page access in Claude Desktop and VS Code could be bypassed using Web Workers, a browser feature that runs JavaScript in background threads. Codex had no mechanism limiting local HTML file access to the project folder in the first place, so files across the system could be read directly. The report says the Codex and VS Code flaws were still unpatched when it was published.

Articles.Title: Security Flaws Found in Five Popular AI Coding Tools, Including OpenAI Codex

stories.Headline: CJI, Law Minister stress on human oversight in AI use - The Sunday Guardian
stories.Summary:
Chief Justice of India Justice Surya Kant and Union Law Minister Arjun Ram Meghwal spoke about artificial intelligence at the Legally Speaking: 4th Law and Constitution Dialogue 2026, organised by the ITV Network in New Delhi. The event also featured senior advocate Mahesh Jethmalani and Rajya Sabha MPs Dr Abhishek Manu Singhvi and Sasmit Patra. The speakers focused on responsible regulation of AI, accountability for autonomous systems and protection of constitutional rights. The Chief Justice said AI was becoming an important subject for judiciaries worldwide, especially in legal research, translation and case management.

The Chief Justice called for international cooperation among courts rather than isolated experimentation, saying that since all courts are learning at the same time it makes little sense for each to learn alone. He highlighted the proposed Judicial Innovation Lab as a platform for judicial institutions to jointly examine emerging technologies. He said technological advancement would not necessarily threaten the justice system as long as human beings remain responsible for judicial decisions. Meghwal discussed agentic AI and asked whether AI could recommend arguments for petitioners and respondents or suggest judicial outcomes. He said technology should assist rather than replace human beings.

Jethmalani said tools such as ChatGPT and Claude are increasingly used by lawyers, and he cautioned against exaggerated fears, arguing that responsible use and an appropriate legal framework could address risks. He said technology must remain the servant of justice and never its master, and he raised concerns about privacy violations, deepfakes and misuse of generated content, referring to the Digital Personal Data Protection Act and 2026 rules on synthetically generated information. Singhvi called for a comprehensive global legal framework for accountability, warning that the autonomy of machines must never become the anonymity of responsibility. He warned that AI trained on flawed historical data could reproduce discrimination, turning yesterday's injustice into tomorrow's automated precedent.

Patra called on lawmakers to understand AI, its algorithms and emerging technologies before framing legislation, and expressed concern over the gap between AI's growing influence and legislators' technological understanding. He said AI could strengthen legislative processes through research and analysis, but decisions on public interest, citizens' rights and social priorities must remain guided by human judgement. He stressed that technological progress must operate within constitutional boundaries, particularly Articles 14, 19 and 21, and recalled Dr Ambedkar's address to the Constituent Assembly on November 4, 1948, on constitutional morality. The articles do not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: CJI, Law Minister stress on human oversight in AI use - The Sunday Guardian

stories.Headline: Runway AI YouTube Scraping Class Action Survives Dismissal
stories.Summary:
On October 30, 2026, Judge Lewis A. Kaplan of the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York denied Runway AI's motion to dismiss a consolidated class action, Ace Cam, Inc. v. Runway AI, Inc., No. 1:26-cv-01362. The ruling lets the case move forward and is not a finding that Runway broke the law. The lawsuit claims Runway violated the anti-circumvention provision of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act, 17 U.S.C. § 1201, by getting around YouTube's measures against bulk downloading to copy creators' videos and train its Gen-3 model. Runway argued the law does not apply because anyone can watch YouTube videos for free, and it asked the court to dismiss the case with prejudice.

The creators allege YouTube uses five technical measures to stop anyone from pulling out the underlying video files, including a rolling cipher, IP blocking and rate limits, session-bound links, CAPTCHA challenges and proof-of-origin tokens. They say Runway used the open-source downloader yt-dlp to defeat the rolling cipher, kept retrieving files after session authorizations had lapsed, and rotated through IP addresses with virtual machines and proxy services. Much of the factual basis comes from a July 2024 report by 404 Media, which the complaint cites, describing an internal spreadsheet listing about 3,968 YouTube channels and more than 100,000 videos. The complaint asks for statutory damages, an injunction against further circumvention and attorneys' fees, and under 17 U.S.C. § 1203 a court may award statutory damages of $200 to $2,500 per act of circumvention.

Judge Kaplan rejected each of Runway's three main arguments for now, writing that scrambling and encryption are examples of access controls, not an exhaustive list, and that the public nature of YouTube content does not leave it unprotected. The court found the creators had plausibly alleged the measures control access, and said the law does not require creators to put the measures in place themselves. Runway's briefs point out that Yout v. Recording Industry Association of America, a 2022 Connecticut decision the judge relied on, is on appeal at the Second Circuit.

The first complaint was filed on February 18, 2026, and a second creator suit followed on February 27, 2026. Judge Kaplan consolidated the cases on March 27, 2026, and appointed Tom Kherkher of Ellzey Kherkher Sanford Montgomery LLP and Gary Klinger of Milberg, PLLC as interim co-lead class counsel. The plaintiffs filed a consolidated complaint on April 27, 2026, Runway moved to dismiss on May 27, 2026, and a third related case was consolidated on June 9, 2026. With the motion denied, the case moves toward Runway's answer and discovery, then the plaintiffs would have to ask the court to certify the class. There is no settlement, no claim form and no deadline for creators to act on.

Articles.Title: Runway AI YouTube Scraping Class Action Survives Dismissal

stories.Headline: AI Labs Pay Lawyers $400 an Hour to Train Models
stories.Summary:
AI labs are paying lawyers, doctors and engineers to help train artificial intelligence models, Bloomberg reported. A civil rights attorney can be offered up to $400 an hour for the work, with no client involved. Platforms such as Mercor recruit and place these specialists with AI labs, while Handshake AI connects students, graduates and professionals with technical training projects. Data annotator now ranks fourth on LinkedIn's list of the fastest-growing U.S. jobs, and experts make up 30% of participants on the British data-work platform Prolific.

Recruiters advertise $400 an hour for attorneys, $170 an hour for condensed matter physics experts and up to $120 for software engineers, all to help train next-generation AI systems. Mercor told Bloomberg its workers average $110 an hour, though it said it did not have data on what share of tasks pay that rate. Mercor's legal listing pays $60 to $150 an hour and asks experts to write a problem from a matter they handled, with the facts, forum and governing law, plus a reference answer that a model's attempt is graded against. Handshake's physician posting lists up to $200 an hour and asks for a medical license and direct patient care experience, while its lawyer posting seeks a law degree, a license and practice experience at $90 to $110 an hour. Fellows are paid by Handshake, not the AI labs, and hourly projects pay for time spent revising and resubmitting work.

Mercor describes the job as applying professional judgment to how a model reasons and responds. Jack Weis, a Princeton chemical engineering Ph.D. who graduated in 2024 and applied to more than 2,300 jobs, took a $70-an-hour Mercor gig in January, The Wall Street Journal reported. He wrote chemical engineering questions for a language model in a program called the Studio, evaluated its answers and tried to improve them, working four to 20 hours a week while the software recorded his screen. Researchers at Scale AI, a rival data vendor, found that checklist-style rubrics built from reference answers written by experts and stronger models produced significantly better models than rubrics generated by AI alone. The work does not always last: Weis received less work over time, and in mid-March Mercor cut his contract, which he learned from a Slack message sent to a group of 810 people.

Mercor was hit with at least seven class action lawsuits in April after a data breach, PYMNTS reported. The suits say the breach exposed contractors' interview recordings, facial biometric data and screenshots of their computers, and allege Mercor monitored those computers, shared the data with clients and used recorded interviews to train AI models. Mercor has said it disputes what it called speculative claims in the suits, and in July it said only a limited subset of experts had sensitive information leaked, Staffing Industry Analysts reported. Mercor announced July 9 that it was buying Deeptune, a startup that builds simulated software environments for training AI agents, and in August Nvidia discussed joining a funding round that would value Mercor at $20 billion, double its valuation from October 2025.

Articles.Title: AI Labs Pay Lawyers $400 an Hour to Train Models - PYMNTS.com

stories.Headline: Latham & Watkins Adds Jason Raeburn As London Partner To Expand AI, Copyright, And Data Disputes Practice
stories.Summary:
Latham & Watkins has added Jason Raeburn as a partner in its London Litigation & Trial Department, the firm announced on November 2, 2026. Raeburn joins from Paul Hastings and will work on artificial intelligence, copyright, privacy, intellectual property, and technology disputes. His practice covers high-value litigation and international arbitration, along with counseling on AI regulation, copyright and data litigation, trade secrets, cyber incidents, and cross-border enforcement. He also advises companies that develop and deploy generative AI technologies.

The firm said the appointment expands its capabilities as AI regulation, copyright litigation over AI development, and data enforcement create complex legal challenges in the UK and Europe. Latham pointed to the European Union AI Act, growing copyright disputes involving artificial intelligence, and intensifying regulatory enforcement as areas driving new demand from technology companies. The firm expects the hire to support collaboration across its litigation, corporate, antitrust, regulatory, copyright, privacy, communications, and artificial intelligence practices. Raeburn is qualified to practice in England and Wales and also serves as a Deputy Master of the Business and Property Division of the High Court of England and Wales, a role the firm said makes him the youngest person appointed to it.

Ed Barnett, managing partner of Latham's London office, said technology is central to the firm's global strategy and that the UK and European markets are critical for leading technology companies, fast growth businesses, and entrepreneurs. Sy Damle, global chair of Latham's Copyright, Privacy & Communications Practice and global vice chair of its Artificial Intelligence Practice, said the EU AI Act, a rising wave of copyright disputes over AI development, and intensifying regulatory enforcement are reshaping the legal landscape in the UK and Europe. Raeburn said some of the most consequential legal battles of the next decade will be fought where technology, AI, and regulation meet. Raeburn received his LLB from the University of Bristol, completed the Legal Practice Course at the College of Law in London, and earned a Postgraduate Diploma in Intellectual Property from the University of Oxford.

Articles.Title: Latham & Watkins Adds Jason Raeburn As London Partner To Expand AI, Copyright, And Data Disputes Practice - Pulse 2.0

stories.Headline: Meet Factory Droid 1.0: A Model-Independent Coding Agent Harness Built on Script Mode
stories.Summary:
Factory released Droid 1.0, the largest update yet to its Droid agent harness, on October 31, 2026. The main change is programmatic tool calling, which is now on by default. In this mode the model writes a program that runs its tools, so one model request can drive hundreds of tool calls. The base prompt is 13,055 input tokens, down 37% from 20,887, and only 2 tool definitions ship up front, down from 11.

Droid 1.0 runs on a macOS and Windows desktop app, a terminal UI, and the Node SDK @factory/droid-sdk. It works with any supported model, including users' own API keys, and users can pick a model or let Factory Router choose a cost-efficient mix. Factory reports a best result of 65.2% on Terminal-Bench 4 with Claude Opus 5.5, at $4.73 per passed task. With GPT-6.1 Sol, Droid takes 10% longer per passed task than Codex.

Factory defines a harness as everything around the model, meaning the prompts, the tools, how tool results return, and the loop. In Script mode the model writes JavaScript that runs in a sandbox with no file, network, or system access of its own. Raw files, search results, and logs stay inside the program, and only printed output returns to the model. Factory says Script mode cuts Droid's cost by 15% versus direct tool calling on Claude Opus 5.5, and it is on by default for 10 models, including GPT-6.1 Sol and Kimi K3.

Factory ran each harness against Droid on the same model, with 3 trials per task from October 23 to 28, 2026. On Claude Opus 5.5, Droid scores 65.2%, while Cursor and OpenCode score 62.1%, Devin 59.6%, and Claude Code 57.6%, and Droid costs up to 24% less. On GPT-6.1 Sol, Droid scores 57.6% at $0.79 per passed task, against Codex at 54.0%, OpenCode at 51.0%, and Devin at 45.0%. Most changes came from an internal Agent Factory loop in which agents read failures and propose changes that engineers review and merge.

Articles.Title: Meet Factory Droid 1.0: A Model-Independent Coding Agent Harness Built on Script Mode

stories.Headline: Cloudflare AI Search billing separates retrieval costs from model charges
stories.Summary:
Cloudflare set November 1, 2026 as the start of usage billing for AI Search, according to an October 1 release note. The change follows October's general availability announcement for the product. The note separates retrieval costs from model charges. Managed Workers AI embeddings and reranking are included in AI Search pricing.

The pricing counts ingestion on the final indexed chunks after parsing and chunking. Overlapping text counts in every chunk where it appears, so the original file's length is not a one-to-one proxy for the ingestion meter. For scanned documents, OCR-extracted text also counts as image-processing tokens in addition to base ingestion. Generation, query rewriting and external model providers continue to use the customer's account and gateway. Their usage is billed and logged through the applicable service.

Cloudflare's release history identifies generation, query rewriting and external model providers as separate from retrieval. The pricing page confirms that their usage is billed and logged through the applicable service. An absent embedding entry in Gateway does not establish that a retrieval workload was unused or free. The articles do not name an individual spokesperson or give direct comments.

Articles.Title: Cloudflare AI Search billing separates retrieval costs from model charges

stories.Headline: The Digital Duty of Care bill reaches services that generate material using AI. That's the chatbot on your website. Here's what it would owe.
stories.Summary:
The Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026 passed the House of Representatives on 28 October, with 23 amendments agreed along the way. The bill places a duty, enforced by eSafety, on whoever is responsible for an online service to keep it safe. In the version that passed the House, the list of covered services includes ordinary websites and any service that generates material using artificial intelligence, with no size threshold. That means a chatbot on an ordinary business website is caught, both as part of the website and as an AI service in its own right.

The person responsible would have to take appropriate action to ensure a safe online environment, including measures to mitigate risks identified in risk assessments. That action would be judged by whether it works and is proportionate to the level of risk, and the cost of the action must not be taken into account. Written risk assessments would be required at least annually and before any significant change, and they would have to be kept for at least six years. The duty starts 12 months after Royal Assent, and the ceiling for breaching it is 60,000 penalty units, which is $21.84 million, or up to $109.2 million for a body corporate.

COSBOA chief executive Skye Cappuccio told SmartCompany on 22 October that the organisation was very concerned the bill as drafted would increase the compliance burden on small businesses that are exceedingly low risk, citing a hairdresser's website as an example. SEO Jim Stewart posted on 28 October that the scope is broad enough to potentially capture ordinary business websites and ecommerce stores. The explanatory memorandum says the definition does not provide for any defence to liability. The only off-ramp is a ministerial power to exempt services that pose little risk to users, and no such exemption can exist until the bill is law.

The Senate committee holds public hearings in Canberra on 9 and 10 November and reports on 20 November. The Coalition opposed the bill, and the Greens want it wider, with real teeth and a right to sue. Section 25A(1) excludes state and territory authorities and agencies, but the bill does not mention local government, so whether a council's chatbot is caught is unclear. It is also unclear how two responsible people share one duty, and the bill does not say who should have caught it when a vendor's model says something harmful on a business's site.

Articles.Title: The Digital Duty of Care bill reaches services that generate material using AI. That's the chatbot on your website. Here's what it would owe. - Webcoda

stories.Headline: Adopt AI technology to boost legal efficiency, Ugandan lawyers urged
stories.Summary:
Justice Geoffrey Kiryabwire of Uganda's Court of Appeal warned on Friday, October 30, 2026, that lawyers who fail to adopt modern information technology and Artificial Intelligence risk being pushed out of the profession. He spoke in Kampala at the launch of the PM Law AI tool. He urged legal practitioners to identify their technological needs and craft strategies to keep pace with digital developments. He said computers will not replace lawyers, but lawyers who use computers effectively will replace those who do not.

The new platform is an AI chatbot accessible through WhatsApp, designed and curated for Uganda's legal landscape. It was developed by Agentic AI, a company based in France and the United States that has been fully incorporated in Uganda. The tool answers complex questions rooted in local jurisprudence that general global AI systems often misinterpret. Dr. Paul Mukiibi, team leader of the PM Law Digital Hub, said internal studies showed WhatsApp is already the primary communication platform for Ugandan lawyers.

He said the chatbot is built on Uganda's legal jurisprudence and avoids hallucinations, giving answers based on the country's statutory framework and court decisions and updating users whenever there is a change. Mr. Anthony Asiimwe, Vice President of the Uganda Law Society, welcomed the innovation and expressed optimism that integrating AI tools into daily practice will streamline research, enhance operational efficiency, and improve access to justice across the country. Justice Kiryabwire said embracing digital transformation is no longer optional and noted that a chatbot on a widely used app like WhatsApp offers an accessible entry point for practitioners. Dr. Mukiibi said technology has moved legal research away from the days of running to the library for a book, and that research can now be done anywhere with the right gadget, internet, and data.

He said the tool is timely for research not only for lawyers but also for members of the bench, academia, and the entire legal fraternity. The launch comes as Uganda's Judiciary increasingly digitizes its operations. Courts across the country are progressively moving away from physical paper filings to electronic court management systems. These systems let practitioners and the public upload documents, track case progression, and monitor schedules online.

Articles.Title: Adopt AI technology to boost legal efficiency, Ugandan lawyers urged

stories.Headline: U.S. Midterm Elections: Market Focus on AI Regulation and Prospects for Divided Government; Major Financial Institutions See Limited Impact
stories.Summary:
U.S. midterm elections are scheduled for Nov. 3, and major financial institutions say the market impact will be limited. The prevailing view is that Democrats will retake the House, while the Senate balance of power is the key focus. Markets are watching the risk of tighter AI regulation and a possible corporate tax hike in 2028. They are also wary of President Trump's rhetoric and actions after the election.

Monica Guerra, an investment strategist at Morgan Stanley, forecasts that Democrats will retake the House, creating a divided government with Trump's administration. She sees Democrats holding an edge in the Senate, and she says a president can veto Congress-passed measures, so Democratic tax and regulatory plans would face obstacles. She said stability that favors the stock market could result if major policy changes become impossible. Citigroup presented three scenarios, including Democrats winning 53 or more Senate seats, which could weigh on stock valuations. Another scenario is Republicans unexpectedly keeping a Senate majority, which could push up the year-end market.

Masahiro Ichikawa, chief market strategist at Sumitomo Mitsui DS Asset Management, is concerned about headwinds if Trump takes a more hawkish stance to project a strong America externally. Ryotaro Sawada, a senior analyst at Tokai Tokyo Intelligence Laboratory, said post-election rhetoric and actions remain a source of uncertainty. He warned that investors could shift to selling all at once if Trump takes unexpected action. Makoto Hattori, head of the equity division at Marusan Securities, said uncertainty will be resolved after the election and stock prices are likely to rise. On AI, he said development will not stop as the U.S. and China vie for supremacy.

The Senate committee composition will influence financial regulation and is tied to approval of Federal Reserve governor nominees. The selection of a successor to Chair Powell will also be affected by Senate political dynamics. At the local level, Democratic governors tend to be cautious on construction permits and land-use zoning for AI data centers, which could delay projects. In Texas, the Republican incumbent governor is considered favored, but support for the party's Senate candidate has declined. Persistent inflation is a headwind for the ruling Republican Party, and some market participants say the current configuration resembles the 2006 midterms.

Articles.Title: U.S. Midterm Elections: Market Focus on AI Regulation and Prospects for Divided Government; Major Financial Institutions See Limited Impact - BigGo Finance

stories.Headline: Arab League urges joint action against disinformation, AI-generated false content
stories.Summary:
The Arab League called on its member states to develop joint mechanisms to verify information and counter media disinformation and false content generated by artificial intelligence. The call was made during a seminar organized by the League of Arab States' General Secretariat in cooperation with Cairo University's Faculty of Mass Communication. Academics and specialist researchers gathered at the seminar to discuss the future of Arab media amid regional conflicts, crises and rapid digital transformation. The initiative aims to strengthen public trust in the media in the wake of regional conflicts and crises.

Ahmed Rashid Khattabi, the league's assistant secretary-general and head of its Media and Communication Sector, said media organizations had become influential players in managing conflicts and shaping public opinion. His remarks were delivered on his behalf by Minister Plenipotentiary Alaa Al-Tamimi. Khattabi stressed the need for media institutions to maintain professional standards and accuracy while confronting rumors, hate speech and misleading content. He also underscored the importance of strengthening the media's role in raising public awareness and rebuilding confidence in information sources, particularly in societies affected by wars and crises.

Discussions at the seminar focused on expanding Arab media cooperation, safeguarding information security and examining the impact of artificial intelligence on content production. Participants also considered how government and institutional communication could help build public trust. They highlighted the need for stronger partnerships and practical initiatives to modernize Arab media and keep pace with technological developments. The League of Arab States was founded in 1945 and comprises 22 member states across the Middle East and North Africa. It was established to promote cooperation and coordination among Arab countries on political, economic, cultural and social affairs.

Articles.Title: Arab League urges joint action against disinformation, AI-generated false content

stories.Headline: It’s time to block reckless AI IPOs and tax billionaires | Naomi Klein and Ilana Glazer
stories.Summary:
Naomi Klein and Ilana Glazer published an opinion article in The Guardian on 2 November 2026 calling for wealth taxes on billionaires and for blocking new tech IPOs. They wrote that the billionaire class gained 40% more wealth in just two years, and that nearly 3,000 global billionaires now hold combined wealth equal to one-fifth of the world's yearly output. Nearly 1,000 billionaires live and do business in the United States, they said. They pointed to Elon Musk becoming an instant trillionaire when SpaceX went public earlier this year, and said he is funding Republican midterm campaigns with a small share of those gains.

The authors said Oracle's Larry Ellison, seventh on the Forbes billionaires list, backed the Paramount-Warner Brothers merger, and that Google's Sergey Brin spent $100m opposing California's Prop 40, a one-time wealth tax for healthcare and public services. They said Anthropic and OpenAI intend to go public soon, that both recently had major security flaws exposed, and that both openly acknowledge huge debts. They argued that when a company goes public, regular Americans end up carrying its risks through their retirement accounts without consent. They called for wealth taxes starting in California and New York, and for legal and legislative avenues to stop the IPOs.

The authors placed responsibility on the Trump administration and tech investors, saying they present IPOs as market success stories while regular people shoulder the risks. They said the 10 most valuable public companies are in tech, leaving the economy dependent on one industry with a history of bubbles, crashes and, in extreme cases like Theranos, fraud. They warned that if the AI bubble bursts it will take everyone down, while billionaires will walk away relatively unscathed. Their first step is passing wealth taxes, and they closed by urging readers to tax the billionaires and block the IPOs.

The article describes a divided country in crisis, with millions struggling to find and keep jobs, rising living costs and lost health insurance despite a sunny forecast from the Trump administration. It cites June's highly contentious SpaceX IPO as already carrying great risk for regular investors, and warns that more speculative tech companies going public would be too much for the market to bear. The authors say the survival of American democracy depends on taxing billionaires. They call for collective action and real change to stop new billionaires being minted and to keep the AI industry's risks from being transferred onto the public.

Articles.Title: It’s time to block reckless AI IPOs and tax billionaires | Naomi Klein and Ilana Glazer

stories.Headline: Eight in 10 judges encounter fake AI court ruling citations
stories.Summary:
A survey by the National Court Administration, an agency under the Supreme Court, found that 80.7 percent of judges handling civil, family and administrative cases in Korea have encountered citations of nonexistent court rulings, and 65.4 percent reported cases in which rulings were falsely cited. The survey ran from Oct. 6 to 16 among 360 judges nationwide, and respondents could select multiple answers. Another 16.9 percent had seen citations of fabricated or nonexistent laws, and 4.1 percent reported citations of fabricated academic papers or other materials. The results were released on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026.

When asked who submitted documents with such citations, 69.5 percent of the judges identified the litigants themselves, and 57.6 percent pointed to lawyers representing parties in civil cases or defendants in criminal proceedings. Some litigants submitted AI-generated fake judgments that copied the format of real Supreme Court rulings, and some documents altered actual rulings or cited them in ways that misrepresented their meaning. Some documents even included excerpts from conversations with AI chatbots, revealing that they had been prepared with AI. Of the judges, 91.7 percent said institutional measures were needed, with 64.8 percent calling them highly necessary. For specific measures, 61.4 percent supported a legal basis for administrative fines, 61.1 percent favored requiring parties to verify the rulings they cite, 60.6 percent backed mandatory disclosure of AI use, and 55.4 percent called for sanctions against lawyers, including disciplinary referrals.

The National Court Administration said citations of fabricated or nonexistent rulings from AI use burden opposing parties and the courts and delay the public's right to a trial. It said ensuring the accuracy of submitted documents is necessary to reduce unnecessary litigation burdens and improve the speed and fairness of judicial proceedings. The agency said it plans to develop countermeasures based on the survey findings, will consult with the Ministry of Justice and other relevant agencies, and will submit recommendations to the National Assembly to amend the Civil Procedure Act and Criminal Procedure Act and establish a legal basis for administrative fines and other penalties. It is also considering guidance for lawyers and litigants on precautions when using AI through the electronic litigation system.

Articles.Title: Eight in 10 judges encounter fake AI court ruling citations - Korea JoongAng Daily

stories.Headline: Case Study: AI Redefines Next-Gen Drilling Vibration Compliance
stories.Summary:
Tomax, a Norwegian specialist company, used artificial intelligence to analyze high-fidelity data from the full drilling process, according to a case study. Ole Andre Høiland, an artificial intelligence adviser to Tomax, monitored the company's 4,000-Hz parallel data pipeline from the driller's cabin as it streamed uninterrupted data to storage. The company targeted an active, modern 150-ton automated drilling rig that was built in late 2025. The rig was equipped with a unique strain and torsion measurement unit, or sub, integrated as an extension to the derrick drilling machine.

The sub unit came from an industry leader in control and diagnostics of rotating machinery, and it was accurately calibrated. Traditional analysis of drilling dynamics often uses data from downhole accelerometers, but those systems typically capture a mix of effects rather than the underlying coupling of forces that cause resonances. On most rigs, surface input and reactive loads are recorded at sparse intervals, typically every 10 seconds or longer. Capturing critical information at a high-fidelity level in this environment presents two challenges, signal integrity and the data pipeline. Modern sensor assemblies can export structural acoustics and stress waves at extreme sample rates, but the bottleneck is the data pipeline and the need for a continuous stream of megabytes of time-stamped data every second into a usable database.

The case study describes a successful solution for data harvesting on a level that is both new and found to meet the requirement for applying AI and machine learning solutions. The study concludes with examples from analysis that reveal the potential from a true image of everything going on in a drillstring. The fundamentals of these resonances reside in the transfer of torsional and axial forces from surface to the bit. The problem of downhole vibrations remains a significant barrier for the drilling industry, and an emerging technology based on direct interception of disturbing resonances is now being used to address the issue. Such solutions rely on a new level of understanding of the true bottomhole assembly dynamics, and AI and machine learning techniques are now helping deliver the full picture.

Articles.Title: Case Study: AI Redefines Next-Gen Drilling Vibration Compliance

stories.Headline: AI adoption could add AUD $93 billion, report finds
stories.Summary:
The Tech Council of Australia released research on artificial intelligence adoption by small and medium-sized businesses, finding that wider use could add up to AUD $93 billion in annual economic value. The report was prepared by Delwood Advisory with support from Employment Hero, Google and Deputy, and drew on data from Deputy, Xero and LinkedIn. It found that only one in four SMEs is using AI, while just 5% have adopted it broadly across their operations. The research was released on 29 October 2026.

The report estimates that an average SME moving from no AI use to broad adoption could achieve annual productivity gains worth AUD $136,000. It cites research showing that 94% of SMEs using AI reported productivity improvements, while 54% of SME employees using AI reported improved job satisfaction. It identifies a gap in adoption between regional and metropolitan businesses, and notes that construction, hospitality and retail are among the industries with the largest differences in uptake between SMEs and larger companies. Barriers to adoption include limited understanding of AI, workforce skills gaps, uncertainty about return on investment, and concerns about security and reliability. The report recommends wider access to affordable training, practical advice and industry-specific examples.

Dr Kate Cornick, Chief Executive Officer of the Tech Council of Australia, said small businesses employ almost two-thirds of Australia's private-sector workforce, so improving their productivity matters to the whole economy. She said most SMEs are not yet using AI and there is a significant gap between what the technology could deliver and what small businesses currently get from it. She said that for owners dealing with rising costs and staffing pressures, even reducing time spent on routine administration can make a difference, and many need practical advice on which applications will be useful and how to introduce them. She said support needs to be better targeted because regional businesses remain behind their metropolitan counterparts and some industries face much greater adoption gaps, and that government and industry can build on existing programs.

Ben Thompson, Co-Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Employment Hero, said payroll, super, awards and compliance consume a small business owner's week and that AI takes real weight off that pile. He said his own company's product teams use AI to move through the roadmap faster, its marketing team tests and refines campaigns in days rather than weeks, and AI agents now handle 95% of routine HR support questions. He said many owners do not know where to start and regional businesses are still behind cities, and that owners need practical training, guidance and tools that work, especially in the regions and sectors furthest behind. The report adds to the wider debate over how quickly small businesses can adopt AI as larger companies move faster and absorb more of the early benefits, and its focus on regional and sector-based gaps suggests policymakers and industry groups may need to target support more narrowly rather than rely on broad national programs.

Articles.Title: AI adoption could add AUD $93 billion, report finds - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Mass+torts+and+AI%3A+Litigation+that+plays+to+technology%E2%80%99s+strength - Virginia Lawyers Weekly
stories.Summary:
Mass tort litigation has become increasingly high-tech, with artificial intelligence tools now used to organize and analyze large volumes of information. Plaintiffs' attorneys say AI allows them to document similar medical complaints from hundreds or thousands of plaintiffs and link their illnesses to drug ingestion, toxic exposure, or consumer product use. Joseph Fantini, managing attorney of mass torts at Rosen Injury Lawyers, said the defense side has generally been ahead of plaintiffs in AI use, but the gap is narrowing over the last two or three years. He said his side uses AI from case acquisition to case workup to settlement and settlement administration.

Christopher M. Placitella, a partner with Cohen, Placitella, Roth & Goslee, said mass tort opportunities often have a short filing window, causing a rush to gather medical records and other materials that AI is crucial for cataloguing. His firm is one of those representing some 70,000 plaintiffs in the mass tort case against Johnson & Johnson over talcum powder exposure. Ashleigh Raso, founding partner of Nigh, Goldenberg, Raso & Vaughn, cautioned that questions litigants ask generative AI programs about their cases can be discoverable, and that inputting proposed settlement terms into AI could void an agreement. Carasusana B. Wall, senior partner at the Bullock Legal Group, said plaintiff fact sheets that used to be 15 pages can now run 60 to 80 pages each.

Kaeo Caindec, chief executive officer and founder of Clarra, said there is no end to the complexity of mass tort cases, with firms struggling with increases in both litigation and litigants. About 100,000 Roundup cases have been settled for about $11 billion, with about 3,000 claims outstanding, and about 69,000 mass tort cases are active in the federal multidistrict litigation over talcum powder before a federal judge in New Jersey. About 3,000 individuals and 800 school districts are plaintiffs in suits claiming Facebook, YouTube and other social media platforms caused psychological or physical harm. Retired Michigan district court judge Brian MacKenzie concluded that a potentially massive social media tort case can be fairly adjudicated under current negligence statutes.

Articles.Title: Mass+torts+and+AI%3A+Litigation+that+plays+to+technology%E2%80%99s+strength - Virginia Lawyers Weekly

stories.Headline: Can AI crack the Cup? The bots are all in on Point Of Law
stories.Summary:
Five leading AI models, Claude, ChatGPT, Grok, Perplexity and Gemini, were each given the same form and data pack on all 24 Melbourne Cup runners. The pack included barriers, weights and penalties, jockeys and trainers, career histories, track and distance records, sectional data and ratings, a speed map and the current market. Each model was asked to build its own model from scratch, price the field to a 100 per cent market and give a top pick, a best value bet, a lay and a probability-based top four. The exercise followed the Cox Plate, where Cosmic Crusader was the top pick for ChatGPT, Grok and Gemini and every model had him and Birdman somewhere in its top four.

Point Of Law is the top pick for ChatGPT, Perplexity, Grok and Gemini, and appears in every top four. ChatGPT rates him $12.05 against a market price of $6.50 and says he is its most likely winner but not worth that price. Claude goes its own way with Shockletz, rated $8.20 against $11, noting she drops 7kg to the minimum 51kg. Soul Of Spain is the value pick for ChatGPT and Grok at $41, while Claude and Gemini land on Zakouma at $27. James J Braddock is the lay for Claude, ChatGPT and Perplexity at $14, and Gemini lays Knight's Choice at $31.

The models agree James J Braddock is too short at $14, citing his seven starts, his failure to race beyond 2420m, his 24-length defeat in the Irish Derby and barrier 24. ChatGPT says Point Of Law has three wins from five starts and arrives off a Geelong Cup victory with 53kg after a two-kilo penalty, but has yet to race beyond 2846m. Perplexity says Soul Of Spain was beaten just 0.26 lengths in the Sydney Cup over 3200m and has the best last-600m figure at the distance range in the field. Grok calls Point Of Law the only runner combining a recent strong win, ideal weight and the right settling profile for the trip.

The bots found more common ground in the Cup than in the Cox Plate, with Point Of Law on top for three of the four and in every top four. Juja Kibo and Shockletz each feature in three of the four top fours, while Hopewell Rock, second favourite at $9.50, makes only two. The value picks split down the middle, with two models on Soul Of Spain and two on Zakouma. The race is on Tuesday.

Articles.Title: Can AI crack the Cup? The bots are all in on Point Of Law

stories.Headline: Revealed: From AI to ageing laptops — what junior lawyers really think about their firms’ tech
stories.Summary:
Legal Cheek published exclusive research on 2 November 2026 from its annual survey of more than 2,000 trainees and junior lawyers. The survey found that firms are investing heavily in AI tools while everyday technology such as case management systems, laptops and work phones is often slow, outdated or broken. One new starter said their firm presents itself as an AI law firm but barely has working tech, with rudimentary laptops that break often. Another said AI will only get you so far if you cannot even open an email. Some juniors praised tools including Claude, ChatGPT and Harvey but rated laptops and IT support as sub-par.

The responses describe a range of setups across firms. One trainee said the tech is very advanced but laptops cannot handle the amount loaded on them and get slow, while another said their case management system is older than they are. One junior reported that their laptop screen fell off, and another said trainees are not given work phones. Some firms were described as slow to adopt AI and apprehensive about committing to one provider, with clunky client management systems. Others were praised for combining AI with high-quality hardware, reliable software and helpful IT support, and one rookie said they could not think of a more advanced firm.

The survey gives no overall figures beyond the 2,000-plus respondents and names no individual firms or people, quoting only anonymous trainees and junior lawyers. No one is identified as responsible for the technology, and the article does not say what firms plan to do in response. It also does not say when the full survey results will be published. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Revealed: From AI to ageing laptops — what junior lawyers really think about their firms’ tech - Legal Cheek

stories.Headline: 😸 Microsoft's enforceable AI privacy standard for schools is now in effect
stories.Summary:
Microsoft, the American Federation of Teachers and the United Federation of Teachers announced the AI Safety & Privacy Standard on September 9, and it took effect on Sunday, November 1. Any U.S. school district can add the standard to a new or existing Microsoft agreement without renegotiation or renewal, according to Microsoft's fact sheet. The standard is written into the contract rather than posted on a webpage, which makes it harder for Microsoft to change later. Once a district writes it into its agreement, the district can cancel and seek damages if Microsoft breaks the rules.

The standard bans training AI models on student or educator data permanently, with one narrow safety and security exception. It also bans selling student data or using it for advertising, tracking students, and AI companions, meaning chatbots built to act like a friend. High-risk decisions require human review, so AI can assist but people decide. Breach reports are due within 72 hours, and violations must be fixed or AI use paused or ended. Microsoft also faces annual certification, audit rights and a deadline to fix security problems.

AFT president Randi Weingarten said older rules like FERPA and HIPAA never anticipated AI, and Fortune noted that COPPA predates generative AI too, so the union went for leverage. UFT president Michael Mulgrew said AI use in grades K-8 isn't appropriate right now, and New York City's public schools had just announced a one-year pause on AI. Weingarten said OpenAI and Anthropic have expressed willingness to sign. An Anthropic spokesperson told Fortune the company has worked with the AFT on a safety and privacy standard, while OpenAI didn't respond.

The standard says nothing about whether classrooms should use AI, only the terms for districts that do, and it binds just one company so far. Microsoft's fact sheet refers to its AI products in general and doesn't name which ones are covered. If OpenAI or Anthropic sign the same standard, a union-negotiated contract starts to look like the default rulebook for AI in schools. If neither does, districts using their tools get whatever terms those companies offer.

Articles.Title: 😸 Microsoft's enforceable AI privacy standard for schools is now in effect - The Neuron

stories.Headline: Op-Ed: Canadian schools need well-considered AI guidance
stories.Summary:
Many Canadian educators began the school year with little or no guidance on managing AI use in their classrooms, according to an op-ed published by Canadian Affairs on November 2, 2026. The piece was written by Joanna DeJong VanHof, director of the education program at Cardus and a PhD student at the University of Toronto. It says just four provinces have formal AI guidelines for educators: British Columbia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador and Quebec. Provinces like Manitoba are still working on their own, and the op-ed says half of the provinces have been quiet on the issue.

The op-ed points to stricter approaches elsewhere. New York City announced a moratorium on AI use in public schools for the 2026-27 year, under a policy published by Chancellor Kamar Samuels, with strong limits for elementary students and limited, guided opportunities for high school students. In early September, Los Angeles passed an even more restrictive policy, imposing a district-wide moratorium on generative AI use by students on all school devices for this school year. The op-ed calls these approaches time-limited and prudent but not a long-term answer. It cites Professor Josh Brake of Harvey Mudd College, who argues in an upcoming book, Beyond School Choice, that a ban can buy time but cannot answer the deeper questions.

The op-ed says that in the absence of provincial guidance, there is a risk that education unions will steer the conversation. It says reports from the Canadian Teachers' Federation emphasize the risks AI poses to members' autonomy and the need for human judgment in the classroom. It raises concern that AI approaches could be shaped by what unions, teachers and education workers will and will not do, rather than by what leads to the best learning outcomes. Brake is paraphrased as saying that forcing students through complicated systems sends the message that their work is not worth doing for its own sake and that they are not trusted to do it honestly.

The op-ed argues that policies should be developed in consultation with educators, parents and students. It says they must start from learner-focused questions about what educational purpose a tool serves, what evidence shows it advances that purpose, and what human capacity its use might strengthen or weaken. It concludes that until those questions can be answered, restraint is a policy choice in its own right. It notes that New York has decided the answer for younger students is, for now, no, and says provinces here should be prepared to follow suit.

Articles.Title: Op-Ed: Canadian schools need well-considered AI guidance - Canadian Affairs

stories.Headline: Massachusetts Sen. Markey Accuses Meta of Shipping Intimate Footage to Overseas Contractors for AI Training
stories.Summary:
Senators Edward J. Markey of Massachusetts and Ron Wyden of Oregon launched an inquiry on October 29, 2026, into reports of privacy violations involving Meta’s AI-enabled smart glasses. The senators said the glasses had captured sensitive imagery of users and bystanders without consent, sent intimate images to overseas contractors, and used highly sensitive images to train Meta’s AI systems. Meta launched the glasses in 2021 even though the company had identified risks to bystander privacy and vulnerable populations beforehand, the senators wrote. The letter follows a March request led by Markey for information about Meta’s reported plans to add facial recognition technology to the glasses. The senators asked Meta to answer by November 25, 2026, a set of questions about the company’s handling of sensitive imagery.

They asked whether Meta’s human rights due diligence specifically evaluated the risk that the glasses could facilitate voyeurism and nonconsensual intimate image capture, including risks from initial capture, local storage, transmission to Meta, access by employees or contractors, use in AI training, and later disclosure. They also asked what testing Meta has done on accidental camera activation, tampering with the recording indicator, and camera-based AI interactions that do not activate the outward-facing recording indicator. Other questions covered safeguards against nonconsensual capture, disclosure, or processing of intimate imagery, the role of Meta teams responsible for women’s safety and intimate image abuse, and whether device owners and people whose images are captured can request deletion of biometric and other data. The senators criticized Meta’s record on the issue. They wrote that Meta’s stated commitment to privacy and preventing intimate image abuse rings hollow if the company cannot show meaningful steps to keep its own products and practices from facilitating those harms.

The letter cites news reports of the glasses being used to sexually harass women, including an October 2025 report by 404 Media that a network of men secretly filmed women while soliciting sexual services using Meta AI Glasses, with the recordings distributed on social media and viewed millions of times. Markey has worked to regulate biometric recognition and other surveillance technologies, including reintroducing the Facial Recognition and Biometric Technology Moratorium Act in September and, with Wyden, Merkley, and Representative Pramila Jayapal, introducing the ICE Out of Our Faces Act in February. The articles do not say what Meta has done in response to the letter or what happens next beyond the November 25, 2026 deadline for answers. They also do not say whether Meta has commented on the reports or the inquiry.

Articles.Title: Massachusetts Sen. Markey Accuses Meta of Shipping Intimate Footage to Overseas Contractors for AI Training

stories.Headline: Mass. ‘Future Booth’ gives residents a direct line to lawmakers as state debates AI safeguards
stories.Summary:
Ari Rosenthal, a local educator and activist, set up a phone booth called the “Future Booth” in communities around Boston, Boston 25 News reported on November 1, 2026. Visitors can plug in their phones and call state legislators to share their views on artificial intelligence. The booth includes phone numbers for six legislators involved in deciding the fate of the bill. Rosenthal is a teacher and co-founder of the Massachusetts AI Action Network.

The booth is meant to draw calls about Senate Bill 3228, which includes AI safety and transparency provisions aimed at large AI developers. Rosenthal says the booth has hosted well over 1,000 conversations about AI. The bill went into conference committee in September, and its final outcome depends on negotiations between House and Senate lawmakers. Lawmakers are debating legislation that would put safeguards in place for AI developers.

Rosenthal said the effort is not anti-AI but focused on safe AI, and he compared it to wanting airbags in a car you love. He said the lack of federal regulation has put more attention on states to address public safety, mandatory reporting, third-party audits and transparency. He said people’s opinions matter and that AI is so technical that many people feel frozen, but it does impact their lives. Critics argue additional regulation could slow innovation, increase costs and make Massachusetts less attractive to AI businesses.

Articles.Title: Mass. ‘Future Booth’ gives residents a direct line to lawmakers as state debates AI safeguards

stories.Headline: In Pursuit of Practicality: 52 real use cases for AI in wholesale distribution today - National Association of Wholesaler-Distributors
stories.Summary:
The National Association of Wholesaler-Distributors published a white paper on November 1, 2026, titled In Pursuit of Practicality: 52 real use cases for AI in wholesale distribution today. The association said it set out to create a structured resource because many distributors still lack clear guidance on implementing artificial intelligence practically, despite widespread enthusiasm. The research effort lasted multiple months and included surveys, interviews, extensive publication scanning, and deep synthesis. It ultimately surfaced more than 50 use cases of AI for distribution.

The white paper is offered free with registration through a form on the NAW website. The form asks for a name, email, country, state or province, company name, and primary sector, and it requires consent to the terms and conditions and the privacy policy. The primary sector list includes Building Materials/Construction Supplies, Electrical, Fasteners, Food & Beverage, Healthcare/Pharmaceuticals, HVACR/Plumbing/PVF, Industrial MRO/Automation/Hose, Jan-San, Machinery, Metals, Office/Paper & Packaging, Plastics, Power Transmission/Fluid Power, Safety, and Wholesale Other. By submitting the form, users agree to receive communications from NAW/MDM about this and other related products and services, and they can unsubscribe at any time through the Manage Preferences link in any email.

The association is responsible for the research and the white paper, and it describes the work as its own multi-month effort. The form states that consent to the use of personal information can be withdrawn at any time, and it points users to the privacy policy for more information. The page also notes that the country and state fields are required by privacy laws. The white paper is sponsored, though the page does not name the sponsor beyond a sponsored by label.

The page lists other white papers from NAW, including an executive summary on making field sales performance repeatable from October 29, 2026, a guide on preparing an industrial distributor for exit from October 1, 2026, and a security paper titled Think Like a Criminal. Defend Like a Pro. from September 11, 2026. The page does not say what happens after registration beyond the offer of the free white paper. It also does not give a publication date for the white paper beyond the November 1, 2026 timestamp on the article.

Articles.Title: In Pursuit of Practicality: 52 real use cases for AI in wholesale distribution today - National Association of Wholesaler-Distributors

stories.Headline: Siemens CEO outlines path to bring industrial AI to smaller manufacturers
stories.Summary:
Roland Busch, president and CEO of Siemens and chairman of the Asia-Pacific Committee of German Business, spoke in an interview with The Korea Herald in Seoul on Friday, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Conference of German Business 2026. He said the gap between the technology Siemens deploys and what small companies can do is still big, and that this challenge exists everywhere, from Korea and Germany to the US and China. He described a step-by-step path for small and medium-sized manufacturers, many of which still run with little or no automation. Showing such a company a highly digitalized factory proves what is possible but gives little guidance on how to get there, he said.

Busch said each company should first define what digitalization means for its business and chart a path from its current capabilities to goals over six months, a year and beyond. He said smaller manufacturers with limited capital often face pressure for quick returns, but must be ready to invest in basics that may bring no immediate payoff, and many still lack systematic ways to manage design tools and store data. He said companies need some courage to invest in their data structure and basic tools before starting the journey, and that this groundwork lets them use digital technologies to improve productivity and stay competitive. Siemens is developing digital training and can offer financing support in some cases, and Busch said the commitment to begin must come from company leaders.

Busch said general-purpose AI models need specialized training on industrial knowledge and data to be used in manufacturing, because the appealing images they generate do not necessarily translate into designs that can be manufactured. He welcomed the Korean Industry Ministry's M.AX manufacturing AI transition initiative, saying its focus on industrial applications plays to Korea's strengths, and that Korea can better use its industrial expertise by adapting available models than by spending heavily to compete with the US and China on leading general-purpose foundation models. He cited work with Samsung across electronics, batteries and semiconductors, SK hynix in semiconductors, and HD Hyundai and Hyundai Motor, and praised Korean partners' engineering expertise and readiness to adopt technology. He described work with HD Hyundai on digital twins, including models of ships with millions of parts and the shipyards where they are built, where AI can speed design and simulation and help engineers find problems before construction.

Busch said AI computing facilities are driving demand for Siemens' electrical infrastructure and control systems, which help manage rapid swings in power demand and their effect on the grid, and that the company is working with Nvidia on next-generation power systems that respond faster and use less energy. Asked about an AI investment bubble, he said he would not call it one, citing major technology companies' financial resources, though he questioned whether every announced project would be built, and he said Siemens does not currently see demand declining through 2030. He said longer-term momentum depends partly on how quickly AI moves from model training to practical applications and whether those applications need GPUs or less expensive chips.
