He said AI will reduce repetitive, rules-based jobs while creating new roles, that preparing people requires changes to school and university curricula and training within companies, and that people are not replaced by AI but by people who use AI.

Articles.Title: Siemens CEO outlines path to bring industrial AI to smaller manufacturers

stories.Headline: S. Korea mulls over longer bans, criminal complaints for use of AI glasses in college entrance tests
stories.Summary:
South Korea’s Education Ministry announced on Oct 29 that it plans to step up enforcement against students who use smart glasses to cheat on the country’s annual college entrance exam. The measures include filing criminal complaints or requesting investigations. The ministry is also considering extending the ban on repeat test-takers caught cheating from one year to up to three years. The announcement follows rules made in July that list smart glasses as prohibited items for the 2027 academic year’s Suneung, the College Scholastic Ability Test.

Under current regulations, wearing or using the glasses invalidates a student’s results and bars them from taking the following year’s exam. Students found with the devices who fail to surrender them before the first session can have their current-year results invalidated. Refusing a proctor’s request to inspect a smart device may also lead to invalidation of the current results and disqualification from the following year’s exam, after a review. The authorities will assign one staff member to each of the 1,312 test sites nationwide to help identify smart glasses and other prohibited devices during this year’s exam.

The ministry said it will urge universities to adopt similarly strict penalties for their own admissions tests in 2026. It also plans to assess radio-signal detectors being developed by specialist institutions, and if deemed feasible, the devices could be distributed to test sites starting in 2027. The ministry said it would protect teachers who diligently supervise exams from being held responsible or disadvantaged when cheating involves smart glasses or other devices. The report came from The Korea Herald and Asia News Network.

Articles.Title: S. Korea mulls over longer bans, criminal complaints for use of AI glasses in college entrance tests

stories.Headline: KAIST develops technology to cut AI fine-tuning time by up to 69.6 percent
stories.Summary:
A research team at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST), led by computer science professor Lee Jae-gil, has developed a large language model fine-tuning technique called CluSTER, KAIST said on Sunday. The method selects data with similar training effects and allocates it efficiently across multiple graphics processing units (GPUs). Fine-tuning is a process that improves performance by training an existing AI model further with domain-specific data such as coding or medicine. Typically, multiple GPUs split the data for processing, but repeatedly processing data with similar training effects can reduce training efficiency relative to the amount of computation.

The team analysed how data affects AI training, grouped data that produces similar effects and used a method that selects the necessary data from each group. It distributed the selected data evenly across multiple GPUs to reduce redundant training while reflecting diverse training information. The team fine-tuned large language models with about 7 billion and 13 billion parameters using three datasets in the coding and medical fields and verified the technique through eight performance evaluations. The experiments showed that using only about 31 percent of the total data reduced training time by up to 69.6 percent while largely maintaining model performance, enough to complete training that previously took 10 hours in about 3 hours. The tests focused on an environment using four GPUs, and the team also confirmed better performance than existing methods in an eight-GPU environment.

Lee said that to improve the efficiency of AI training, it is important not only to use more GPUs but also to choose intelligently which data to train on. He added that the study is meaningful in that it can reduce the training burden of large-scale AI models by using existing GPU resources more efficiently. The study also included KAIST computer science department doctoral student Kim Hyun-jin as first author. The findings were presented in October at EMNLP 2026, an international conference in the field of natural language processing.

Articles.Title: KAIST develops technology to cut AI fine-tuning time by up to 69.6 percent - 디지털투데이

stories.Headline: Tech services firms face a talent decision, not a shortage, in $100-200 billion AI race, says Boston Consulting Group
stories.Summary:
Boston Consulting Group released a report on Thursday, October 29, 2026, saying technology services firms do not face an AI talent shortage but a talent decision. The report says AI-led services are expected to add $100-200 billion of net new work by 2030. It says firms can staff much of that work from people they already employ. The findings draw on more than 2,500 AI-tagged job postings and over 50,000 professional profiles across more than 15 firms, plus BCG's own skills database.

BCG identified 40 distinct Applied AI roles, each linked to an existing technology role. A data scientist or full-stack developer can grow into a forward-deployed engineer, a DevOps engineer into an AI Ops engineer, and a data engineer into a semantic engineer. Moving a data scientist into a forward-deployed engineer role takes roughly three times the upskilling effort of moving a data engineer into an AI data engineer role. Firms that hire against the new titles pay up to roughly 35% over the comparable traditional role.

Sreyssha George, Managing Director and Partner at BCG and a co-author of the report, said the people who can deliver Applied AI are largely already on the payroll. She said clients are moving from paying for hours to paying for outcomes, which changes how work is staffed and rewarded. The report sorts the 40 roles into four groups, with a distinct action for each: buy the scarce anchor roles, build the scale drivers at volume, retain the delivery core, and watch the early signals. It also proposes five career tracks from a single role, with lateral moves between them and progression tied to demonstrated capability.

The report says the decision that turned existing talent into supply was role architecture, including a skill taxonomy, proficiency gates, bands and a dedicated job family, so each Applied AI role has a title, a level and a band attached. It closes with five questions for leaders to answer this quarter, including whether pay bands and career paths would hold against an AI-native offer. The global services market is projected to grow from roughly $1.6-1.7 trillion in 2025 to $2.2-2.4 trillion by 2030. AI-led services contribute $300-400 billion of that growth through building and running agentic solutions, work that becomes outsourceable as agentic tooling matures, and the human oversight and governance clients may not hand to a model.

Articles.Title: Tech services firms face a talent decision, not a shortage, in $100-200 billion AI race, says Boston Consulting Group

stories.Headline: Nearly 1,900 U.S. Schools Are Within 1 Mile of an AI Data Center, Prompting Health Concerns for Children - Science, Public Health Policy and the Law
stories.Summary:
Research highlighted by the National Education Association identified 1,878 U.S. public schools within one mile of existing or proposed data centers, including 602 in California and 101 in Virginia, according to an article by Henrick Karoliszyn published October 31, 2026. The finding comes as researchers study the environmental effects of a rapidly growing AI industry whose electricity demands are expected to rise sharply. A 2024 study by the University of California, Riverside, and the California Institute of Technology estimated that air pollution from AI infrastructure could contribute to as many as 1,300 premature deaths a year in the U.S. by 2030, with public health costs approaching $20 billion. Those projections cover pollution, including fine particulate matter linked to respiratory and cardiovascular disease, from electricity generation and diesel backup generators.

The concerns center on diesel-powered backup generators, which can release nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide and fine particulate matter, and large facilities can house hundreds of them. The Environmental Protection Agency has linked generator pollution to asthma attacks, reduced lung function and impaired lung development in children. A 2026 analysis by Virginia Commonwealth University found that clusters of data centers can produce combined annual emissions that in some cases exceed those of nearby power plants. Researchers also flagged industrial noise, water consumption and electricity demand, and a 2024 Department of Energy report cited federal projections that data center electricity consumption could nearly triple by 2028. A 2026 study in Frontiers in Climate examined noise and water use from Virginia's data center industry.

Shaolei Ren, a UC Riverside engineering professor and co-author of the 2024 study, said tech companies' sustainability reports focus on carbon emissions and sometimes water but do not mention unhealthful air pollutants, which he said are already creating a public health burden. Damian Pitt, lead author of the Virginia Commonwealth study and an associate professor there, said the researchers were surprised to learn that in terms of total annual air pollution, living next to a natural gas power plant may be preferable to living next to many data centers. Alison L. Steele, executive director of the Environmental Health Project, said children are especially susceptible because they breathe proportionally more air than adults and their bodies are still developing, and she said the technology is outpacing the scientific community's ability to study it and the government's ability to regulate it. Julie Cink, a teacher, said she was not necessarily opposed to data centers but questioned why one was placed so close to her school and homes.

In Frederick County, Maryland, plans for the roughly 2,100-acre Quantum Frederick Data Center Campus about 500 feet from Carroll Manor Elementary School led officials to install air monitoring equipment. In Palm Beach County, Florida, teachers and parents opposed a proposed 4 million-square-foot data center about 1,200 feet from Saddle View Elementary School, with plans including more than 600 industrial cooling fans, and county commissioners rejected the proposal in July. Virginia's Department of Environmental Quality launched an air monitoring initiative near data centers in Loudoun County, including at schools, to assess local air quality and determine whether more testing is needed. The article notes that research directly linking data center proximity to specific illnesses among schoolchildren remains limited.

Articles.Title: Nearly 1,900 U.S. Schools Are Within 1 Mile of an AI Data Center, Prompting Health Concerns for Children - Science, Public Health Policy and the Law

stories.Headline: Autonomous Mind | Congress scrambles to keep pace with AI
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is advancing faster than Congress can regulate it, and Colorado’s congressional delegation is largely united that the technology needs guardrails, though members differ on how those guardrails should work. The debate has grown more urgent as AI companies develop increasingly powerful systems that experts warn government oversight is struggling to keep pace. Steve Beaty, an MSU Denver professor of computer science, said AI presents a different challenge from nuclear weapons because the technology is advancing so quickly. He said researchers understood how to train neural networks decades ago but lacked the computing power to make them broadly useful until graphics processing units could handle enormous amounts of computation. Beaty said a major turning point came in 2017 with a research paper titled “Attention Is All You Need,” which introduced the transformer architecture behind modern large language models.

Democratic U.S. Rep. Brittany Pettersen, who served on a bipartisan congressional AI task force, said Congress has failed to respond with the urgency the technology requires. She said Congress should establish independent audits of AI systems, require companies to report significant incidents and create a federal regulatory structure with the resources and technical expertise to oversee the technology. She also said the federal government needs to require companies to identify unintended consequences and report negative findings from internal testing. Pettersen accused U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson and President Donald Trump of failing to prioritize the issue. After a recent meeting with Johnson and top AI executives, Trump appointed Jay Clayton as director of national intelligence and to lead a new federal AI task force, which Trump said would coordinate the federal effort to keep America leading the world in super intelligence.

Republican U.S. Rep. Gabe Evans argued that Congress needs guardrails too, but he places greater emphasis on ensuring regulation does not cause America to surrender its technological edge to China. He said the United States must lead AI development to influence how the technology is used, and he compared the situation to the Cold War space race. Evans pointed to legislation he has worked on involving AI chatbots, open-source AI and the data centers required to power AI systems. One measure, the Ratepayer Protection Act, passed the House 417-3 before the Senate blocked it, with Colorado Sens. John Hickenlooper and Michael Bennet playing a key role in killing the legislation, which had sought to keep data center electricity costs from shifting to other customers.

Beaty said the U.S. should lead but that leadership should not exclude discussions with China, comparing the situation to nuclear weapons, where America and the Soviet Union maintained communication and negotiated arms-control agreements despite being rivals. He said AI is already used in cybersecurity and military applications, including systems that can help identify targets, and has potential benefits in medicine and scientific research. Beaty cautioned against interpreting recent developments as evidence that AI has become conscious or will inevitably turn against humans, but he said the technology is beginning to move toward systems that can modify or improve aspects of their own software, a process he described as recursive self-improvement. He said the speed of those changes makes traditional regulation particularly difficult, because AI capabilities can change substantially between congressional hearings.

Articles.Title: Autonomous Mind | Congress scrambles to keep pace with AI - Denver Gazette

stories.Headline: AI Lawsuit Croatia 2026: Eligibility, Payouts, Deadlines
stories.Summary:
Croatia began enforcing the EU AI Act in full on August 2, 2026, and the first wave of AI lawsuits is now before the Zagreb County Court, with more than 40 cases filed. The claims target banks, employers and government agencies over biased algorithms, including AI credit scoring and hiring tools. AZOP, the Croatian data protection agency, has opened investigations into three major Croatian banks over biased credit scoring models, and a case filed in Zagreb in early 2026 involves over 800 rejected job applicants who say an AI system downgraded resumes with employment gaps. AZOP also issued its first AI-related fine in early 2026, penalizing a Zagreb marketing firm 150,000 euros for feeding customer data into an AI system without consent.

The legal basis combines the EU AI Act, the GDPR and the Croatian Civil Obligations Act. AZOP handles data privacy and AI data processing, with fines up to 20 million euros, the Ministry of Justice handles high-risk AI compliance and can order market bans and recalls, and the European AI Office handles cross-border and general-purpose AI cases, with fines up to 35 million euros. Penalties reach up to 35 million euros or 7 percent of global annual turnover for banned practices, 15 million euros or 3 percent for high-risk failures, and 7.5 million euros or 1.5 percent for administrative breaches. Any EU resident harmed by an AI system in Croatia can file, and family members, consumer organizations and small businesses can also bring claims. Payouts typically range from 500 euros to over 50,000 euros per claimant, depending on the harm.

Under the AI Act the burden of proof shifts toward the AI provider, and employers must conduct bias audits before deploying high-risk employment tools. The articles do not name the banks under investigation, the employers in the hiring case or the marketing firm, and they give no statements from the companies or authorities involved. The standard filing deadline is three years from discovery of the harm, data privacy complaints to AZOP should be filed within one year, employment discrimination claims have a six-month window, and challenges to government AI decisions have 30 days. The articles say over 12,000 Croatian residents could be affected, that early claims tend to receive higher payouts, and that the filing window is closing, but they do not say what happens next in the courts.

Articles.Title: AI Lawsuit Croatia 2026: Eligibility, Payouts, Deadlines - LawFold.com

stories.Headline: Brazilian lawyers busted for attempting to manipulate court's AI with prompt injection hidden in filing — court's AI flags hidden text that demanded superficial legal scrutiny, lawyers fined $16,000
stories.Summary:
Two Brazilian lawyers were caught trying to manipulate a court's artificial intelligence system by hiding a prompt injection in a legal filing, according to a report from Tom's Hardware dated November 1, 2026. The hidden text demanded that the AI give only superficial legal scrutiny to the case. The court's AI flagged the concealed instructions rather than following them. The lawyers were fined $16,000 over the attempt.

The filing contained hidden text that acted as an instruction to the AI, a technique known as prompt injection. The injected demand asked the system to carry out only a shallow review of the legal material. The court's AI detected the hidden text and did not comply with it. The lawyers were fined $16,000 as a result of the attempt.

The lawyers were the ones responsible for placing the hidden instructions in the filing. The articles do not say whether they commented on the fine or the attempt. The court's AI is credited with flagging the concealed text. The fine of $16,000 was imposed on the lawyers.

The articles describe the episode as an attempt to manipulate a court's AI through a filing. They do not give further context on how the injection was discovered beyond the AI flagging it. They do not say what happens next in the case or whether the lawyers plan to respond. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Brazilian lawyers busted for attempting to manipulate court's AI with prompt injection hidden in filing — court's AI flags hidden text that demanded superficial legal scrutiny, lawyers fined $16,000 - Tom's Hardware

stories.Headline: The Flaw in AI Economic Estimates
stories.Summary:
An opinion piece published on Daily Kos on October 31, 2026, by a community writer using the name ExCorpFlunky argued that estimates of AI's economic benefits are flawed. The piece said the firm Anthropic recently made very optimistic predictions about how AI will boost economic growth. It said the firm has an interest in convincing potential investors because it is preparing an initial public offering of its stock. It also said many investors and politicians hype AI's economic gains to support higher stock prices and more data centers in their districts.

The article argued that productivity is a measure of worker productivity, and that economic growth depends on productivity times growth in the number of working people. It said Anthropic predicts in one scenario that over 15% of office workers may need to move to more manual jobs, and that lower pay in those jobs would lower productivity and growth. It said AI proponents often ignore the negative effects of worker disruption. It also said AI could speed up the business cycle and competition, and that if volume rises 15% while prices fall 15%, there is little economic growth.

The writer said he uses AI for free every day and expects it to be everywhere. He said AI models and agents are self-learning and self-replicating, so results will likely be available almost everywhere for free or at very low prices. He said other countries and companies also have AI, so competition will spread and competitive advantage will be destroyed quickly. He said the lowest cost producer, whether in China or at some new cheap company, should be expected to win in a commoditized industry.

The piece said every technological revolution has caused unemployment and disruption, citing the industrial revolution, the Michigan copper mine where the steam drill doubled productivity, and the computer revolution that replaced secretaries. It said AI will target the knowledge industry and that many high-skilled, high-paying jobs will be lost. It said the assumption that AI will double the economy every few years with little downside is wrong, and that the assumption all AI companies will make massive profits forever is also wrong. It said the auto industry shrank from 90 US companies to three, and it called for common sense regulation, people-first solutions and billionaire taxation.

Articles.Title: The Flaw in AI Economic Estimates

stories.Headline: As AI makes law firms more efficient, clients ask: ‘Where’s my discount?’
stories.Summary:
Law firms have been rolling out artificial intelligence tools and promoting their use. Sullivan & Cromwell introduced Agreement Analyzer for reviewing deals, Cooley brought out Go Public for drafting the S-1 before an initial public offering, and Ropes & Gray said it was developing a tool that could produce a detailed, issue-level diligence report in hours, not weeks. Google and Anthropic have also released AI tools for lawyers in the past year, firms have begun hiring chief AI officers, and Kirkland & Ellis has announced big investments in its own AI systems. Because the industry bills by the hour, clients are now asking when that efficiency will lead to lower legal bills.

Some clients are using AI to argue for discounts. Jennifer Leonard, founder of Creative Lawyers, said firms and clients have used AI agents to find line items where AI could have saved hours, then struck them out and asked for a discount. Kyle Poe, vice president of legal innovation at the software company Legora, said in-house legal teams often ask firms to cut bills by 20% to 30% across the board. Firms often push back, saying AI does not yet save that much time and is changing the mix of hours toward more substantive analysis. Norm AI, a technology company with an affiliated law firm, raised $260 million in July at a $1.2 billion valuation from Khosla Ventures, Blackstone and Bain Capital, and now counts those firms among its clients.

Firm leaders say they are open to new arrangements. Jon Ballis, chair of Kirkland & Ellis, said in a July interview that more fixed-price and project-based pricing is already happening a bit and will continue. Neill Jakobe, vice chair of Ropes & Gray, said the firm discusses AI use with clients at the start and end of each project and that he has become more open to fixed fees. Poe of Legora said nobody wants to be the first firm to really lead the way, and that firms want to be ready to pivot if and when the shift happens. In a Citi survey of 55 large law firms last year, 35% expected to change their billable hour models in the next year because of AI, and 65% expected to do so by 2035.

The billable hour remains deeply embedded in law firm operations, from insurance to performance management, and few in the industry expect it to disappear entirely. Revenue at large firms grew more than 12% on average in the first six months of the year, and average standard billing rates rose by double digits, according to Wells Fargo. Researchers at the legal placement firm BCG Attorney Search wrote that bespoke litigation, major transactions and urgent strategic counseling will remain largely hourly, while repeatable or portfolio work will increasingly support fixed or hybrid pricing. Leonard said she expects more firms to price the AI-heavy, repeatable parts of a matter in new ways and to keep judgment-heavy work like strategy, negotiation and advocacy on the hourly model.

Articles.Title: As AI makes law firms more efficient, clients ask: ‘Where’s my discount?’ - The Seattle Times

stories.Headline: Right Law Group Founder Alexis Austin Litle Speaks on AI Security and Vendor Risks at MaxLawCon 2026
stories.Summary:
Alexis Austin Litle, founder of the Colorado criminal defense firm Right Law Group and the legal technology company LexAxiom, spoke at MaxLawCon 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia, on October 8 and 9. Her presentation was titled "How to Read the Matrix: A Framework to Help You Evaluate Legal Tech AI Companies." She gave law firm owners a practical way to assess AI products before bringing them into their firms. The session focused on what happens to confidential client information, how secure the software is, and whether vendors can back up their claims.

Litle introduced a framework meant to help attorneys evaluate legal AI companies without needing an extensive technical background. Rather than relying on product demonstrations or sales materials, it encourages law firms to ask specific questions about how a vendor handles information, what security measures are in place, and whether its claims can be independently assessed. She has published supporting materials on her personal website, including an AI Vendor Evaluation Scorecard with 12 questions attorneys can use when reviewing legal technology products. Her resources also include a guide to assessing vendor security claims and an explanation of common AI marketing terminology.

Litle said lawyers are being flooded with AI products and every vendor claims its technology is secure and will save lawyers time. She said being secure is not the same as protecting client confidentiality. She said lawyers have an obligation to ensure AI models are not trained on clients' confidential data and that the data is not stored on LLM servers or accessible by third parties. She said that in criminal defense this opens clients' data up to possibly being subpoenaed and used against them, and that under rules of professional responsibility lawyers must understand how these tools work, where the data goes, and who may have access to it.

Litle founded Right Law Group in 2018 after working as a Colorado prosecutor, including as Chief of the Domestic Violence Unit in the state's 10th Judicial District. Earlier in 2026 she presented "Ethics and AI in Law: From Deepfakes to Defense Strategy Memos" for the El Paso County Bar Association. At Right Law Group, every attorney is a former prosecutor, and the firm has offices in Colorado Springs, Castle Rock, Highlands Ranch, and Denver. The firm handles DUI, domestic violence, assault, drug offenses, and other misdemeanor and felony cases, and offers free initial consultations and 24/7 availability.

Articles.Title: Right Law Group Founder Alexis Austin Litle Speaks on AI Security and Vendor Risks at MaxLawCon 2026 - EIN Presswire

stories.Headline: Etsy Bans AI-Generated Listings but Sellers Say It Still Isn't Working
stories.Summary:
Etsy introduced new rules on October 22 that ban AI-generated patterns, recipes and other instructional content, the kind of listing where a buyer has to put in effort to reach a finished product. Sellers must now show at least one unedited photo of the actual item against a real background. Anyone who edits photos with AI has to disclose it in the listing. Fully automated listings, generated and posted with no human involvement, are no longer allowed. The ban covers knitting, crochet, sewing, embroidery, quilting and beading patterns, along with woodworking plans and instruction manuals, while AI-generated art can still be sold if the seller had a real hand in making it and says so.

The numbers behind the policy are stark. Etsy's active seller count fell 10.9% to 5.5 million last quarter, and more than 17,000 listings were pulled in early 2025 over AI disclosure violations, many of them genuinely handmade. A new reporting tool lets buyers flag suspected AI listings, but at first it will only collect information rather than trigger immediate action. Removals still depend on the same detection systems sellers already distrust. Kruti Patel Goyal became CEO on January 1 after running Depop, inheriting a marketplace where cheap AI-made goods were already undercutting human sellers.

Viktor, a UK-based illustrator, told Marketplace that people have stopped trusting sites like Etsy because they are tired of AI slop infecting the platform. Sellers say AI-supported listings still outrank their own and undercut them on price, and nothing in the October 22 announcement changes how search ranking works. A disclosure requirement only matters if Etsy can tell who is lying, and the same detection tools that wrongly pulled thousands of listings last year are expected to do that job now. Etsy needs buyers to believe the crackdown works and sellers to believe enforcement is fair, and neither side is convinced.

Fortune reported that buyers may be returning following the policy change, but sellers wrongly flagged last year have little reason to expect better this time. The business reasons for acting are real, since Etsy spent much of 2025 watching its seller base shrink as sellers cited a crackdown on fakes and new fees alongside the flood of AI-made goods. The turnaround is still fragile, even as active buyers and sellers have recently returned to growth. The core complaint is not that Etsy picked the wrong rules but that it has a track record of enforcing them unevenly, pulling real handmade listings while AI-flooded ones keep appearing in search.

Articles.Title: Etsy Bans AI-Generated Listings but Sellers Say It Still Isn't Working

stories.Headline: Disquiet grows in Albanese’s back yard as Grayndler artists unite against ‘insane’ AI proposal
stories.Summary:
Artists and creative businesses in Anthony Albanese’s inner west Sydney seat of Grayndler are pushing back against a federal government proposal that would let AI companies scrape everything Australians create online. The seat is home to more than 3,000 cultural and creative businesses, and 10% of its workers are employed in cultural and creative fields, compared with 4.2% nationally. Labor is considering the copyright changes as part of a suite of AI reforms covering datacentres, energy and the economy. The proposals were leaked in September as senior personnel from OpenAI, the creator of ChatGPT, met Labor ministers and warned that Australia’s copyright laws were preventing the company from training models locally. The government’s draft laws are expected by the end of the year, with consideration in parliament due in 2027.

Albanese has promised the strongest possible protection and warned it would be theft if creatives were not paid for their work. Some AI companies have said licensing agreements under existing copyright law would be too difficult, while Anthropic has suggested an opt-out model that would allow it to scrape content unless a rights holder objected. Coalition senators and the recording industry have warned this could amount to an acquisition of property by the government. Screenprinter and Greens councillor Pete Strong, whose business is based in Grayndler, said he was completely against the proposal and described AI as an extraction industry mining for profit for the few. Designer and artist Lu Campbell-Smith said having to opt out was outrageous and asked why anyone would want to make anything and post it online if they were creating free content for an AI machine.

H Morgan-Harris, an author, curator and director of the Tortuga Studios artist-led space in St Peters, said there was a risk the Australian creative ecosystem could be decimated and that artists are the first to be thrown under the bus. She said her copywriting industry had already been heavily impacted by AI. Jason Zoidberg, a co-founder of Monster Mouse Studios in Marrickville, said the AI industry had already stolen artists’ collective labour without consequence and that it felt insane the government was inviting companies in. He said he was seeing a surge in interest in traditional, hands-on art forms, though he described it as a niche inner west bubble.

Grayndler has been an ultra-safe Labor seat, and Albanese has won it on first preferences alone at recent elections. At the next federal election he will be challenged by 28-year-old Hannah Ferguson, co-founder of Cheek Media, running as an independent. No sitting member has lost their seat from such a margin at a federal election. Guardian Australia’s latest Essential poll shows Albanese’s disapproval rating at 56%, the equal highest since he took office.

stories.Headline: US SEC's top cop says agency is monitoring AI corporate disclosures
stories.Summary:
The US Securities and Exchange Commission is examining how artificial intelligence companies describe their businesses to investors, the agency's enforcement director told Reuters on Friday, October 30, 2026. David Woodcock, who became enforcement director in May, said the agency is watching corporate AI disclosures as investor worries grow about a possible AI bubble. Big Tech stocks sold off this week as companies disclosed they are burning through cash to fund AI expansion while interest rates are rising. That raised questions about whether AI spending can be sustained.

Woodcock said the agency does not want to stand in the way of tech innovation, but it must make sure issuers give investors the full picture on potential risks. He said the main concern is that people make accurate disclosures about material information so investors know what they are getting into. Where such disclosure does not happen, he said, enforcement will be present. He also said AI and superintelligence have made scams much easier and cheaper to produce at scale, raising risks for more people, and that brokers and other firms need processes to protect retail investors.

Woodcock said the SEC will keep looking at private markets, and the enforcement team's asset management unit is very focused on conflicts of interest and valuations. He said that when people do not make accurate disclosures, whether about valuations or anything else, there is a role for enforcement, and he expects more activity in this space. He also said the SEC has a role in overseeing prediction markets, which are led by Polymarket and Kalshi and have grown in popularity over the past two years. He said enforcement staff are working with policy officials and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission to monitor and regulate these markets.

Asked about possible cases against firms that do not register with the agency, Woodcock said the agency does not want to regulate the new industry through enforcement actions. He said the agency wants to be involved where it makes sense, but not in a way that crushes innovation. Law360 reported that agency attorneys are watching for at least two types of AI-related fraud: those that use AI to trick social media users and those by companies that fail to properly disclose their use of the technology. Reuters previously reported that the SEC was probing a type of private equity fund as part of its broader interest in opaque markets.

stories.Headline: Pope says 'most urgent' challenge facing AI race is need for institutional ethical framework - The Tribune-Democrat
stories.Summary:
Pope Leo XIV spoke on Friday at a Vatican gathering of artificial intelligence researchers and experts. He told the meeting that the most urgent challenge in the AI race is to identify international institutions that will put ethical principles for AI development into practice. The American pope has made AI a key priority. He said the principles are already known, but the institutions that can effectively safeguard the global common good are missing.

The gathering was held in the Vatican and co-sponsored by the Pontifical Academy of Life, the Vatican's bioethics think tank, and the Future of Life Institute. It gave the Vatican's in-house AI commission a chance to engage with experts in the field. Leo's 2026 AI encyclical, "Magnificent Humanity," called for robust regulation of AI and for its developers to work for the common good rather than profit. On Friday he highlighted many of the encyclical's key points, especially that the future of AI is not predetermined and that much will depend on the choices developers and political leaders make today.

Leo said the framework calls for shared standards, independent oversight and clear mechanisms of accountability. Decisions about the development and use of AI should be examined, challenged when necessary, and met with appropriate remedies for any harm caused, he said. He also stressed that machines are tools, not persons, and should not be granted legal status or be delegated to make life-or-death decisions. He said the institutional ethical framework was the most urgent of all the challenges facing the AI field.

The company says it has rebuilt its platform for AI agents. The funding was reported by Techmeme on November 2, 2026. The round values Hex at $1.2 billion.

Separately, Dataline announced a $10.6 million funding round on October 31, 2026, co-led by Lattice and Samsung-backed Dispersion Capital, with participation from Symbolic Capital. stories.Headline: How AI is impacting the midterm elections
stories.Summary:
As midterm candidates made their final pitches to voters in late October 2026, experts spoke out about how artificial intelligence had shaped the election cycle. Chris Borick, a political science professor at Lehigh University, said AI had become a major issue in several races over the previous few months. He noted that the rhetoric around it differed from other new technologies, saying that while tech had traditionally been liked as part of the political economy, that changed in the past year, with a more neutral and sometimes negative political position on AI. Borick said the political calculus around AI had gone from positive to negative in both red and blue states after the backlash, picking up on broader public concerns about AI's effects on society, the economy and communities.

The articles give several figures on money in the cycle. More than $16 billion was raised ahead of the elections, with ad spending in House and Senate races topping $4 billion, according to AdImpact, which called it the most expensive cycle on record. Two leading AI super PAC networks, affiliated with OpenAI or Anthropic, spent $50.7 million on the primaries but only $8.5 million in the lead-up to the general election. A CNBC analysis from early October found that 14 of the 20 largest donors and donor groups exclusively or nearly exclusively backed GOP candidates or aligned groups. A recent poll of Iowa and Ohio voters, published online for SEMAFOR, found the vast majority wanted greater regulation of artificial intelligence.

Shobita Parthasarathy, a public policy professor at the University of Michigan, said Republicans had been in a much closer position with AI companies over the past year or more, so they tended to talk more about the cost issue and were less likely to discuss broader issues or a moratorium. Borick said that at the local level, conservatives, liberals, Republicans and Democrats often align in opposition to data centers or in concerns about AI, which creates the potential for political realignments. Intercept managing editor Maia Hibbett said the data showed AIPAC was still spending a lot of money on many races and more often than not its candidates were still winning. Intercept politics reporter Matt Sledge said the AI super PACs were mainly about setting the tone for future federal regulation, and that such groups often run ads with vague names that are not associated with crypto or AI.

Sledge said polls showed it was not a great environment for Republicans, so the spending may have softened the blow but could still be overwhelmed by a blue tide. Hibbett said that no matter which party won control of either or both houses of Congress, many people elected would have gotten there on the backs of Big Tech and special interests. Sledge added that the groups were backing many people in safe seats without tight elections, and the goal may simply be to buy a few friends in Congress, since having people who can stop regulation can be as good as having people who can shape and pass laws. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the elections.

stories.Headline: What if AI Doesn't Work? Apollo's Torsten Slok Sees "No Signs" of AI Productivity Growth.
stories.Summary:
On Saturday, Apollo economist Torsten Slok published research arguing that AI has not yet delivered expected gains. His analysis found no signs that AI is boosting productivity growth, despite hundreds of billions of dollars invested in AI data centers. The research also found that since the third quarter of 2022, when ChatGPT launched the AI boom, the Magnificent Seven tech companies have seen higher profit margins and higher revenue per worker. The other 493 companies in the S&P 500 have not, with comparatively flat productivity and profitability as a group.

Slok's research found that most AI spending is concentrated among a small number of companies that sell AI-related services, such as cloud computing. He warned that mainstream corporate America does not need the latest model and is unwilling to pay for it. The Motley Fool article, published on Oct. 29, 2026, says other sources have suggested some S&P 500 companies are already seeing meaningful gains from new AI tools and automated business processes. It notes the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF has delivered annualized returns of about 13.8% in the past five years, and that yields on U.S. Treasuries have recently surpassed 5%.

Atlassian's "State of Product 2027" survey of 1,000 product professionals found that 80 percent of respondents are shipping faster with AI, but without customers seeing value any sooner. Forty-nine percent said they have had to check agents to keep them on task, 49 percent reported reprompting AI chats, and 48 percent retraced an agent's steps after something went wrong. Sixty-one percent of product managers said AI has created more technical debt, and 82 percent said team members at least sometimes produce low-effort AI work and revise it based on feedback. Axel Sooriah, product management evangelist at Atlassian, said companies need a broader accounting of what AI productivity costs, and that whoever sends AI-generated material owns it.

Sixty-nine percent of the Atlassian respondents said decision-making has not accelerated alongside product development, even as AI makes it easier to produce specifications, prototypes and features. The respondents worked at companies with 500 to 10,000 employees in the U.S., Germany and France. Newsweek's AI Impact newsletter said Firdaus Bhathena, executive vice president and chief technology and transformation officer at S&P Global, will join Dr. Ranjit Tinaikar for a webinar on Nov. 4 called "What Enterprise AI Looks Like When It Works." The Motley Fool article says there is no guaranteed way to protect against stock market risks, and that AI might still deliver the hoped-for gains.

stories.Headline: Nasdaq 100 losing momentum as AI trade divides
stories.Summary:
On Friday, October 30, 2026, the Nasdaq 100 fell 3.46 per cent to close at 28,384.85, after touching an intraday low of 28,093.24, which was 10.0 per cent below the October 6 record close of 31,224.47. That low briefly put the index in correction territory during the session, but buyers lifted it back before the close, leaving it 9.1 per cent below the record. The selling began in chip stocks, with Intel dropping 28.6 per cent after guiding fourth-quarter revenue to US$15 billion to US$16 billion, below the US$16.5 billion it had just reported. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 7.2 per cent, its worst day since June 23, and lost 15.4 per cent for October. The VIX hit 23.93 during the session but closed at 19.41, up 12.91 per cent.

The Federal Reserve held its policy rate at 3.75 per cent to 4 per cent on October 28, a pause after September's hike, on a split vote with multiple dissents. Chair Kevin Warsh struck a balanced but hawkish tone, played down any influence from the midterm elections and left a December increase on the table. Third-quarter GDP grew at a 3.4 per cent annualised pace, headline PCE inflation accelerated to 3.6 per cent in September, and jobless claims held near multi-decade lows, pushing the 10-year Treasury yield back towards 5 per cent. Alphabet fell around 10 per cent after results as search growth disappointed and cash burn mounted, dragging the index down roughly 1.6 per cent on Thursday, while Microsoft was rewarded earlier in the week for converting AI investment into cash. Apple slipped 1.23 per cent and, at US$5.03 trillion, passed NVIDIA as the most valuable company, while NVIDIA fell 4.2 per cent to US$204.64, leaving it worth US$4.94 trillion.

Joe Tigay, a portfolio manager at Equity Armor Investments, said the market was moving out of the hopes and dreams phase of the AI trade and into the show me phase. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said the company still expected 2026 cash capital expenditures of approximately US$220 billion. On Intel's call, management said data center demand exceeds supply but guided fourth-quarter gross margin to 38 per cent, compared with 44.1 per cent in the third quarter, and warned of a PC slowdown linked to memory prices. The Business Times reported that the index had slipped below its 20-day, 50-day and 100-day simple moving averages, at 30,050, 29,812 and 29,559, while remaining above a rising 200-day average at 27,912.

This was the third time in 2026 that the index fell more than 10 per cent below a record, after closes of 23,132.77 on March 27 and 27,192 on July 29, and both times it later set new records. The Business Times said the immediate task for bulls was to reclaim the 29,559 to 30,050 band, with 30,500 and 31,200 as hurdles above, and the late-October low near 28,800 as first support, with a break exposing the 28,000 region and then the 200-day average. Upcoming events include Apple's expected report after the close on November 2, the US midterm elections on November 3, the October jobs report on November 6, NVIDIA's report in mid-November, and a Trump-Xi meeting at the Apec summit in Shenzhen on November 18-19. The US-China trade truce is set to expire on January 10.

stories.Headline: "Meta Spends, Doesn't Make Enough"... Is an 'AI Shock' Coming?
stories.Summary:
S&P, one of the world's top three credit rating agencies, revised its credit outlook for Meta from stable to negative, according to a report published on November 1, 2026. The agency said Meta's ability to generate revenue through AI investments is more limited than that of competing companies. It also said the scale of Meta's future facility investments remains unclear and that its multi-year AI investment plan is highly aggressive. The report noted that Alphabet and Amazon fell short of market expectations in the third quarter, and that Intel's stock price dropped 45 percent during October. During its third-quarter earnings announcement last month, Meta spent 2.1 billion dollars more on investments than it earned from business operations, and its free cash flow turned negative for the first time since its 2012 IPO.

The company still announced plans to spend up to 145 billion dollars on facility investments this year. S&P projected that Meta's funding shortfall could grow to 710 billion dollars next year, which is about 95 trillion won. A separate report said Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, Amazon and Oracle have a collective 3 trillion dollars or more in AI spending commitments over the coming years, including 1 trillion dollars for Alphabet and 800 billion dollars for Meta. Meta said it disagrees with S&P's assessment and countered that the company remains solid. Matt Kennedy, a senior strategist at an IPO-focused investment firm, said everyone knows growth is possible, but the core of investment decisions is whether that can actually translate into profits.

S&P said the cost burden keeps growing because of increased AI investments, while future profit-generating capability remains uncertain. If the credit rating is actually downgraded, Meta would have to pay higher interest when borrowing money, which would further increase its funding burden. Concerns in the market are growing, as other digital big tech companies ramping up AI investments, such as Alphabet and Amazon, are also seeing their cash flows turn negative one after another. The report described skepticism spreading across industries over whether AI, which requires massive investment costs, can actually generate corresponding profits. It referred to this as the "AI bubble theory" affecting big tech and semiconductor companies.

stories.Headline: Value Options: AI Can Change the World—and Still Crash the Market
stories.Summary:
Alphabet, the parent company of Google, lost about $500 billion in market value on Oct. 29, 2026, when its shares fell 12.6% to close at $283.82 on the Nasdaq. The drop was the steepest single-day decline since Alphabet's initial public offering and the second-largest one-day loss in Wall Street history, behind only Nvidia's $593 billion decline in January 2025. The selloff followed third-quarter results that missed expectations, with revenue of $127.6 billion, up 25% year on year, and earnings per share of $2.12 against a forecast of $2.99. Google Search revenue rose 12% to about $63 billion, below the $65 billion consensus, and paid search click growth slowed from 13% in the second quarter to 8%.

The quarter also brought a free cash flow deficit of $9.1 billion, the company's first two consecutive quarters of negative free cash flow since it listed. Capital expenditure reached $51.3 billion in the third quarter, up from $44.9 billion in the previous quarter, and Chief Financial Officer Anat Ashkenazi reaffirmed a projection that annual capital expenditure could reach as much as $205 billion. The quarterly filing showed contingent commitments of about $98.5 billion, up roughly $23 billion from the previous quarter, separate from purchase commitments and future lease obligations exceeding $1 trillion. Google Cloud revenue more than doubled year on year.

Chief Executive Officer Sundar Pichai said search query growth was at its fastest pace in five years, but Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler acknowledged that lower monetization of AI Mode queries had weighed on revenue. On the Value Options Podcast, Tim Travis said the big technology companies had long funded spending from operating cash flow but are now turning to debt and equity as capital expenditure runs into hundreds of billions of dollars. He said long-term Meta or Oracle bonds might yield 7% or 9%, while a company like Corweave is financing itself at 15% in the debt markets. He added that Meta could raise close to $100 billion in equity across this year and next.

Travis said he likes most of the big companies and finds Amazon and Meta compelling at current valuations, citing Meta's Muse product and its distribution network. Tobias Carlisle said the chip makers benefiting from the spending, such as Micron and SK Hynix, may be over-earning at the top of a cycle, and he raised the possibility of an early 2000s-type scenario in which the technology is real but stocks still crash. Travis said that if the hyperscalers struggle to raise capital affordably, demand for chips could fall and supply could rise, which might ultimately make the AI build-out more affordable and sustainable. Carlisle also noted that Anthropic's pre-IPO filing showed an $80 billion loss in the six months to June on $16 billion of revenue, which he said partly reflected accounting for convertible notes converting into equity.

stories.Headline: Anthropic orders AI tool Claude to stop remaking video games
stories.Summary:
Anthropic added a new rule to Claude Code on October 27, 2026, according to X user Chasm, who spotted the change. The rule is listed under "tengu_heron_brook" and tells the tool to build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user's own designs and assets. It also says not to build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original. Chasm reported that there is no way to disable the rule.

Anthropic confirmed the change and said it had added two sentences to Claude Code's prompt on Opus 5.5. Addy Osmani, a member of Anthropic's technical staff, said the aim was to steer the tool away from recreating someone else's specific game. He said using Claude to infringe IP is against the company's usage policy. He added that original games, genre games, and games built from a user's own designs and assets are meant to keep working, and that Anthropic will keep iterating to strike the right balance. He also said that if Claude turns down something that is yours, you should send it his way.

The change follows weeks in which Steam was overrun with AI slop and the game development community raised outcries. Fear over fast-follow AI remakes that might beat the copied game to market has spread among independent developers in recent weeks. Digital Sun Games was one of several studios to cancel its upcoming public playtest for fear someone might ingest the demo into an AI tool and release their own version of its upcoming game ReVamp. Developers also pressed Valve to explain how it can prevent shady clones from supplanting their games on Steam, prompting the company to offer a rare explanation to developers in South Korea earlier in the week.

The rule may only deter the most low-effort copycats, since scientists and reporters have repeatedly documented that safety limits on generative AI tools can be sidestepped with rhetorical tricks. It is also unclear how the software would interpret whether or not a user owns a game idea or game assets. As many users responding to Chasm pointed out, if Claude becomes too difficult to use, vibe-coding cloners can turn to open-weight models that have no such restrictions. GameDeveloper.com said it had reached out to Anthropic for comment and would update the story upon its response.

stories.Summary:
United Systems Inc., a Quincy-based technology services provider, announced new artificial intelligence tools for small and midsize businesses. The tools transcribe phone calls and gauge caller sentiment, the company said. The announcement was reported by whig.com on November 1, 2026. The company said the tools use live transcription, which turns a conversation into searchable text as it happens.

The system includes real-time sentiment analysis, which the company said detects when a caller's experience may be turning negative. In a customer service setting, it can alert a supervisor during the call so the supervisor can help the employee, provide information, or step in. The company said transcripts and sentiment reports can also help managers spot patterns, such as repeated complaints about billing, scheduling, or a particular product. Employees can stay engaged with the caller instead of taking notes, then search the transcript later to find a deadline, customer concern, or pricing question.

Mike Melton, the company's president, said important information is exchanged during employees' phone calls every day. He said AI can help capture those conversations automatically and turn them into meaningful data. Melton said the technology raises employee productivity, which in turn increases profitability and improves customer service. The company said a salesperson, for example, could return to a 30-minute prospect call and locate a specific point without relying on memory or handwritten notes.

Separately, Aehr Test Systems added former Meta infrastructure leader Vijay Rao to its Board of Directors, according to a Simply Wall St article published on Yahoo Finance on October 31, 2026. The article said Rao brings three decades of AI, data center, and semiconductor experience to the company's semiconductor test and burn-in focus. It said Aehr's share price was down about 45% over the past month and around 31% over 90 days, while the year to date share price return was up 148% and the 1 year total shareholder return was 111%. The article said Aehr last closed at $54.89, while the most followed narrative pegs fair value at $130, and it cited a record backlog of about US$100.6 million and a fiscal 2027 revenue outlook of US$130 million to US$150 million.

stories.Headline: Developers Are Fed Up With Their Games Being Cloned Using Claude and Other AI Tools, So Major Companies Could Introduce New Restrictions on Their Technology
stories.Summary:
Independent game developers have complained in recent months that their games are being cloned through vibe coding and reverse engineering, practices that have become more common as AI technology advances. Some studios and creators have stopped releasing demos or sharing updates on social media because they fear someone will steal their ideas and copy their projects before launch. As a result, they have demanded greater AI regulation from the industry's biggest companies. Reports claim that Anthropic, the company behind Claude, has already taken the first step.

According to recent reports, Anthropic introduced new restrictions to prevent the modification, reverse engineering, and decompilation of video games. Specifically, the Claude Opus 5.5 model reportedly blocks attempts to recreate any existing game. So far, Anthropic and other AI companies have not made any official announcements. Nevertheless, many believe that regulation of these tools is inevitable, and everything suggests that broader restrictions will arrive over time.

The new restrictions could help curb cloning, but the same barriers have also affected creative professionals. Legitimate developers have reported that they can no longer use Claude to move their projects forward because the AI refuses to complete certain basic tasks. The tool now reportedly declines to help with fundamental problems related to video game development. As a result, there is speculation that companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI will make significant changes to strike a balance between different uses.

Cloning and porting games can involve copyrighted material, creating potential legal risks, and AI has already caused problems for companies such as PlayStation, Nintendo, and Xbox. Major companies appear to be taking precautions to avoid legal disputes with developers and studios over the use of their tools for reverse engineering. Players are also affected, since they are increasingly exposed to low-quality games or titles based on stolen ideas. Any effort to balance different uses could also make AI less accessible to everyday users.

stories.Headline: E2E Networks Plans 5.4 MW NVIDIA Blackwell AI Expansion in India
stories.Summary:
E2E Networks announced plans to add 5.4 megawatts of AI computing capacity in India, using NVIDIA's Blackwell architecture. The company said the addition would raise its total AI infrastructure to about 14.6 MW, an increase of nearly 59 percent. The expansion will include NVIDIA HGX B300 systems and other Blackwell GPUs. The announcement was reported on October 28, 2026.

The new capacity is intended for foundation model training, post-training, production inference, agentic AI and multimodal applications. E2E Networks said demand is coming from higher education institutions, research organisations, foundation model developers, AI-native startups, enterprises and public-sector programmes. The company also plans to offer infrastructure hosted within India for customers whose data must stay under domestic jurisdiction, including regulated and data-sensitive environments. E2E Networks has not disclosed when the infrastructure will be commissioned, the capital expenditure planned, or the total number of GPUs to be deployed.

Tarun Dua, founder and managing director of E2E Networks, said Indian AI developers are moving beyond pilot-stage deployments and increasingly need infrastructure for production-scale workloads. He said customers also need infrastructure operating within their organisational boundaries to help protect data in line with national laws. On October 30, 2026, shares of E2E Networks hit their 5 percent lower circuit limit amid a global sell-off in technology stocks. Investors were concerned about rising spending on AI infrastructure, returns from those investments and rising borrowing costs, while earnings growth has failed to match the scale of investments.

The sell-off followed earnings announcements from major companies including Amazon.com and Intel, and Alphabet shares posted a record decline after its results. Jai Malhi, a senior equity strategist at Vanda Research, told Bloomberg that tech earnings have proven a major hurdle with investors becoming capex vigilantes, and that tech names are being punished if revenue growth does not beat a high bar given higher funding costs. Other AI-related Indian shares also fell, including Netweb Technologies, MTAR Technologies, Black Box, ESDS Software Solution, Hitachi Energy India, GE Vernova T&D India, CG Power and Industrial Solutions and Anant Raj. In the US, chipmakers Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices fell 2.8 percent and 6.9 percent respectively in premarket trading.

stories.Headline: How AI data centers could affect Pennsylvania’s water and electricity
stories.Summary:
Pennsylvania is becoming an attractive location for artificial intelligence data centers, and the facilities' growing demand for electricity and water is raising questions about their impact on local communities, according to a report from 90.5 WESA published on November 2, 2026. Brian R. King, an associate professor of computer science at Bucknell University, says data centers house the powerful computers used to train and operate AI models. Those computers rely on graphics processing units, or GPUs, that require substantial amounts of electricity. King says Pennsylvania's energy resources and its location near major East Coast cities make it appealing to companies developing these facilities, but he also says the rapid expansion of AI is contributing to growing energy demand.

The impact extends beyond electricity, according to the report. Dr. Benjamin Hayes, program director of Watershed Sciences and Engineering, says many large data centers use water to cool their equipment. Their overall footprint can also include water used to generate electricity, new infrastructure, pressure on public water supplies and the conversion of farmland to industrial development. Hayes says the effects can reach beyond the companies building the facilities, potentially affecting neighbors and taxpayers through electricity costs and the availability of public water.

Hayes argues that communities need to consider how multiple projects could affect the same watershed or power supply, rather than evaluating each proposal in isolation. He says there is no single clearinghouse for how a data center project is reviewed, and he calls for statewide or regional analysis that accounts for electricity and water demand, drought conditions, land use and the needs of local communities. King says another part of the solution could be developing smaller AI models designed for specific tasks, rather than relying exclusively on increasingly large models that require extensive computing resources. As Pennsylvania weighs the opportunities and challenges of data center development, both researchers say energy use, water availability and local infrastructure are important parts of the conversation.

AI’s Biggest Water Problem Isn’t The Data Center. It’s The Power Plant

stories.Headline: Explainer: How AI muddies the waters ahead of U.S. midterm elections?
stories.Summary:
AI-driven disinformation is spreading through voters' feeds ahead of the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3, 2026. The Wesleyan Media Project, which tracks AI-generated political advertising, said in October that it had found 220 such advertisements worth more than 137 million dollars. That is a large jump from 50,000 dollars in the 2024 election cycle, and the project called the figure an almost certainly low estimate because AI use is hard to detect. Much of the content carries no disclosure that AI was used, and analysts warned it could mislead voters and damage election integrity.

Some of the ads have been provocative, including one showing a Republican candidate for governor embracing Hillary Clinton under the slogan "Clinton Lover. Trump Hater." Another depicted Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed laughing at cards reading "Death to America" and "Celebrate 9/11." A third showed James Fishback, a Republican primary candidate for Florida governor, hosting a party with Iranian leaders attacking the Star of David. Frances Haugen, a former Facebook data engineer turned whistleblower, said an information operation can now be run with quality that was impossible in 2016 for very little money, and that tweaking posts slightly each time can get some past content moderation.

A survey by the American Association of Political Consultants Foundation found that only 1 percent of respondents considered AI their most credible source of election information, yet one in five voters plans to use AI to look into a race on their ballot. Twice that proportion has already received election details through an AI search summary. Groups are now advising candidates on how to shape what AI says about them, with the left-wing group Run for Something launching a platform called CampSight and the Center for Campaign Innovation publishing research on how AI models answer questions about candidates. Eric Wilson, the center's executive director, told The Atlantic that they are campaigning for the AI vote now.

The AI giants are spending millions on lobbying to block unfavorable legislation, and The Wall Street Journal reported last year that Silicon Valley was channeling more than 100 million dollars into political-action committees and advocacy groups. Leading the Future, a super PAC backed by OpenAI President Greg Brockman and Andreessen Horowitz, reportedly spent 8 million dollars trying to unseat Democratic New York State Assemblymember Alex Bores over his sponsorship of the RAISE Act, an AI safety bill signed into law last December. In December, President Donald Trump issued an executive order creating an AI litigation task force to challenge state laws deemed more than minimally burdensome and directing the Commerce Department to consider withholding federal broadband funds from states with onerous AI regulations. Susan Hyde, a political science professor at UC Berkeley, said the deeper concern is whether voters can make informed decisions when they can no longer trust the information they receive, and the Brennan Center for Justice said policymakers need to act quickly to curb bots' tendency to create or ignore election disinformation.

stories.Headline: Copilot AI Predicts Solana Could Hit $2,500 if This Landmark Event Happens
stories.Summary:
On November 1, 2026, Microsoft Copilot AI predicted that Solana could reach between $1,000 and $2,000 by January 1, 2027, with a stretch target toward $2,500 or more. Alex Ioannou reported the prediction for 99Bitcoins, and Yahoo Finance republished it. Solana was trading near $95 at the time. The forecast assumes a full crypto bull market returns and is boosted by a landmark event, which the article describes as a major global consortium adopting Solana as its blockchain for consumer applications and real-time payments.

The article says Solana had been recovering and consolidating in the $115 to $125 region after reclaiming key levels from earlier lows, and that it was holding above important intermediate moving averages. It says a sustained break above $130 to $150 would open the path toward the prior all-time high near $296, and that clearing that high could trigger measured-move extensions and multi-cycle Fibonacci projections. It lists nearer-term support zones at $110 to $115 and $100 to $105, and says the RSI was in neutral-to-constructive territory with room to run. It also says only an extraordinary surge in real-world, high-throughput adoption could justify the multi-thousand-percent move the targets imply. The article lists five catalysts: scrutiny of traditional banking products, geopolitical instability, interest rate cuts, Bitcoin's next rally and institutional investment.

A separate NTT DATA article by Sandeep Kaushik, published August 21, 2026, says AI agents are moving from emerging technology into everyday enterprise use and are becoming part of how companies operate. It says agents need identities, defined access, governance, policies, observability, accountability and lifecycle management, much like employees. It describes Microsoft tools including Copilot Chat, Microsoft 365 Copilot, Copilot Cowork and Microsoft Scout, and says the opportunity is to redesign work itself rather than just save time per user. It says the risks change once agents take action, such as retrieving sensitive information, triggering workflows or updating business systems, and it distinguishes agents that borrow a person's identity from agents with their own managed identity.

The NTT DATA article says CIOs, CISOs and other business leaders must answer who owns an agent, what data it can access, what actions it can take, how it is monitored and how its behavior is stopped or changed. It says organizations should extend their existing trusted infrastructure rather than build a new governance model, using tools such as Microsoft Entra, Defender, Purview, the Microsoft 365 admin center and Microsoft Agent 365. It recommends assessing AI readiness, prioritizing use cases with measurable value, building a secure foundation with least-privilege access and agent registries, scaling through a repeatable agent factory, and treating AI as an ongoing transformation. It says a partner can shorten the path from experimentation, and the text ends there. The Solana article does not say what happens next beyond its price scenarios.

stories.Headline: October dive for AI-related shares tests broader US stock market's resilience
stories.Summary:
In October 2026, shares linked to artificial intelligence fell sharply, testing how well the wider US stock market could hold up, according to a Markets Daily report dated October 31, 2026. The report was posted by Michael Walen and looked at three AI stocks to watch. It named Tempus AI, Hut 8 and SentinelOne as the three AI stocks to watch that day, based on MarketBeat's stock screener tool. The report said these companies had the highest dollar trading volume of any AI stocks in the last several days.

The report described the three companies and their businesses. Tempus AI is a technology company that uses artificial intelligence mainly in healthcare to advance precision medicine. Hut 8 acquires, builds, manages and operates data centers for digital assets mining, computing and artificial intelligence in the United States, across four segments. SentinelOne is a cybersecurity provider whose Singularity Platform uses AI to prevent, detect and respond to threats across endpoints, cloud workloads and identity credentials. The report said AI stocks can offer growth tied to the expanding AI industry but can also carry elevated risks from high valuations, intense competition, technological changes and regulatory uncertainty.

The report did not name anyone as responsible for the October share decline or give any statements from companies or officials about it. It gave no figures for the size of the drop and no dates for when the fall happened beyond the month of October. The only named person was Michael Walen, who posted the report. The only named source was MarketBeat's stock screener tool, which the report said identified the three stocks.

The report did not say what happens next for the market or the three companies. It offered no forecast and no comment on whether the decline would continue. It listed the three stocks as ones to watch and linked to research reports on each of them. It also included recommended stories and promotional text, which are separate from the main report.

stories.Headline: Andy Jassy Says West Is 'Very Hungry' For More Western Open Source AI Models as Amazon Adds China's Kimi and GLM to Bedrock
stories.Summary:
Amazon.com Inc. added China's Kimi and GLM open models to its Bedrock AI platform, the company said during its third-quarter earnings call on Thursday. The additions join Bedrock's mix of proprietary and open models. CEO Andy Jassy said Bedrock now offers closed models from Anthropic and OpenAI alongside open models such as Moonshot's Kimi K3 and Z.ai's GLM 5.3. He also referenced SpaceXAI's Grok 4.7 model on Bedrock. Earlier in October, Bedrock added Z.ai's GLM 5.3 open-weight model, which the company said offers enhanced capabilities for agentic coding and complex software engineering with AWS security and compliance protections.

Jassy said the Western world is very hungry for additional Western open models, and that he believes this will happen over time. He called Bedrock's potential gigantic and suggested the platform could ultimately become comparable in scale to AWS's EC2 cloud computing offering. He emphasized Bedrock's security structure, saying customer inputs and outputs are not shared with model providers or used to train their foundational models. He expects six to eight models to handle more than 95% of workloads within two to three years.

The expansion follows the broader rise of Chinese-developed open AI systems. Last week, former Google CEO Eric Schmidt said China was roughly six months behind the U.S. in AI, but warned that free products could still give China a strategic advantage. He said China's cheaper, often free and open-weight models could gain traction in developing markets, and attributed the country's progress partly to access to restricted advanced chips and the use of distillation to replicate Western AI capabilities. In July, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang called Chinese models excellent and argued Washington should use rather than ban high-quality open-source technology. He dismissed fears that Chinese open models pose security risks or threaten U.S. tech firms, arguing wider adoption of models like DeepSeek and Kimi will boost demand for Nvidia chips and infrastructure.

stories.Headline: Vehicle curbs, WFH and AI surveillance: From today, Delhi goes into full pollution patrol mode
stories.Summary:
Delhi's government began enforcing special winter pollution restrictions on November 1, 2026, and they will last until January 31, 2027. The measures include vehicle-entry limits, reduced office attendance, staggered working hours, higher parking charges and curbs on dust-generating construction. The policy was unveiled in July and replaces reliance on pollution-triggered restrictions with a notified set of measures applied every winter. It will run alongside the Graded Response Action Plan, and stricter provisions under that plan will take precedence.

The vehicle rule could keep more than 10 lakh vehicles registered in neighbouring National Capital Region districts out of Delhi. It applies to vehicles registered outside Delhi that do not meet BS-VI norms and are neither CNG nor electric, while ambulances, fire tenders and police vehicles are exempt. Government and private offices must limit physical attendance to 50 percent, with the rest working from home, and parking charges at authorised sites will double from November 1 to February 28, except at facilities owned or managed by the Delhi Metro. Outdoor dust-generating demolition and civil construction are banned from November 1 to January 31 except for essential public infrastructure, with a stricter ban from December 10 to January 20, and the Commission for Air Quality Management has halted construction and demolition across the region from November 5 to November 20.

Fuel outlets will dispense petrol, diesel, CNG and LPG only to vehicles with a valid pollution-under-control certificate, with electronic verification permitted. Enforcement will use special teams, automatic number plate recognition cameras and an AI-enabled Integrated Command and Control Centre, according to a Delhi government statement issued on Saturday. Chief minister Rekha Gupta appealed to residents, vehicle owners, construction agencies and institutions to comply, use public transport or carpool, avoid open burning and report violations. The government also urged through-traffic to use peripheral expressways instead of entering Delhi, naming the Eastern and Western Peripheral Expressways, the Delhi-Meerut Expressway and the Kundli-Manesar-Palwal Expressway as alternatives.

Vehicles violating the entry restrictions may face automatic e-challans and traffic police action including impounding, while dedicated teams will inspect construction sites and can issue stop-work notices, levy environmental compensation and start sealing or legal proceedings. The government hopes the combined measures will reduce emissions and dust. Activist Amit Gupta criticised the distinction between Delhi-registered and out-of-state vehicles, saying it is unfair that a Delhi-registered BS-IV or older vehicle can ply while an equally compliant NCR-registered vehicle with a valid certificate is barred, and that pollution is a region-wide problem. The articles do not say what happens after the measures end or how their effect will be assessed.
