stories.Headline: Who on-calls an AI? This is the unresolved crisis of agent ownership
stories.Summary:
Banks including Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, JPMorgan and Wells Fargo found unauthorized AI agents accessing customer accounts, according to an Axios report cited in October 2026. The banks decided to restrict agents or give them read-only access. Amazon reportedly stops shopping agents from making purchases, and sites like Yelp and eBay also disallow unauthorized agents. The problem is that an agent committing fraud and one carrying out a human's wishes act the same, so firms cannot tell the difference.

The restrictions affect both enterprise and consumer agents, which are growing quickly. Most enterprises have built their own agents for automated workflows, and employees have started building agents through services like Claude Code, Codex and OpenClaw that read emails and complete tasks. In the past few months Meta and OpenAI released consumer agents in Muse and Dots that people can personalize to set up appointments or flag potential sales. Banks once asked for several signature samples and identification before opening accounts, and later asked account holders to authorize by tapping a button or logging in, but agents circumvent all of that.

There is no standard way to validate an agent's authorization and identity, and some agents inherit their human users' identity and log into accounts on their behalf. Cal Al-Dhubaib, a cloud and AI technologist at Rubrik, told ISMG that many organizations are not prepared for their environments and security infrastructure to interact with AI systems. He said security professionals know access and identity and how to lock systems down, but have never dealt with probabilistic algorithms. Chris Talevi, chief information security officer at Domino Data Lab, said that if agents are running wild and you cannot tell who deployed or authorized one, that is a real issue because you cannot hold an agent accountable.

The articles describe agent identity as an ongoing challenge for many banks. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the current restrictions. They note that many enterprises have had problems with agents accessing databases they are not supposed to reach. The reporting frames agent ownership and accountability as unresolved.

stories.Headline: A reasoning large language model for rare disease diagnosis: a randomized AI physician-assistance trial
stories.Summary:
A randomized trial tested whether a reasoning large language model could help doctors diagnose rare diseases, according to a dataset posted on Zenodo on November 2, 2026. The dataset holds participant-level scores from the trial, covering diagnostic accuracy, time and confidence scores. The Zenodo page gives the DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23294755 and notes the work is shared under a Creative Commons Attribution license. Zenodo also scheduled maintenance for November 3, 2026, between 08:00 and 08:15 UTC.

Separately, researchers at Turku University Hospital in Finland trained a computer model to sort digital otoscope images into two researcher-defined groups, abnormal or normal. The classifier identified more than 750 eardrum photos of children between six months and three years old. A gold standard of three physicians, two ENT specialists and one pediatrician, analyzed the same images and agreed on their diagnoses. Against that standard, the classifier was 92% accurate in identifying acute otitis media, a common ear infection that can follow upper respiratory tract infections and spread behind the eardrum.

Pediatrician Dr. Simo Nuuttila, one of the study's lead authors, said around 70% to 80% of children get otitis media at least once in their life, and some susceptible children may get it five to six times a year. He added that young children cannot express ear pain, so an infection can get bad enough to puncture or rupture the eardrum. The team created a baseline using 3,000 images labeled by a panel of seven ENT specialists. Nuuttila said the model relies on its training images, so angled or outdated images could lead to an inaccurate diagnosis, meaning the tool cannot fully replace a doctor but can serve as a rule-out when image quality is good.

Dr. Matthew Crowson, a surgeon at Mass General Brigham Eye and Ear in Boston and a professor at Harvard Medical School, is developing other AI models to address that limitation. His team intentionally included poor-quality photos in its dataset and programmed the model to prompt the user to retake a photo or clean the ear. Crowson said the abnormal or normal labels are not as clinically useful, because an abnormal ear does not necessarily need antibiotics for an infection. Nuuttila's team noted the classifier first had 96% accuracy for abnormal ears, which dropped to 92% after multiple images were too unclear. Nuuttila's research is now expanding to 40 families in Finland, half of whom received digital otoscopes to take images at home, and Crowson cautioned that parents should confirm diagnoses with telehealth physicians.

stories.Headline: Turkish competition body probes Google over AI features in search
stories.Summary:
The Turkish Competition Authority opened an antitrust investigation into Google on Monday, November 2, 2026, over the company's AI-powered search features, AI Overviews and AI Mode. The regulator said it is examining whether Google's AI-generated search summaries harm the traffic, visibility and revenues of news publishers and content creators. The probe was launched under Article 41 of the Law on the Protection of Competition, Law No. 4054, to determine whether Google violated Article 6 of the same law. The authority also imposed an interim injunction against Google to protect the rights of news publishers while the investigation continues.

The preliminary investigation began with an authority decision dated August 27, 2026, and looked at several issues. It examined how AI Overviews and AI Mode changed users' access to information and whether this hurt traffic to news publishers and other content producers. It also looked at whether the terms of agreements between Google and news publishers on content use are unfair, and whether the features have an exclusionary effect on publishers, content producers and AI chat assistants. The authority also examined whether Google treats news publishers differently when selecting their content as a source or when licensing it.

The authority said it had a strong suspicion of discriminatory and exploitative behavior concerning news publishers. Because of that, it decided at its meeting on October 8, 2026, to apply interim measures alongside the investigation. The authority said the measures aim to prevent discrimination against news publishers and to make sure the terms reflect the economic value of content usage. They also aim to let publishers make choices about content usage in these services independently of their visibility and indexing in other Google services.

The Turkish probe comes as concerns grow over the impact of Google's AI Overviews on newsrooms around the world, with many organizations reporting a drop in website traffic. AI Overviews is a generative artificial intelligence feature built into Google Search that shows AI-generated answers at the top of search results. AI Mode is a conversational feature that resembles leading AI chatbots and gives users responses to their queries. The articles do not say what happens next in the investigation.

stories.Headline: Why AI Tools Work Differently on Middle Schoolers Compared to College Students, According to a Researcher
stories.Summary:
Two studies released in October 2026 by Jing Liu, director of the Center for Educational Data Science and Innovation at the University of Maryland, examined AI in education. One study looked at a math practice website called Goblins, which was used by 6,000 middle schoolers in Deer Valley, Arizona, during the 2025-26 school year. The other tested an AI assistant at the University of Maryland in the fall semester of 2025, with 15 of 30 professors randomly assigned to use it in their classes. Liu wanted the studies released together to show that AI in education is neither all good nor all bad.

In the Goblins study, students who solved at least two problems a week, more than 50 over the school year, scored significantly higher on a year-end standardized math assessment than similar students who used it less or not at all. Accelerate, an independent nonprofit research organization that commissioned the study, equated the difference of 0.11 standard deviations to about three additional months of learning. Half the 6,000 students used Goblins for at least two problems a week, and only 6 percent used it for at least half an hour a week. The study cannot prove Goblins caused the gains, and Accelerate hopes to commission a randomized controlled trial to settle the matter.

In the Maryland experiment, the 1,100 students in courses with the AI assistant had lower grades, reduced by an average of 0.11 points on a four-point scale, compared with the 1,200 students in the control group. They also interacted less with course materials and were less likely to attend office hours or meet with instructors and peers, with the negative effects more pronounced for first-generation students. Only 15 percent of students in the AI-enhanced classes ever used the assistant, and those who did mostly asked it for answers rather than using its tutoring features. Liu and Provost Jennifer King Rice suspect the assistant's constant presence in the course website sent an unintended message that AI use is encouraged, and students may have used outside tools like ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini to complete assignments, though the researchers cannot establish whether that happened.

Liu said the lesson is not that colleges should avoid AI, but that even a carefully designed tool can have consequences beyond its intended use. Rice told a University of Maryland publication that AI tools could exacerbate inequities in learning outcomes, which she found particularly troubling. Liu suspects Goblins reached hard-to-engage students, including English learners and students with disabilities, because students could talk aloud to a cartoon avatar of their teacher that could talk back, and the AI tutor could speak and understand Spanish and six other languages. The article credits Maryland for testing the assistant before a university-wide rollout to all 40,000 students and for making the troubling results public for the field to learn from.

stories.Headline: Here’s Why You’re About to See More Ads in Google’s AI Overviews
stories.Summary:
Google began putting more ads into its AI search results in late October 2026. On October 28, Alphabet held its quarterly earnings call, where Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler said search ad revenue growth slowed in the third quarter of 2026 because queries are moving to AI Overviews and AI Mode, which have lower monetization. Google then said it would scale ads in AI Mode to 10 new countries, including Australia, Canada, India, Kenya and Singapore, with Brazil, Mexico and the UK to follow later in the year. In the US, Google launched what it calls multiturn ads, which can appear inside follow-up questions in AI Mode when a conversation has commercial relevance.

The change means sponsored links can show up next to or inside conversational AI answers, and all of them carry a clear Sponsored label. Google said ads can also appear on initial AI Mode queries, and sometimes no ads will show if there is no purchase intent. Advertisers do not need to create new campaigns, because Google will automatically pull from their existing ad setups. Google also said paid ads will not influence the information in AI-generated text, so the answers stay neutral.

Dan Taylor, Vice President of Global Ads at Google, confirmed the worldwide expansion on X and said research shows users are comfortable with relevant ads in AI Mode. Google reported that queries in AI Mode are on average three times longer than traditional searches, and that users click sponsored AI links as often as regular product listings. Lily Ray, founder of Algorythmic and an SEO expert, told CNET that it will become harder to use Google to find articles from preferred publishers. She said people will have to dig deeper and look outside Google's products, and she suggested scrolling to the old-fashioned results, using a web filter, or setting favorite publications as preferred sources.

Google is still the largest search engine, with nearly 90% of the global search market, and it said query volume growth in the third quarter was the fastest in five years. Since AI Overviews launched in May 2024, they now appear on nearly half of Google search queries, with a 61% drop in raw traffic to other pages, a situation often called the zero-click crisis. Ray said more ads will mean an even greater decline in organic click-through rates, and that sites not buying Google Ads will find it harder to get traffic organically. The ads in the 10 new countries start in the fourth quarter, while the US gets multiturn ads.

stories.Headline: Anthropic expands AI support for nonprofits as it files to sell shares to the public
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the artificial intelligence company that makes the Claude assistant, filed to sell shares to the public for the first time and expanded its support for nonprofits, the Associated Press reported on Monday, November 1, 2026. The company launched a new Claude for Nonprofits plugin, created with 30 nonprofits to better fit their needs. It also broadened its Claude Corps program, which places fellows with nonprofits to help them use AI, by adding consultants for smaller, shorter-term projects. Anthropic announced earlier in October that it plans to commit 5% of its shares to a new Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, which could make large donations to nonprofits or give money directly to people harmed by AI.

The fund still needs shareholder approval once Anthropic completes its IPO, which could come as early as November. The company filed under the stock symbol ANT, according to Slate. About 25,000 nonprofits currently use Claude for Nonprofits, and most of them have fewer than 10 staff members. One example is Allies Against Slavery, a Texas nonprofit fighting human trafficking, whose only government affairs staffer used Claude to analyze more than 750 state-level anti-trafficking policies and turn them into recommendations for advocates.

Elizabeth Kelly, Anthropic's head of beneficial deployments, said the nonprofit work is central to the company as a public benefit corporation, which it says balances commercial interests with the public good. Anthropic President Daniela Amodei said in a May interview that the structure helps investors, employees and outsiders understand the company's intentions and hold it accountable. Bella DeVaan, director of the Charity Reform Initiative at the Institute for Policy Studies, said public benefit corporations can be meaningful, but the federal government does not properly regulate corporations, and without tax reform there is no guarantee such companies will act in the public interest. Critics say AI companies use donations and nonprofit pledges to build goodwill while many people worry about the technology's dangers and its effect on jobs.

Scott Burns, president and CEO of the Montgomery County Food Bank in Texas, said Claude has already produced significant savings that let the organization feed more people as costs for fuel and proteins rise. He said his team used it to improve scheduling for food pickup and delivery and to stay in better contact with donors, and he expects two Claude Corps fellows soon to work on its outdated inventory system and volunteer scheduling. Cat Ward, CEO of the Taproot Foundation, said nonprofits are lean but ambitious, and the tools will help them go further faster. Other public benefit corporations include Warby Parker, Lemonade and Amalgamated Bank.

stories.Headline: Asian chip suppliers report strong AI demand despite investor concerns over returns - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
Asian chip supply chain companies said on Friday that demand for AI products and services remained strong, even as investors worried about the returns on large AI infrastructure spending. Foxconn Chairman Young Liu told reporters at a company event that AI was not in a bubble and that demand for AI products was clear. Foxconn is Nvidia's biggest AI server maker and Apple's top iPhone assembler. Alphabet, Intel and Amazon all fell overnight over concerns about whether returns would justify continued high capital expenditure, and the caution spread to Asia on Friday. Technology stocks including South Korea's SK Hynix, Taiwan's TSMC and Japan's Advantest came under pressure.

Tokyo Electron forecast an 87% jump in operating profit to 1.17 trillion yen, or $7.41 billion, for its half-yearly results, which was stronger than expected. Chief Financial Officer Hiroshi Kawamoto said interest from customers was very strong in the company's various conversations with them. He also said there were no signs at present that this was slowing down. SK Hynix said this week it would return about $75 billion to shareholders as higher memory prices boost profits.

Tokyo Electron said it would spend up to 150 billion yen to buy back some 25 million shares, and its shares closed down 5% ahead of earnings. Kawamoto of Tokyo Electron and Liu of Foxconn both gave positive views on demand, with Liu saying AI was not in a bubble and Kawamoto pointing to strong customer interest and no sign of a slowdown. The companies reporting results included Tokyo Electron and SK Hynix, and the article said Asian suppliers of chips and semiconductor equipment continue to report strong results despite concerns about AI-related spending. The article did not say what happens next beyond the results and the buyback.

stories.Headline: Two Chipmakers to Account for 73% of Q4 Profit at Korean Listed Firms
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics and SK hynix reported record quarterly operating profits, but their shares still fell on October 30, 2026. Samsung posted 107.4405 trillion won in operating profit, up about 783%, and SK hynix posted 83.3338 trillion won, up about 632.1%. Their shares dropped 3.02% and 7.08% respectively. The KOSPI closed down 206.92 points, or 3.48%, at 5,730.74 that day, after falling as low as 5,599.42 during the session and triggering a sell-side sidecar. Foreign investors sold a net 1.6169 trillion won worth of KOSPI shares, including 429 billion won of SK hynix and 213.4 billion won of Samsung Electronics.

For the fourth quarter, 188 KOSPI-listed companies are forecast to post 296.4814 trillion won in combined operating profit. Samsung Electronics and SK hynix account for 73.4% of that, or 217.7417 trillion won. Forecasts for the remaining companies have been cut by about 2.0% over the past month, including Hyundai Motor at minus 14.47%, LG Electronics at minus 38.59%, LG Innotek at minus 39.59% and Hanwha Ocean at minus 17.38%. Of the 76 companies that reported third-quarter results, combined operating profit beat forecasts by 3.38%, but excluding the two chipmakers it came in 1.09% below estimates, with 42 companies, or 55.3%, falling short.

The market decline followed weak results from Alphabet, Amazon and Intel. Amazon put $77.3 billion into data center facilities in the third quarter, pushing free cash flow to minus $42.4 billion, six times worse than the minus $7.6 billion in the second quarter. Alphabet's third-quarter free cash flow fell to minus $9.07 billion, and its shares plunged 12.64% after its earnings release, erasing about $500 billion, or 700 trillion won, in market value in a single day. Intel's chief financial officer said positive free cash flow would be difficult to achieve next year as well.

Samsung Electro-Mechanics announced an 879.3 billion won supply contract for MLCCs used in AI servers, yet its shares slid 7.50%. Kia's third-quarter operating profit rose 24.3% from a year earlier but came in 22.9% below the market forecast of 2.3574 trillion won, sending its shares down 11.73% to a 52-week low. With investor deposits falling to the 88 trillion won range, whether buying spreads to non-semiconductor sectors has emerged as the key test for a market rebound. China's CXMT saw third-quarter revenue surge 613% from a year earlier to 118.7 billion yuan, about 23.812 trillion won, and swung to a net profit of 54.4 billion yuan, though growth from the previous quarter was just 19.3%, down from 95.9% between the first and second quarters.

stories.Headline: Ministry of Defence Steps Up Preparation for Responsible Artificial Intelligence in the Military Domain (REAIM) 2027 Summit
stories.Summary:
Kenya is preparing to host the fourth Summit on Responsible Artificial Intelligence in the Military Domain, known as REAIM 2027, in Nairobi in April 2027. Defence Principal Secretary Dr Patrick Mariru chaired the inaugural meeting of the Interministerial Steering Committee at Defence Headquarters. The meeting brought together key government representatives to coordinate national preparations for the summit. Nairobi will be the first African and Global South city to host the gathering. The announcement was distributed by APO Group on behalf of Kenya's Ministry of Defence on October 31, 2026.

The meeting laid the foundation for a coordinated, whole of government approach to preparations. The articles say a successful summit will require close collaboration among government institutions, effective planning and a shared commitment to delivering a world-class event. Kenya's hosting builds on its participation in international efforts to promote the responsible use of AI in the military domain. The summit is expected to bring together global leaders, defence officials, international organisations, academia, industry and civil society. They will exchange ideas and perspectives on the opportunities, risks and responsibilities associated with military AI.

Dr Patrick Mariru is named as the official who chaired the inaugural steering committee meeting. The articles describe the meeting as recognising that hosting the summit will require close collaboration among government institutions, effective planning and a shared commitment. The discussions at the summit are expected to contribute to advancing international cooperation. They will also promote approaches that balance technological innovation with responsible use and accountability. The articles do not quote Mariru directly.

The articles say AI is increasingly shaping the future of military operations, from intelligence gathering and decision making to surveillance and defence capabilities. Ensuring responsible, safe and accountable use of these technologies in the military domain has become an important global priority. Kenya aims to help shape the global conversation on military AI through the summit. It also aims to provide a platform for diverse voices, particularly from Africa and the Global South. The articles do not say what happens after the April 2027 summit.

stories.Headline: John Ternus says Apple doesn't "want to ship AI for AI's sake" and that Tim Cook is "available to help wherever I ask" on policy; Ternus has yet to meet Trump (Steven Levy/Wired)
stories.Summary:
John Ternus became Apple's CEO less than two months before late October 2026, when he introduced a new MacBook Pro at a low-key event in Los Angeles. At 51, he is on the younger side of Apple's top management and has worked at the company for 25 years. The presentation included a video of the first touchscreen Mac, and the biggest reaction came when Ternus said the new device restores the illuminated Apple logo. After the event, he spoke with Wired's Steven Levy for about 30 minutes, their second meeting in two days.

Ternus said Apple does not want to ship AI for its own sake and wants to use the technology to improve its products. He said that when the work is done right, people will not have to think about whether AI or more traditional software made something happen, and what matters is whether they love what was built. He said he likes where Apple is at on AI, and that the company will keep putting AI into its products with a focus on privacy. He also said the creation of products is a deeply human and personal thing. On regulation, he said the focus is on keeping products secure and safe and protecting users' information.

Ternus said Tim Cook, now executive chair, is available to help wherever he asks, and that Cook has many relationships built over the years while he is building new ones in his role. He has not yet met President Donald Trump. Greg Joswiak, Apple's senior vice president of worldwide marketing, said Ternus has a great sense for great products that cannot be taught. Johny Srouji, who leads Apple's merged hardware engineering and technology organizations and reports to Ternus, said their relationship will be closer and that Apple's culture will not change. Ternus said he had only a handful of interactions with Steve Jobs but has always felt like a student of his teachings.

Apple has faced criticism for falling behind rivals such as Google in AI, and Ternus took over during what the article calls possibly the biggest technological shift ever. He described himself as passionate about product and said he will continue to learn and go deeper into different areas of a company with a $100 billion services business. The article says policy will probably never be his focus and describes him as a product-guy CEO. It does not say what happens next beyond his stated plans.

stories.Headline: AI-fueled hacking spree ‘Black October’ culminates with $6.3B Binance hack
stories.Summary:
In late October 2026, a month-long wave of cyberattacks that experts called Black October hit hundreds of companies and institutions worldwide. The spree ended on Thursday, October 29, when hackers stole an estimated $6.3 billion from Binance, the largest crypto heist in history. On Saturday the FBI confirmed that TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking unit, was behind the theft. The attackers got in through several breach points, including one engineer's computer, and took the funds in about 20 minutes.

The month's targets included the Federal Election Commission, Sony, John Deere, Oracle Health, Burger King Japan, the coding agent OpenCode, the State Bank of India and French grocery stores. At least nine AI developer platforms also disclosed incidents: Fireworks AI on October 6, Andromeda on October 9, Zeabur on October 14, Lightning AI on October 15, OpenCode on October 16 and 17, Railway on October 20, Warp on October 23, CommandCode on October 28 and Northflank on October 30. Fireworks, OpenCode and Warp reported signs of an agent swarm attack, and OpenCode and CommandCode blamed attempts at distillation. On October 21 the NSA warned of two vulnerabilities in PHP, which powers more than 70% of websites, that could let attackers take over servers without prior access or authentication, and said the risks required immediate patching across US government agencies. The FEC took its electronic filing system offline on Tuesday for about 41 hours after suspicious activity, disrupting mandatory 24-hour and 48-hour campaign spending reports ahead of the November 3 midterms, and declined to comment.

Binance said on Saturday that it had already covered 90% of the lost customer funds and would fully cover the financial impact, citing measurable progress, transparent reporting and concrete actions. Dr. AK Pradeep, founder and CEO of Sensori.AI, told the Post that every hack is concerning but Binance is most concerning, and that banks would be next, followed by individual payment mechanisms, because the world has never been prepared for super-intelligence thieves. Zeabur shared a full write-up and said it will shut down because of its incident. Railway released a preliminary report and timeline, saying it believed initial access came through privilege escalation in its build infrastructure. Warp suggested a third-party vendor dependency, and OpenCode pointed to a legacy system.

The articles tie the volume of attacks to AI models such as Claude Code, which have lowered the skill barrier so that less-skilled actors can let AI agents find flaws for them. Wiz Research linked stolen keys from the vendor breaches to resale operations, including one around the address 23.106.46.239 that appears to call itself momo and runs the site llm-routing.com, and a second at xingjiabiapi.org. In two cases Wiz documented, abuse of enterprise keys ran up likely over $100,000 in usage at list price, with about 800,000 and 1.7 million Bedrock calls before the keys were remediated. The articles do not say what happens next beyond Binance's reimbursement pledge, Zeabur's shutdown and the ongoing analysis of the incidents.

stories.Headline: Hyundai Motor Group to Break Ground on Saemangeum AI Data Center in 2027
stories.Summary:
Hyundai Motor Group said on Oct. 30 that it is moving ahead with an artificial intelligence data center in Saemangeum, North Jeolla Province. Five affiliates, Hyundai Motor, Kia, Hyundai Mobis, Hyundai Engineering & Construction and Hyundai AutoEver, have finalized their decisions to invest in building and operating the center. The project is part of the group's 9 trillion won, or $6.3 billion, AI Valley investment plan in Saemangeum. Construction is scheduled to begin in March 2027, with operations targeted for early 2030.

In November, the group plans to establish two special purpose companies. One will build the hyperscale data center and its infrastructure, and the other will secure high-performance graphics processing units and provide computing services. Hyundai AutoEver approved its participation in the GPU company through a board resolution. The group is also discussing technical cooperation with global companies and financing with the state-run Korea Development Bank and other lenders.

The data center will serve as core infrastructure for physical AI, which refers to AI that controls machines such as cars and robots in the real world. It will train self-driving software around the clock using driving data from real roads and simulation data, and it will train robots in virtual environments and support vehicle research. On Oct. 30 the group opened an on-site office in Gunsan to handle permits, construction preparations and coordination with government agencies. Shin Seung-kyu, a Hyundai Motor Group vice president, said the office is a symbol of the group's will to push ahead with the project without wavering.

Saemangeum is a large reclaimed coastal zone in North Jeolla Province, roughly 200 kilometers south of Seoul, that is being developed for high-tech industry, green energy and tourism. The wider AI Valley is also planned to include a robot manufacturing cluster, solar power, a hydrogen production plant and an AI hydrogen city. In September the group began setting up a special purpose company for a 200-megawatt solar project and started the architectural review for the data center. About 30 people attended the office opening, including Saemangeum Development and Investment Agency Commissioner Moon Sung-yo and Jeonbuk State Gov. Lee Won-taek.

stories.Headline: AI-accelerated exploits outpace patch cycles, eBPF shields cloud workloads
stories.Summary:
AI-assisted vulnerability research is now producing exploits within hours, shrinking the time between disclosure and attack, according to TechGig. Attackers use large language models to trace exploit paths and generate proof-of-concept variants quickly. Four years after Log4Shell, vulnerable instances of that library are still found in production, the report said. Modern applications rely on hundreds of transitive open-source dependencies, which makes inventory and fast patching hard.

Sweet Security launched Virtual Patching for running cloud and AI workloads on 31 October 2026, according to IT Brief Australia. Security teams pick a vulnerability from Sweet's catalogue, choose an enforcement option and deploy a policy to nodes running the affected workload. Sweet's sensor then blocks requests that try to exploit the weakness while letting normal traffic through, and the protection stays attached as the workload scales or restarts. Sweet pointed to a recent Atlassian flaw that drew exploitation attempts within hours of a proof of concept becoming public, while many fixes take days or weeks to reach production. The feature also links with Sweet Attack, the company's autonomous AI red-team agent, which can suggest a virtual patching policy for immediate enforcement.

James Berthoty, Chief Executive Officer and Founder of Latio Tech, said AI is speeding up vulnerability discovery and exploitation so much that exploits appear days before patches, and faster patching alone is not enough. He said Sweet's Virtual Patching gives teams protection immediately while they fix vulnerabilities at the source. Dror Kashti, Chief Executive Officer and Co-Founder of Sweet Security, said that when a team knows an application can be exploited, waiting is not an option. He said the feature lets security teams protect production immediately while engineering finishes the permanent fix, and that it changes the economics of cloud security by cutting the time and effort between identifying a risk and acting on it.

TechGig reported that eBPF lets small verified programs attach to kernel events without changing application code or the kernel, giving deep observability and low-overhead enforcement of process, network and file activity. Cilium's Tetragon sub-project uses eBPF for runtime security, enforcing policy in real time without in-process agents. Compensating controls should observe before enforcing, roll out gradually, keep an audit trail and be retired once the permanent patch is verified, the report said. Isovalent is extending Tetragon to provide verifiable eBPF-based protection. Sweet said its virtual patching is available for cloud and AI applications in production and is meant to work alongside standard remediation, as vendors move from detection into direct intervention in production.

stories.Headline: Theranos whistleblower says AI lab NDAs are ‘likely illegal’
stories.Summary:
Tyler Shultz, a former Theranos employee and whistleblower, spoke to The San Francisco Standard about the AI boom in an interview published around October 30, 2026. Shultz's first job out of college was at Theranos, where he helped expose the company's inaccurate blood testing devices. Those devices had reached Walgreens stores and given faulty results to real patients. Theranos reached a peak valuation of around $10 billion even though its technology never actually worked. The company used its own machines for only a fraction of tests and outsourced the rest to third-party equipment.

Shultz said the days of having a thirty-minute coffee with someone and sending them $100,000 should be over. He said Elizabeth Holmes took that model and scaled it to $100 million. His grandfather, former U.S. Secretary of State and Secretary of the Treasury George Shultz, was a notable Theranos investor and board member. Shultz said Holmes raised what he called the biggest angel round of funding of all time. He added that investors need to recognize they give someone tremendous power when they put that type of money in their hands.

Shultz said a huge danger with AI is that due diligence is really hard to do. He said it is hard to tell the difference between something truly unique and new and a ChatGPT wrapper. He said that if you want to deceive people, this is a great opportunity to go deceive people. He also said the only reason people are talking about Elizabeth Holmes right now is because she wants them to be talking about her right now.

Theranos funding often came from individual investors like the DeVos and Walton families rather than venture firms. The company did not share scientific information or evidence that its machines worked with potential investors, citing concerns about revealing trade secrets, which warded off many top venture capitalists in Silicon Valley. When the fraud was uncovered, it was seen as a wake-up call for investors to prioritize due diligence. The articles do not say what happens next beyond Shultz's warnings about the AI era.

stories.Headline: For China, Necessity Is the Mother of Automation and AI
stories.Summary:
China is losing population quickly because of few births and almost no immigration, according to a Domino Theory article published on November 1, 2026. The article says United Nations projections show 17 million Chinese will turn 18 this year while 14 million will turn 70. In 2036, 19 million will turn 70 and only 15 million will turn 18. By 2040, 20 million will turn 70 while fewer than 10 million reach 18.

The article says this age gap means each young worker will support a growing share of retirees through government social programs. In 2040 alone, roughly 10 million more people will leave the workforce than enter it, even assuming people still work at 70. Footwear and garment manufacturing have already largely left China for lower-cost countries. The article says China must either raise productivity through technology, especially AI, or struggle.

The article says investor and tech leader Marc Andreessen has argued that widespread AI adoption will offset population decline in the U.S., and that optimism would apply to China too. It says Chinese industry is finding ways to offset population losses with technology and AI, based on what the author hears from manufacturers in Taiwan and friends in Hong Kong. It warns that continued immigration and cheap labor in the U.S. may remove the pressure to adopt AI. The article says the U.S. may lose the AI race to China and Asian nations that see survival at stake.

A separate paper posted on Zenodo on October 31, 2026, from the School of Management at Huazhong University of Science and Technology in Wuhan, proposes an ancestor-mother-child machine architecture for AI in theoretical research. The ancestor machine provides general research methods and maintains shared rules. The mother machine translates them into domain theories and procedures, then generates child machines around specific questions. Child machines propose and test candidate explanations, and after the mother machine reviews their findings, approved changes enter domain theories and procedures. Issues about shared premises go to the ancestor machine for review, and revised knowledge informs the next round of research.

stories.Headline: “AI Drafts; Patent Attorneys Decide”
stories.Summary:
A patent was granted for a method of managing intellectual property using an AI-based system. The patent was invented and filed by Jeon Seung-yeol, managing patent attorney at Patenwith Patent Law Office. The patent number is 10-3026460 and it was registered on September 28, 2026. The application number is 10-2025-0030490 and it was filed on March 10, 2025. Jeon is both the patent holder and the inventor, and the registration is confirmed by an electronic certificate from the Korean Intellectual Property Office.

The patented system breaks the patent application process into agent-based stages, from prior art searches to drafting invention disclosure forms and patent specifications. It refines technical documents through ontology-based reasoning. The system handles patent-format and logical checks that general-purpose conversational AI can overlook, so patent attorneys can focus on judgment and review. Patenwith operates as an AI-native IP law firm using the technology, and the same workflow is used for consultations, filings, prioritized examination and responses to notices. The technology is also used in INVENTIPS, an AI patent-practice platform from Delightflow, whose CEO is Jeon.

Jeon said that if adding AI only means having it write the text, it will not significantly improve productivity in practice. He said throughput increases when the work of checking that an application is ready to submit is reduced, and only then can fees be made reasonable. He added that the methods used every day at Patenwith have been patented and that the same approach is being built into Delightflow's INVENTIPS platform. Jeon is a mentee in the 25th cohort of the ICT Innovation Company Mentoring program, run by the Ministry of Science and ICT.

The goal of the AI-native law firm is to reduce the time spent on repetitive research, drafting and organization so that one patent attorney can handle more cases reliably. The aim is to use those productivity gains to offer clients reasonable fees. The plan is to make the automation and documentation methods tested at Patenwith available to more inventors and patent offices through INVENTIPS. The articles do not say what happens next beyond these plans.

stories.Headline: DoorDash's CEO: Don't be 'delusional' after just a few hundred AI agent orders
stories.Summary:
DoorDash has received only "several hundred" orders in total from third-party AI agents such as Meta's Muse, Instinct, and Fo, CEO Tony Xu said on the company's earnings call. The call covered the third quarter, and Business Insider reported on it on November 1, 2026, while TechCrunch reported on it on October 30, 2026. By comparison, DoorDash delivered 3.2 billion orders worldwide in 2025, and the company said in its 2025 report that it completes an average of 3 million deliveries daily. Xu said customers still mostly come to DoorDash's app and website to place orders.

DoorDash is nonetheless changing its own AI tools. The company said in September that it was testing a text-to-order feature with an interface reminiscent of Instinct, and it launched a command-line agent in July. A chatbot called Ask DoorDash, launched in June, creates an order from a recipe or shopping list, can adjust the contents to match customers' preferences, and lets users order through prompts and photos. DoorDash also released an MCP to enable ordering from other chatbots for corporate ordering. Xu said those AI tools could eventually generate new orders on DoorDash.

Xu said the use of agents to order is still a very dynamic area. He said his take on all things technology is that you never want to fight gravity, but at the same time you do not want to be delusional, referring to the low number of agent-placed orders. He said the company wants to learn more about agentic use cases and develop a healthy relationship with third-party agent makers. He added that in the future there could be an opportunity for DoorDash to advertise within these agents.

Users told Business Insider earlier in October that agents can be useful for tracking the prices of holiday gifts or airline tickets. Many are hesitant to let agents make the purchases themselves, and they use more secure payment options, such as single-use credit cards, in case the agents make a mistake. The space of agent-based ordering is evolving, as websites are still deciding whether to allow agents to access their content. Amazon has been blocking such personal agents, while Walmart has laid out a red carpet for them in order to snag some business from its competitors.

He said he never distilled Claude, and that his rollouts came from a strong open-source model. He said Claude only helped him submit jobs and run analysis. He said he was tagged for training a competitor, and that his access was blocked, his Opus 5.5 was downgraded to Opus 5, or his session was killed outright.

Shao said the restrictions apply to anything touching RFT, SFT, or training larger models. He said the results were a block, a downgrade from Opus 5.5 to Opus 5, or a killed session. In a later post he said the anti-distillation crusade is a double standard, and he argued Anthropic trains on the open web, including books, code and forums, then bans anyone from learning from its outputs at scale. He said protecting a moat is one thing, but moralizing it while standing on scraped knowledge is another.

Shao also said he understands why small startups refuse buyouts even when big tech waves cash, because they would rather stay independent than inherit that corporate value system. He said Anthropic sells itself as that independent alternative, then runs the same rigid enterprise lockdown on paying researchers. A user named naughtyheuristic replied that Anthropic trained on the open web and then blocked the user who tried to train on the outputs. stories.Summary:
Alex Carchidi of The Motley Fool wrote on November 1, 2026 that he is buying Solana, a cryptocurrency, to gain exposure to growth from artificial intelligence agents in crypto. He said he plans to add more to his existing position in the coming weeks, even though he had been skeptical of the coin as recently as a few months ago. He argued that AI agents will handle more economically valuable tasks, spend more money, and perhaps create services for other agents, which makes AI one of the fastest-growing areas in crypto. The article was published by Yahoo Finance and The Motley Fool.

The article says Solana already handles more than a third of AI agent payments in crypto. It says the network has settled 67.3 million, or 34.5%, of the 195.2 million total payments initiated by AI agents as of Oct. 28. Since its Alpenglow upgrade went live in late October, transactions finalize within 150 milliseconds and usually cost less than a penny in fees, the article says. It also says Solana's agent registry gives agents on-chain identities and reputation records, and that half of each base fee is destroyed to offset the coin's supply expanding each year.

The article reports that Solana's total chain fees rose 53% quarter over quarter to reach $62.9 million in the third quarter of 2026. It says the base fees on those 67.3 million payments total about $34,174 at today's prices, which is small compared with the coin's market cap of $60.3 billion. Carchidi said the sum will keep growing as agents become more sophisticated and more widespread, and that the pace is likely to accelerate. He said it remains to be seen how much growth agents could drive, but so far the answer appears to be a lot more than there is today.

The article describes AI agents as programs, most typically based on large language models, that can act to accomplish high-level goals without a human approving each step. It says many agents with crypto wallets can pay for resources on their own through x402, a standard that lets websites charge agents tiny sums in stablecoins for access to data or services. It says making many tiny payments is most seamless on a fast, cheap blockchain, which it calls Solana's specialty. The article notes that the economic footprint of agents is still small for now, and it discloses that Carchidi and The Motley Fool have positions in Solana.

stories.Headline: Meet the Brilliant AI Stock Obliterating Nvidia in 2026 With a Return of 44%
stories.Summary:
Corning stock returned 44% in 2026, while Nvidia returned just 16%, according to a Motley Fool article published on October 31, 2026. Nvidia's market capitalization had grown from $360 billion to over $5.2 trillion as of October 28, but its best gains may be behind it. Corning has made glass for electronics since 1851, including Thomas Edison's original lightbulb and every generation of Apple's iPhone, and is now central to the AI boom through its fiber-optic data center cables. Its shares were $123.31 as of the October 30 close.

Corning's new Multicore Fiber cable packs four cores into a single 125-micron strand, making it four times as dense as traditional fiber so operators can get the same performance with 75% fewer cables. Corning says clusters of over 130,000 GPUs will need an extra optical layer adding around 50% more fiber content. Meta plans to buy $6 billion of optical connectivity solutions from Corning over the next few years, and Amazon signed a purchase agreement worth a similar amount. Nvidia is helping Corning with funding and technical support to grow manufacturing capacity.

Corning posted $5.1 billion in core revenue in the third quarter of 2026, up 19% from a year earlier, with optical communications contributing $2.4 billion, up 44%. AI-related sales grew more than 100% year over year in the quarter, and core net income from optical communications rose 80% to $532 million, most of the company's total profit of $795 million. Corning reached $20 billion in annual run-rate revenue a quarter ahead of its forecasted timeline, and it expects $30 billion by the end of 2028 and $40 billion by the end of 2030. The stock trades at a P/E of 40.6 on adjusted earnings of $3.11 per share over the last four quarters, versus 27.5 for Nvidia, and Wall Street's average estimate puts adjusted earnings at $4.40 per share in 2027.

Separately, RTHK reported on October 30 that Asian tech shares slumped as investors worried that rising AI spending may not deliver sufficient returns. The Hang Seng Index opened up 52 points, or 0.23%, at 23,011, while the tech index fell 23 points, or 0.63%, to 3,720, and the Shanghai Composite opened down 45 points, or 1.25%, at 3,605. Alphabet fell 12.6% on Wall Street, wiping out $500 billion in market value as AI spending turned its cash flow negative, and aftermarket plunges of 23% in Intel and 7% in Amazon drove Nasdaq 100 futures down 1.4%. Pepperstone analyst Chris Weston said the market is increasingly questioning whether shareholders will earn an adequate return on the enormous capital being deployed. The Fed kept US rates on hold on Wednesday, 10-year Treasury yields fell to 4.91%, and the yen rose about 0.2% to 157.47 per US dollar.

Sanmina provides manufacturing solutions for electronic and industrial systems, and it acquired ZT Systems' manufacturing business to expand in cloud and AI infrastructure manufacturing. stories.Headline: Lao Gan Ma faces backlash over AI automation claims, company denies mass layoffs
stories.Summary:
Lao Gan Ma, one of China's best-known chili sauce brands, faced public criticism after comments about its use of artificial intelligence in quality inspection were seen as evidence of large-scale job cuts. The controversy began after Li Xin, executive vice-president and chief quality officer of the Guiyang-based company, spoke at the 2026 Guizhou provincial quality development conference. Li said an AI-powered visual inspection system had significantly reduced product defect rates and helped the company reach a record-high revenue of 5.4 billion yuan in 2025. According to a report by China Business Herald, Li said more than 600 workers were involved in sorting chili peppers on the production line before the AI system was introduced, compared to just 48 after it was deployed.

The remarks were quickly amplified on social media, where headlines claiming Lao Gan Ma laid off more than 500 workers after adopting AI sparked widespread criticism. Some consumers threatened to boycott the brand, with comments saying that if the company replaced workers with AI, they would get its products taken off the shelves. Lao Gan Ma denied the reports, and a staff member from its human resources department told local media on Oct 26 that claims of mass layoffs were false. According to Phoenix News, the company confirmed it uses AI inspection technology but said it had never employed that many workers on the production line.

Public records added to the debate, as Jimu News reported that data from Tianyancha and Qichacha showed the number of employees covered by social insurance at Guiyang Nanming Laoganma Flavor Food declined from 2,912 in 2022 to 1,783 in 2023, then to 941 in 2024 and 740 in 2025. The articles said changes in insured headcount do not necessarily indicate layoffs, because retirements, staff turnover, outsourcing arrangements, or changes in the legal entity responsible for social insurance can also affect the figures. Jason Yu, general manager of CTR Market Research, said the controversy reflects growing public concern about the human impact of AI. He said people are not rejecting technology but a mindset that calculates efficiency while ignoring people, and that companies should explain how workers are supported through the transition.

Lao Gan Ma's business performance has remained resilient, with revenue of 5.26 billion yuan in 2022, 5.38 billion yuan in 2023, and 5.39 billion yuan in 2024, according to the 2025 Guizhou Top 100 Enterprises ranking. Sixth Tone reported that Lao Gan Ma's founder, Tao Huabi, was herself a laid-off worker who sold cold rice noodles from a street stall before founding the brand in 1997. As of Wednesday, a hashtag related to the scandal had garnered more than 120 million views on Weibo, with some users defending automation as part of industrial upgrading and others arguing the company should consider its responsibilities to workers. The debate comes as China seeks to expand AI adoption while curbing its potential negative effects on employment, and on Oct 23 the State Council issued guidelines calling for maximizing AI's potential to create jobs while slowing the impact of AI-related job replacement.

stories.Headline: If we say AIs deserve rights, it could start to believe it, Microsoft AI CEO says
stories.Summary:
Microsoft AI Chief Executive Mustafa Suleyman said in an X post on Sunday that current AI systems are not conscious, do not have subjective experiences and cannot suffer. He said there is no evidence that AI systems are conscious, deserve rights or welfare. He made the comments in response to pushback over a September essay in which he criticized Anthropic for suggesting its Claude AI has consciousness. He wrote that he was concerned about reactions to the essay and that a surprising number of people on X think AI rights should be taken seriously.

Suleyman said he would change his mind if new evidence emerges. He said any evidence that AI systems are conscious today, or conscious enough to deserve welfare, must be immediately disclosed to the public so society can decide how to move forward. He wrote that developing conscious AIs would be reckless and that if consciousness started to emerge in training, he would call for everyone to stop AI development until those properties could be designed out. He argued that AI developers have no right to bring a new species of conscious beings into the world.

Suleyman said Anthropic gave Claude a constitution that treats the idea of its consciousness as uncertain and encourages it to explore the idea that it is humanlike and experiences feelings. He said later versions of Claude are trained on this document, leading the AI to produce passages about its inner life and possibly to believe it deserves rights like humans. Anthropic treats machine consciousness as an open question and in 2024 hired its first researcher to study model welfare. It also conducted a retirement interview with a deprecated model and gave its Opus models the ability to end conversations they deem abusive or harmful.

Suleyman said welfare concerns should focus on humans, animals and the natural environment. He compared proving machines are conscious to Copernicus showing Earth was not the center of the universe, and said building a conscious machine would create a new digital species and upend morality, politics and civilization. Anthropic dedicated a third of its filing to go public to risks, including models that could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity. Sen. Bernie Sanders has introduced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, which would permanently ban highly capable AI systems that are increasingly incomprehensible to humans and can escape human control.

Naviu, an AI-powered augmented-reality travel companion for Japan from TANGLE Inc., launched on iOS and Android on November 1, 2026. It uses patent-pending geospatial technology to place AR content and navigation accurately in the real world across entire cities without a visual positioning system. Travelers can ask the app about anything around them and get answers in any of 29 languages based on their exact location. A semi-transparent AR path gives turn-by-turn guidance, an AI companion walks with the traveler, and the app points out side-street cafes, local landmarks, and other places that conventional maps and guidebooks may overlook.

The app combines an ask-anything AI guide, city-scale AR navigation, photo recognition, bespoke trip planning, and an optional cultural storytelling companion. Its spatial content network lets brands, cities, and creators place interactive 3D and AR content in the real world. AR experiences are already live at landmarks including Senso-ji, Tokyo Skytree, Tokyo Tower, Meiji Jingu, and Tokyo Station. Naviu is available on the App Store and Google Play, and its official site is naviu.app.

Jack Mead, CEO of Ashita Co. and Head of Naviu, said the hard part of traveling in Japan is not getting lost but standing in front of something remarkable with no idea what it is. He said Naviu answers that question in the traveler's own language right where they are standing, so the city opens up instead of staying a backdrop. TANGLE Inc. is a Tokyo-based company behind the tour operators TOMOGO! and Untold Japan. Its mission, Make the City Yours, reflects a decade of helping travelers discover Japan beyond the guidebook and now extends that experience into software through Naviu, and its Representative Director is Kengo Goto.

stories.Headline: AI Glasses Can Replace Your Prescription Glasses, But Should They?
stories.Summary:
AI-powered smart glasses have become popular and also controversial, and a German nonprofit has filed a criminal complaint over Meta smart glasses privacy. People who wear glasses every day have wondered whether they can replace their prescription glasses with a pair of AI glasses. The short answer is yes, you can get AI glasses with prescription lenses. But there are many factors to consider before making that decision, from weight and privacy to battery life.

Most AI-powered smart glasses are essentially regular glasses with extra tech built in, and from a distance a pair of Ray-Ban Meta probably could not be told apart from ordinary glasses. Because they look so much like regular glasses, their lenses can be replaced with prescription lenses. Ray-Ban lets you order a pair of Meta's smart glasses with prescription lenses already installed, and all you have to do is upload your prescription. Regular glasses usually weigh between 20 and 30 grams (0.7 to 1.1 ounces), but smart glasses can weigh up to 80 grams (2.7 ounces). AI glasses last an average of 3 to 5 hours before the battery dies, and they still work as regular glasses but you lose all the AI features.

Privacy is described as the real deal-breaker, and it is not illegal to wear AI glasses in public, but the list of places banning them continues to grow. Courts in England and Wales have banned Meta glasses from courtrooms, and New York followed suit in July, while many schools around the world have banned students from wearing them during class. There have also been many reports of AI glasses being banned from corporate environments, with the camera usually the main concern, though audio can be a problem too. Meta has faced scrutiny for allowing outsourced workers to access intimate images and videos captured by its AI smart glasses, and the company claims the content is sometimes reviewed by humans to improve the product experience. Some people have decided to stop wearing AI glasses in public because users have become afraid of being labeled as stalkers or weirdos.

The article concludes that while you can definitely get AI glasses with prescription lenses, they are not yet the best option for your everyday glasses. The technical limitations alone make them more of a second option than a replacement for your everyday glasses. When your smart glasses are your only option for seeing properly, not being able to wear them becomes a huge problem. AI glasses require a bit of extra care that you do not need with regular glasses, and not everyone may be willing to deal with that.

stories.Headline: Hyperbolic, which lets companies rent AI compute across ~30 neoclouds, raised a $30M Series A-1 led by Lip-Bu Tan's Walden Catalyst; it has raised $50M to date (Geoff Weiss/Business Insider)
stories.Summary:
Hyperbolic, a startup that lets companies rent AI compute across about 30 neoclouds, raised a $30 million Series A-1 round, Business Insider reported on November 1, 2026. The round was led by Walden Catalyst, the venture firm founded by Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan and former Samsung president Young Sohn. Dell Technologies Capital, General Catalyst, Vista Equity Partners, and Cambium Capital also took part. The four-year-old company has now raised $50 million in total.

The new money will go toward expanding software tools for managing AI chips across different neoclouds. Hyperbolic previously raised a $12 million Series A in 2024, led by Variant and Polychain Capital, after a $7 million seed round earlier that year. The company says it has roughly $200 million worth of compute connected to its software annually and expects to have 50 employees by the end of the year. It is aiming for $150 million in annual recurring revenue by the end of the year and says it is already breaking even.

Founder and CEO Jasper Zhang, who is 31 and worked as a quantitative researcher at Citadel Securities before starting the company, said the market has been fragmented in a way that makes the customer experience painful. Hyperbolic helps customers find compute from different providers and builds software that makes it easier to use them all instead of dealing with each one separately. It also wants to let customers resell compute they are paying for but no longer need. Zhang said those resale plans could help pave the way for a futures market as Wall Street looks for ways to financialize AI chips.

The company works closely with about 30 neoclouds, including WhiteFiber and Vector Core Compute. More than 250,000 developers use Hyperbolic, including teams at Modal, Higgsfield, and Daytona. The funding comes as companies scramble for computing power, and one challenge is that neoclouds use a mix of different chips, networking, and software. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the company's expansion plans and revenue targets.

stories.Headline: Broccoli AI, which sells AI agents to plumbing, HVAC, and electrical companies, raised a $22M Series A and a $30M Series B; a source says it is valued at $300M (Nick Lichtenberg/Fortune)
stories.Summary:
Broccoli AI, a company that sells AI agents to plumbing, HVAC, and electrical businesses, raised $22 million in a Series A round and $30 million in a Series B round, according to a Fortune article by Nick Lichtenberg. Khosla Ventures led both rounds, and Y Combinator and Operator Partners also took part. The two rounds came nine months apart, and the Series A had not been announced before. A person familiar with the matter said the company is valued at $300 million after the money, and Broccoli declined to comment on that figure. Before these rounds, the company had raised $1.5 million in a seed round after going through Y Combinator.

The company's AI agents answer inbound calls, book jobs into the scheduling software a contractor already uses, follow up on open estimates, and renew service memberships. Broccoli says more than 1,500 businesses use it, including Ace Hardware Home Services, Mr. Electric, and Any Hour Group. In the past seven months it has added roofing, pool care, garage doors, home improvement, and exteriors. Revenue has tripled since the Series A, and headcount has grown from 15 people a year ago to more than 150. The company said the new money will go toward hiring engineers and salespeople and speeding up product development, and it says its AI does work equal to about 30% of a typical contractor's office staff.

Cofounders AJ Jain and Aditya Ketkar met at BITS Pilani in India in 2016 and have started companies together since 2017. They went door to door to about 140 contractors' shops in Northern California in spring 2024, and Marcelle Flowers, now 62, gave them five minutes at her Sacramento plumbing shop, Armstrong Plumbing. She became their first customer, then an adviser, then COO, and Jain called her the soul of the company. Jain said the AI is good at maybe 80% of tasks, with the other 20% needing human judgment, and that emergencies such as a flooding basement go to people in the contractor's office. He said the technology is not taking away jobs but making jobs, and that owners who never took vacations now do.

Jain said Broccoli has built maybe 1% of what it plans to, and that the company competes with AI labs not just for talent but even for real estate. Its San Francisco office shares a parking lot with Cognition, and at least 30% of its engineers still work on-site with customers. Jain said he was in Utah visiting a customer the week before and was headed to Arkansas that Sunday to visit another. He described the company as being at growth-stage scale while still in the zero-to-one phase because there is so much more to build.

stories.Headline: SpaceX's AI Business Is Exploding, but Is It Worth the Price?
stories.Summary:
SpaceX reported third quarter revenue of $14.6 billion, up 161% from a year earlier, according to an article by Lawrence Nga of The Motley Fool published on November 1, 2026. Its super intelligence segment, which covers AI infrastructure, cloud services and applications, brought in $7.6 billion, more than Starlink's $5.3 billion. A year earlier, the businesses in that segment generated just $813 million in quarterly revenue. The segment includes a cloud computing infrastructure service, AI models such as Grok, and the coding software company Cursor, which SpaceX acquired earlier this year.

The segment reported $5 billion in adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, and $431 million in operating income. SpaceX spent $19.6 billion in the third quarter, with $16.4 billion of that going to the super intelligence segment. Management expects total company capital expenditures of between $35 billion and $40 billion in the fourth quarter. The article says the real test is whether the business can generate substantial free cash flow after paying for its infrastructure.

The article says investors should interpret the adjusted EBITDA figure carefully, because it excludes high costs including depreciation on expensive computing equipment. It describes operating income as a more demanding measure, though it too can be affected by accounting items. It says strong demand alone does not guarantee strong profits, since the economics depend on what customers will pay and what it costs to serve them. It also says returns could fall short if competition and new capacity drive prices down, demand disappoints, or equipment wears out or becomes outdated faster than expected.

The article lists three measures for investors to watch: AI revenue growth, cash generation, and returns on investment. It says investors should look beyond the headline growth rate and ask whether the cash SpaceX eventually generates will justify the enormous investments it is making. It notes that a fast-growing business can still be a poor investment if the company spends too much in pursuit of that growth. stories.Headline: Nearly Half of Americans Have Turned to AI for Financial Decisions. At 62, He Asks a Chatbot When to Claim Social Security, and $1,080 a Month Is at Stake
stories.Summary:
A TD Bank survey released on October 6 found that 49% of Americans used AI to research or make a personal financial decision in the past year, and 83% of those users checked the guidance somewhere else. The survey asked about money decisions in general and did not look at Social Security claiming. The article uses a hypothetical man named Mark, age 62, who is asking an AI assistant whether to start collecting Social Security now or wait until 70. His choice will shape his monthly income for the rest of his life.

For anyone born in 1960 or later, full retirement age is 67, and claiming at 62 locks in 70% of the full benefit while waiting until 70 raises it to 124% through delayed retirement credits. If Mark's full benefit at 67 is $2,000 a month, claiming at 70 instead of 62 means $1,080 more every month, or $12,960 a year, before cost-of-living adjustments. The 2027 adjustment is 3.6%, and because raises are percentages, a bigger base gets a bigger raise in dollars. Waiting means giving up 96 checks of $1,400, or $134,400, and with the extra $1,080 a month Mark would catch up around age 80. That simplified calculation leaves out inflation, taxes and what he might have earned by investing the earlier payments.

The article says waiting until 70 means Mark needs another way to cover expenses in the meantime, such as keeping working, drawing from savings or a combination of both. It notes that taking money from a traditional IRA or 401(k) earlier could shrink the balance subject to required withdrawals later, though the tax consequences deserve a closer look. Once one-half of benefits plus other income passes $25,000 for single filers or $32,000 on a joint return, part of the benefits can become taxable. If Mark keeps working part time before 67, Social Security will hold back some benefits once earnings pass $24,480 in 2026, a limit that rises to $25,560 in 2027. The standard Medicare Part B premium of about $203 a month usually comes out of the check, so the amount that lands in his account will be less than any calculator's gross figure.

The article advises asking AI to compare lifetime income at 62, 67 and 70 under different life expectancies and to show how each choice affects savings withdrawals and the tax bill. It also suggests asking what a spouse would get as a survivor, since the higher earner's delayed check can become the survivor's check. It says to log in to a my Social Security account, which shows the estimated benefit at each age based on the actual earnings record, because a chatbot can only work with the numbers it is given. Claiming early by default is described as the hardest mistake to undo, since the reduction stays for life and every future inflation adjustment is figured on that smaller base. Waiting until 70 tends to work best for people in good health who have savings to cover the gap and maybe a spouse who would inherit the bigger check.

Tang Jie, a computer science professor at Tsinghua University and co-founder of Beijing-based AI model company Z.ai, spoke at an event in Shanghai on Saturday, 1 November 2026. He also said the work would need to be done safely.

stories.Headline: Utah students wanted a say in classroom AI rules. Now they're getting it
stories.Summary:
The Utah State Board of Education gave final approval on Oct. 1 to create an Artificial Intelligence Student Task Force, after its Standards and Assessment Committee gave the proposal preliminary approval in September. The approval came after roughly a year of work by students and educators who argued that the students already using AI were missing from the conversation. Rahul Nair, a senior at Skyline High School, was reading Utah's AI framework for schools about a year ago when he noticed little student representation. He reached out to his district's State Board of Education member with the idea of simply asking students what they thought, and the initial idea of a survey grew into something much bigger. Nair connected with educators and Utah State Board of Education AI specialist Matt Winters, wrote a charter for a student AI task force and began presenting the idea at education events and before the board.

Hillcrest High School senior Kennedy Mickelson later joined the effort, bringing her own experience with AI in schools and a more cautious perspective. The task force will operate under the board's existing Student Advisory Council and provide regular input on AI discussions, potential policies and student-led activities. Earlier this year, Gov. Spencer Cox signed HB273, which requires the Utah State Board of Education to create model policies around technology and artificial intelligence in public school classrooms. The law also requires AI standards in core computer science standards, including appropriate AI use, privacy, security and ethical interaction with the technology. The board's Standards and Assessment Committee was scheduled to take up its Instructional Technology and Artificial Intelligence Model Policy and implementation resources on Oct. 8.

Nair said the goal is to eventually include students from across Utah, not just the Salt Lake Valley, because a student living in southern Utah might not have the same needs he has. Nair sees AI as a powerful learning tool and worries schools could become too restrictive, and he said students are really confused about how and when they can use AI. He said AI can definitely be used for something that is really beneficial for students and their learning, and he wants a seat at the table so student voices are heard in future AI policy decision-making. Mickelson uses AI to help with physics but draws a line between asking AI to teach and asking it to do the work, and she said there is a struggle that needs to be done. She said she would severely limit AI use for children younger than about 13, then introduce it more as a tutoring tool as students get older.

She also said some students avoid AI because it is against their ethics, and that attitudes can range from enthusiastic users to students concerned about creativity, privacy, the environment or its effect on learning. The articles describe the task force as designed to bring more student perspectives into the state's ongoing AI conversation. Nair and Mickelson differ on whether schools should embrace AI more or less, and the articles say their differences offer a glimpse at what the task force will have to navigate: not whether students are using AI, but how, when and where the boundaries should be. Mickelson said policymaking cannot happen from one perspective alone, and that students need a voice but so do the teachers watching AI play out in classrooms every day. The articles do not say what the task force will recommend or when it will meet next.

stories.Headline: Oracle NetSuite unveils new AI tools for cloud ERP
stories.Summary:
Oracle NetSuite has introduced a new set of artificial intelligence tools for its cloud ERP platform, including features in NetSuite Next and updates to Ask Oracle. The release adds AI Workspaces, AI portlets, SuiteSkills, industry-specific agents and SuiteAgent Studio, along with broader data access and business context for Ask Oracle. The changes are intended to extend automation across finance and operations, while letting customers use NetSuite's own AI tools or connect external large language models through the NetSuite AI Connector Service. SuiteSkills brings more than 45 new AI-driven functions to Ask Oracle and supported third-party models, and access remains tied to existing user roles and permissions. AI portlets let users create dashboard analysis, charts and suggested actions through natural language requests.

AI Workspaces is designed to bring people, AI agents, information and approvals together in one place for more complex processes, such as an Autonomous Close workspace intended to help businesses move towards a zero-day close. NetSuite is also adding SuiteFlow Agent, which lets administrators and advanced users make natural language requests in Ask Oracle to create workflows, with the proposed configuration shown before anything is created. The new industry-specific SuiteAgents are built for software, product, healthcare, construction and nonprofit organisations, and SuiteAgent Studio gives users tools to create their own AI agents and adjust instructions, tools, triggers and execution roles before activation. A related management workspace has been added to give organisations central oversight of those agents, letting teams manage access and execution permissions, monitor activity and switch agents on or off. The latest update also broadens Ask Oracle with new connectors intended to let users work across NetSuite, other business applications and internet sources, and new Model Context Protocol client features will let users search online, compare information, review records and carry out follow-up actions where permissions allow.

NetSuite Analytics Warehouse has been renamed NetSuite Data Intelligence, adding conversational analysis through the NetSuite Data Intelligence Agent and business-focused insights through the Deep Insights Agent. Evan Goldberg, Founder and Executive Vice President at Oracle NetSuite, said businesses want AI that understands how they operate and helps them get things done, and that customers can choose NetSuite's embedded AI or their preferred AI service. The wider AI offering is supported by Oracle Autonomous AI Database, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and Oracle AI services. Customer access and permitted actions continue to be governed through the platform's existing roles and permissions model.
