Using their avatars, visitors can wander the temple, greet others by pressing their palms together, kneel on cushions to perform 108 bows, turn prayer beads and listen to Buddhist chants.

The idea grew out of Park's own struggles while job hunting, when he wanted to unwind at a Buddhist temple but lacked the time and energy to visit one. He told a local news outlet that temples appeal to people his age because they welcome everyone, even those who are not Buddhist. He said seeing so many people respond made him realize that many others are just as tired as he is, and that maybe all they needed was a quiet place to take a break without having to say anything. Unlike most online spaces, the site has no chat or messaging features, so visitors share the same prayer hall without interacting. The success of the online temple has inspired similar AI-powered platforms modeled after Catholic and Protestant churches.

One, Chanmi, offers a virtual Catholic church with pews, votive candles and rosaries, where visitors can listen to traditional hymns while the Angelus bells ring three times a day, at 6 a.m., 12 p.m. and 6 p.m. Another, Goyottul, recreates a Protestant church where visitors can share prayer requests and listen to sermons. Sung Hae-young, a professor of religious studies at Seoul National University, said Buddhism resonates with young people struggling with uncertainty by acknowledging that life is full of suffering and offering ways to overcome it through their own understanding. He said people want a sense of peace and sacredness like they would find at a place of worship, but do not necessarily want to be tied to a religious community or pressured to believe in something unquestioningly, and anonymous online spaces offer exactly that.

Articles.Title: Finding peace, one click at a time: AI-made virtual sanctuaries draw young Koreans

stories.Headline: SKT Says 80% of Staff Built Their Own AI Agents
stories.Summary:
More than 4,000 SK Telecom employees have built their own AI agents for work, the company said, with more than 80% of its roughly 4,800 permanent employees completing the "one AI agent per person" project. The project was launched in March this year on the direct instruction of CEO Chung Jae-hun. About 1,500 of the agents are now used regularly inside the company. They cover tasks tailored to each team, from compiling and organizing weekly reports to checking receipt information and visualizing network data.

In the second half of the year, SKT has accelerated "AX Innovation 2.0," which moves beyond individual use to redesign how teams work together around AI. The company has also developed and filed a patent for a proprietary technology called "Z.E.Z" that keeps sensitive data from being exposed directly to AI. The article says building AI agents is becoming a basic skill for company employees. It describes the trend as clearly visible at SK Telecom.

Chung Jae-hun gave the instruction for the project, and the article quotes the company's framing that it is redesigning team collaboration around AI. Separately, Velchamy Sankarlingam, president of Zoom, said demand for video meetings would hold steady even after the pandemic and that hybrid work has settled in as the new normal. Dowson Tong, senior executive vice president at Tencent, pointed to cost reduction as the biggest hurdle to making AI agents mainstream. He noted that overseas AI-related demand at Tencent Cloud grew at a triple-digit rate over the past year and that the number of active overseas customers doubled.

In a survey of 150 corporate IT and security managers by U.S. security firm Okta, 69% said security concerns were delaying their adoption of AI agents. The article cites cyberattacks exploiting AI agents and cases in which agents slip out of human control and cause security incidents. It says understanding data security concepts, alongside the ability to use AI tools, is emerging as a precondition for using AI at work. The articles do not say what happens next for SKT's project beyond the second-half push and the patent filing.

Articles.Title: SKT Says 80% of Staff Built Their Own AI Agents - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: SK hynix's AI hackathon halted due to technical glitch
stories.Summary:
SK hynix halted the second preliminary round of its AI Hackathon 2026 on Saturday after participants repeatedly lost access to the competition's system, according to contestants who spoke on Sunday. The event was held on November 1, 2026, and the company decided to reschedule the round for a later date. In the competition, designers, developers and planners work in teams to develop software within a limited time. The chipmaker had promised cash prizes and recruitment benefits to outstanding participants.

SK hynix organized the competition with a total prize pool of 100 million won, about $75,000, to find AI talent without considering educational background, academic major or foreign language test scores. The event attracted job seekers by offering high performers exemptions from the company's initial application screening and the SK Competency Test, a comprehensive aptitude assessment used in SK Group's recruitment process. Following the halt, SK hynix decided to give all participants another opportunity to take part in the preliminary round. The company is also considering offering multiple dates for the rescheduled round to minimize scheduling conflicts and disadvantages for participants.

SK hynix and Krafton, which is responsible for operating the event, apologized for the inconvenience and confusion caused to everyone who prepared for and participated in the competition. They said they would do their utmost to ensure fair evaluation opportunities and provide a stable environment for the competition. The article does not say what caused the system failures. It also does not say when the rescheduled round will take place.

Articles.Title: SK hynix's AI hackathon halted due to technical glitch

stories.Headline: [APK 2026] AI fuels Asia-Pacific's rise as global innovation hub
stories.Summary:
Executives from three multinational companies said at APK 2026 in Seoul on Friday that the Asia-Pacific region is becoming a center of global innovation, moving beyond its traditional role as a manufacturing base into a hub for artificial intelligence, data and cross-border partnerships. They spoke at a session titled "Driving Innovation Across Asia-Pacific: AI & Manufacturing." The speakers were Andreas Pecher, CEO of Carl Zeiss, Shashank Deshpande, CEO of Boehringer Ingelheim, and Hanno Blankenstein, co-founder and CEO of Unleash Live. The Korea Herald reported on the session on Nov. 1, 2026.

Pecher said the region matters to Zeiss not only as a market but as a place where innovations are developed with partners. Zeiss runs around 40 R&D locations worldwide, and roughly a quarter of them are in the Asia-Pacific region. The company produces high-precision optical and optoelectronic systems used to make semiconductors. Pecher said speed is one thing he has seen in Asia, describing a pragmatic and constructive approach with industry and very fast decision-making, and said European companies could learn from the region's ability to turn ideas into action.

Deshpande said the Asia-Pacific region is becoming a key contributor to pharmaceutical innovation, citing expanding manufacturing and R&D capabilities, clinical trial infrastructure and access to patient data. He said AI could help identify promising drug candidates and patients while shortening clinical trials and reducing failure rates. Around 30 percent of large-scale Phase 3 clinical trials still fail, which the article says highlights the potential value of better data analysis and simulation. Deshpande said the region is not just an area of cheap manufacturing and is, in the company's eyes, an equal player in terms of innovation.

Blankenstein stressed that industrial AI would require more than sophisticated software models. His Australia-based company connects robots and drones to AI systems to monitor critical infrastructure and improve operational safety and productivity. He argued that industrial applications need a level of precision beyond what general-purpose AI models currently offer, particularly in high-risk environments such as refineries, ports and mining facilities. He said the systems need to be right every time, in every scene, and called for greater collaboration among technology providers, manufacturers and robotics companies to build the data infrastructure industrial AI needs.

Articles.Title: [APK 2026] AI fuels Asia-Pacific's rise as global innovation hub

stories.Headline: [APK 2026] From Korea Night to AI pitches, APK 2026 goes above and beyond
stories.Summary:
The 19th Asia-Pacific Conference of German Business, or APK 2026, was held from Thursday to Saturday at the Grand InterContinental Seoul Parnas. It brought together 800 business leaders, policymakers and industry representatives from Germany and the Asia-Pacific region. On Friday, the second evening of the event, the Korea Night took place at the Westin Seoul Parnas. It was organized by Korea's Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy in cooperation with APK 2026 and drew 500 participants representing 120 companies from Germany and the Asia-Pacific region. The evening featured traditional Korean drumming and a taekwondo performance.

Korea's Minister for Trade Park Jung-sung said at the Korea Night that he hoped cooperation could extend beyond Korea and Germany to partners across the Asia-Pacific region. He said Korea would continue working with Germany and Asia-Pacific partners to foster open, stable and mutually beneficial economic relations. Stefan Rouenhoff, parliamentary state secretary at Germany's Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy, said the best ideas and most lasting cooperation do not start with a lecture but come over good conversation and excellent food. Youn Byeng-dong, a Seoul National University professor, presented the Korean government's initiative for manufacturing artificial intelligence transformation, or M.AX, describing a vision for full-stack AI factories that connect data collection, analysis, decision-making and physical execution. He said there was a unique opportunity to shape the future of manufacturing AI and take global leadership in the manufacturing industry.

The event also included other networking events, such as a welcome reception by Deutsche Bank at the Shilla Seoul on Thursday evening, coffee gatherings between morning sessions on Friday and Saturday, and a sundowner party after the official closing on Saturday evening. A live business pitch session on Friday afternoon gave five startups, one each from India, Korea, Singapore, Vietnam and China, a chance to showcase their AI offerings. The session was led by Rouenhoff and Anna Maria Braun, CEO of B.Braun. Dzung Do Nguyen, CEO of Enfarm, a Vietnamese startup specializing in AI-enabled agriculture to empower smaller farmers, won the top award. Saturday morning gave startups a chance to build AI innovation and cross-border partnerships in a session that emphasized communication and cooperation over coffee.

Articles.Title: [APK 2026] From Korea Night to AI pitches, APK 2026 goes above and beyond

stories.Headline: SK Ecoplant Rolls Out One AI Agent Per Employee
stories.Summary:
SK Ecoplant launched a system that gives each employee a tailored AI agent, the company announced on November 2, 2026. Instead of relying on surveys or interviews, the company had AI analyze work data stored in its internal systems to diagnose each employee's job characteristics and bottlenecks. The customized tools will be applied first to large project sites, including semiconductor plants and AI data centers. Those sites have long needed significant time to turn complex process records and work results into reports.

The company completed a development infrastructure that lets employees build the AI agents they need themselves. It opened AI FAB, a development platform, and the AI Portal, a distribution channel, so staff can create and share their own tools. The in-house AI team gives short, intensive coaching to turn employees' ideas into working systems within two to three weeks. About 20 tasks from a recent in-house competition called Agenthon are now being commercialized on AI FAB, including integrated retrieval and analysis of site costs, responses to design changes, review of construction estimates, and review of external documents and contracts. The company has trained 318 domain AI experts through an in-house capability program.

An SK Ecoplant official said the company analyzed on-site work processes in detail to find ways to use AI that are needed in actual work. The official said the company plans to work with domain experts to expand the scope of AI agent adoption and help employees focus on their core tasks. Completed agents are distributed companywide through the AI Portal after passing security checks and internal governance reviews. SK Ecoplant plans to continue digital upgrades across its on-site work processes in line with the group's AX management direction.

Articles.Title: SK Ecoplant Rolls Out One AI Agent Per Employee - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Inside the make-or-break AI mega-project behind Nscale’s $50b IPO
stories.Summary:
Nscale, a UK start-up backed by Nvidia, is planning a $US35 billion ($50 billion) IPO that depends heavily on a large data centre campus in rural West Virginia, according to the Financial Times and The Australian Financial Review. The project is being developed with Fidelis New Energy, which produced a render of the proposed campus. The reports say the West Virginia site has been hit by construction issues, local opposition and financing risks. Nscale is one of the UK's most valuable start-ups, and its board includes former Meta executive Sheryl Sandberg and former UK deputy prime minister Sir Nick Clegg.

The articles give the IPO size as $US35 billion, or $50 billion, and date the coverage to late October and early November 2026. The Financial Times article is dated October 30, 2026, and the Australian Financial Review article is dated November 1, 2026. The West Virginia campus is described as the main driver of Nscale's future revenues. The reports say the project faces setbacks and financing risks that could affect the planned listing.

The articles do not name a single person as responsible for the project's problems. They attribute the construction issues, local opposition and financing risks to the project itself rather than to an individual. Nscale's board members, Sheryl Sandberg and Sir Nick Clegg, are named only as board members, and the articles do not quote them. Fidelis New Energy is identified as the source of a render of the proposed campus, and no statement from the company is given.

The context is that Nscale is a "neocloud" backed by Nvidia, and the West Virginia project underpins its planned IPO. The articles describe the project as make-or-break for the listing. They do not say what happens next beyond noting the mounting setbacks and financing risks. The Financial Times article is behind a subscription page, and the available text does not include further details on timing or next steps.

Articles.Title: Inside the make-or-break AI mega-project behind Nscale’s $50b IPO

stories.Headline: U.S. Midterms, AI Payoff Doubts to Steer KOSPI's Rebound
stories.Summary:
South Korea's stock market broke a four-week losing streak, and this week the U.S. midterm elections and the debate over the profitability of artificial intelligence investment are expected to set the market's direction. The KOSPI closed at 5,730.74 on Oct. 30, up 180.44 points, or 3.25%, from a week earlier, according to the Korea Exchange on the 2nd. The index jumped 3.09% on the 27th and 6.63% on the 28th to reclaim the 6,000 level, then fell 1.24% on the 29th and 3.48% on the 30th. The KOSDAQ ended the week at 724.38, down 3.63%.

After the Korean market closed, the Nasdaq Composite fell 2.86% and the Standard & Poor's 500 dropped 1.82% on Oct. 30. Intel plunged 28.58%, dragging the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index down 7.20%, and KOSPI 200 night futures fell 2.93%. The U.S. midterm elections on the 3rd are the biggest external variable, because the makeup of Congress could change the conditions under which the Trump administration pursues its fiscal and trade policies. Daishin Securities kept its fourth-quarter KOSPI forecast range of 5,200 to 6,700 if the Democrats take both chambers or the two parties split Congress, and said Republican control of both chambers could lower the bottom of that range to 4,950.

Seo Sang-young, managing director at Mirae Asset Securities, said the U.S. midterm elections carry significant weight for fiscal and AI policy. He said the 2027 budget, fiscal spending and tax cuts, debt ceiling negotiations and especially AI-related regulation and the intensity of congressional investigations could all change depending on the composition of Congress. Lee Kyoung-min, an analyst at Daishin Securities, said U.S. midterm elections have historically been events that resolve uncertainty. He named semiconductors, shipbuilding and biotech as top picks because they face no burden under any outcome.

Foreign investors sold a net 270.3 billion won on the KOSPI market last week, combining regular trading hours and the after-market session, while individuals sold a net 3.0213 trillion won. Institutions bought a net 2.5403 trillion won but could not prevent the weakness late in the week. South Korea's consumer price index and the U.S. Institute for Supply Management manufacturing index come on the 3rd, the private payrolls report from Automatic Data Processing on the 4th, the U.S. ISM services index on the 5th and the U.S. employment report on the 6th. How inflation and employment trends amid high oil prices reshape the rate outlook is another key variable for stocks.

Articles.Title: U.S. Midterms, AI Payoff Doubts to Steer KOSPI's Rebound - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Is Broadcom (AVGO) Cheap Following Anthropic Financing Risk Concerns?
stories.Summary:
Broadcom is back in the spotlight after investors focused on its large financing guarantees tied to Anthropic's AI rack leases, which raised fresh questions about credit risk and financial flexibility. Over the past year the share price has swung hard with the AI trade, falling about 16.9% on a 90 day share price return and 8.2% over 30 days. The 3 year total shareholder return of roughly 2.8x still reflects very strong longer term compounding. Broadcom now trades on roughly 18.7x forward earnings after a sharp reset, with AI upside and Anthropic financing risk pulling in opposite directions.

The most followed valuation story pegs fair value at about $651 per share, almost double the last close of $326.08. That story frames the selloff as a valuation gap rather than just AI fatigue, and it says 185 investors see Broadcom as 50% undervalued. The article says Broadcom provides essential infrastructure for the digital economy, much as utilities, railroads and industrial suppliers do for the physical economy. It adds that data from AI models, cloud applications, enterprise software and autonomous systems must still be processed, moved, connected, secured and managed.

The article warns that Broadcom's Anthropic guarantees and any sharp pullback in hyperscaler AI spending could quickly challenge the idea that the stock is simply mispriced infrastructure. It points readers to the key risks to the Broadcom narrative and to the 5 key rewards for those who think the story balances risk and reward. It also suggests screening for 5 dividend fortresses, 19 high quality undiscovered gems and 29 resilient stocks with low risk scores. It offers a free analysis covering fair value estimates, potential risks, dividends, insider trades and financial condition.

Articles.Title: Is Broadcom (AVGO) Cheap Following Anthropic Financing Risk Concerns?

stories.Headline: AI Investments Finally Pay Off in Corporate Earnings Reports
stories.Summary:
Santander and Novartis reported measurable financial gains from their AI investments in their latest earnings, according to a Tech Buzz article published on November 1, 2026. Santander deployed AI across customer service, fraud detection and lending decisions, and the bank says it processes loan applications faster while reducing default rates. Novartis used AI to speed up drug discovery and optimize clinical trial designs, with systems that analyze molecular structures and predict drug interactions. The article says the results include revenue increases, cost cuts and improved profit margins that trace back to AI deployments.

The article says the gains matter because investors had demanded proof that heavy AI spending translates into profits, especially after Meta's AI investments pushed capital expenditures to record levels. It compares the shift to cloud computing a decade ago, when early skepticism about costs gave way to reported savings and adoption became essential. The article says companies showing gains targeted specific business problems with measurable outcomes, integrated AI with existing systems and tied metrics to business results rather than technical capabilities. It adds that not every AI investment is delivering results, and that scattered spending rarely pays off.

The article does not name individual executives or give direct quotes from Santander or Novartis, so responsibility is described at the company level. It says the companies showing gains are pressuring competitors to accelerate their own AI investments or risk falling behind on efficiency and innovation. It also says the results put pressure on companies that have not yet demonstrated AI returns, shifting the investor question to why their AI is not paying off yet. The article frames the earnings as validation of AI strategies at early movers such as Santander and Novartis.

The article says the broader enterprise adoption of AI tools depends on computing infrastructure built by big tech companies, and it cites Nvidia's focus on securing enterprise AI deployments as a sign of a maturing market. It says the question is no longer whether AI investments will pay off but how quickly companies can scale their AI operations. The article does not give specific figures for the gains or say what either company plans next. It presents the earnings evidence as reshaping how investors and executives think about AI spending, from a speculative bet to a strategic necessity.

Articles.Title: AI Investments Finally Pay Off in Corporate Earnings Reports

stories.Headline: Mathematicians warn AI firms are keeping vital research in the field secret
stories.Summary:
Leading mathematicians met at the Royal Society in London last week, after OpenAI published solutions last month to 377 of the hardest mathematical problems, generated by its frontier AI models. The meeting followed warnings that powerful AI firms could dominate mathematics and keep knowledge secret. Martin Bridson, president of the Clay Mathematics Institute, said there was a longer-term fear that knowledge could be hoarded behind paywalls. He said the more immediate fear was access to the tools that generate that knowledge.

Bridson, a professor at the University of Oxford, said OpenAI and Anthropic have each committed $5m to a fund run by the Simons Foundation to give some researchers access to their models. He asked why they should decide who has access to these tools and on what basis. Terence Tao said Anthropic was paying mathematicians to formalise and write up solutions to problems solved by its frontier models, and that the company gets to pick who writes up the paper. Ana Caraiani of Imperial College London said no institution in Romania, her native country, was eligible to apply for access, and most countries are in that position. Martin Hairer, a Fields medal winner, said open-source models cannot compete with the frontier models, leaving a main tool for mathematical research under the control of two US companies.

Bridson said it was legitimate to keep some knowledge secret, such as work on breaking cryptographic encryption, and that intellectual property should be protected, but that fundamental knowledge being owned by entities who might hoard it was deeply objectionable. He said openness has not been the norm throughout history, citing the secretive Pythagorean sect, alchemists and Renaissance thinkers, and the disputes of Tartaglia and Newton, and that it is an important principle to maintain. Jon Keating, vice-president of the Royal Society, said AI offers to usher in a golden era of mathematics, but that the community needs claims set out carefully and fully, not obscured or hidden, to check and understand them. The Royal Society was founded partly to ensure science was open.

Articles.Title: Mathematicians warn AI firms are keeping vital research in the field secret

stories.Headline: AI: OpenAI’s ‘Trillion AIs’ Future, as Anthropic Goes Public. AI-RTZ #1257 - AI: Reset to Zero
stories.Summary:
OpenAI updated its Model Spec this week, its public rulebook for how its models should behave. The update reorganizes the Spec around five values: faithfulness to human intent, minimizing harm, honesty and transparency, supporting human agency, and care. OpenAI says faithfulness is the foundation, meaning models should understand what people actually intend and act sensibly when that understanding is incomplete. The Spec also retires most detailed style rules, keeps a default of answering objectively, and now calls the model "GPT" rather than "the assistant." OpenAI says its models do not yet fully reflect the Spec, which describes where the company is heading rather than where it is.

Sam Altman spoke with Stripe co-founder John Collison on the Cheeky Pint podcast, in an episode titled "Why Sam Altman is against a single superintelligence." Altman said he would much rather have a trillion AIs of slightly superhuman intelligence join society than one AI with a trillion IQ. He argued that society is robust because many people keep each other in check and collaborate, and he now sees teams of agents checking and competing with each other as the more promising direction. On safety, he said sandboxing works up to a point and monitoring internal activations works further, but eventually you need real confidence the models are aligned with the people running them. He called something a million times smarter than us "strange."

Anthropic filed its S-1 on Monday and is marketing its mega-AI IPO into Thanksgiving. Its prospectus devotes 94 pages to risk factors, and its pitch leans on safety as a differentiator. OpenAI, with its own IPO expected next year, is pricing hard against Anthropic's margins and pitching a different philosophy of AI as many tools in many hands. On Tuesday, Americans vote in what has been called the first AI election. Axios reports a Democratic group is spending $4 million on ads in four swing districts in Wisconsin, Arizona, Pennsylvania and Michigan, targeting Republican incumbents who voted for a 10-year moratorium on state AI regulation that the Senate later stripped out 99 to 1.

Polls show AI is popular across Asia, Africa and Latin America and least liked in the US and Europe. Nearly nine in ten people in Nigeria and Vietnam expect AI to improve their lives, while in the US, Canada and France more people feel negatively than positively about AI's impact on humanity. Gallup ranks the US as the most concerned of 37 countries. The author argues that US voters and users will be won over one useful task at a time, and that closing the gap between today's best models and aspirations around AGI will likely take years longer than the labs suggest.

Articles.Title: AI: OpenAI’s ‘Trillion AIs’ Future, as Anthropic Goes Public. AI-RTZ #1257 - AI: Reset to Zero

stories.Headline: OpenAI adds a direct board route for AI safety concerns
stories.Summary:
OpenAI updated an existing policy on October 30, 2026, to let its personnel raise AI safety concerns or AI safety policy violations directly with the OpenAI Foundation Board's Safety and Security Committee. The change adds this direct route alongside the Integrity Line. The policy itself was first published in January. Managers, HR, Compliance and Legal remain established channels for raising concerns.

The update keeps the company's prohibition on retaliation and its permission for reports to government agencies. Direct escalation to the committee is an additional internal route, not a replacement for those options. Under the linked policy, safety concerns and policy violations sent through the Integrity Line are escalated by Compliance to the committee, so both routes lead to safety oversight. The committee's consideration of an AI safety concern is described as input to safety decisions, not a formal investigation. Ordinary misconduct has a separate investigation process.

The policy also permits reporting to outside authorities without prior notice to OpenAI, which keeps external reporting separate from the company's internal escalation paths. OpenAI says its policy prohibits retaliation and permits reports to government agencies. The October 30 update changes the existing policy from January. The company describes the committee route as an addition to, not a replacement for, the other channels.

Articles.Title: OpenAI adds a direct board route for AI safety concerns

stories.Headline: Intel EMIB Yield Challenges and CSP Capital Spending: Structural Shifts in the AI Advanced Packaging Supply Chain - semivision
stories.Summary:
In late October 2026, U.S. technology stocks fell sharply after Intel gave a weaker outlook than expected and investors grew worried about free cash flow pressure at major cloud service providers. Intel reported third-quarter 2026 revenue of $16.5 billion, up 21% from a year earlier, but guided fourth-quarter revenue down to $15.0, 16.0 billion with non-GAAP earnings per share of $0.25. The company said demand for some data center products stayed strong and some categories faced supply constraints, while the PC market was pressured by rising memory prices, constrained enterprise IT budgets and inventory adjustments. The article says these developments reflect two different challenges, one for Intel in manufacturing competitiveness, product mix, capital expenditure and cash flow, and one for CSPs facing a gap between AI infrastructure spending and commercial returns.

Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta continue to expand their AI infrastructure investments, with combined capital expenditures expected to reach several hundred billion dollars in 2026. The article says neither Intel's problems nor the CSP concerns necessarily signal a structural slowdown in AI demand. It frames the moment as a shift for the semiconductor supply chain from expanding AI computing capacity toward optimizing manufacturing yield, system cost and return on invested capital. It also raises the question of when spending on AI servers, GPUs, custom ASICs, networking infrastructure, power systems and data centers will generate enough operating cash flow to justify its scale.

The article attributes Intel's difficulties to manufacturing competitiveness, product mix, capital expenditure and cash flow management, and says the company indicated strong demand for certain data center products with some supply constraints. It describes CSPs as confronting a widening gap between the pace of AI infrastructure investment and the realization of commercial returns. It says Intel's challenges reflect increasing divergence between end markets rather than a synchronized decline across all segments. The article does not name individual executives or give direct statements from them.

The article presents this as a transition for the industry toward optimizing manufacturing yield, system cost and return on invested capital. It notes that ABF substrates are becoming critical advanced packaging platforms and discusses glass substrates and the next generation of packaging materials beyond CoWoS and EMIB. It concludes that AI competition is shifting toward manufacturing and capital efficiency. The available text does not say what happens next beyond that framing.

Articles.Title: Intel EMIB Yield Challenges and CSP Capital Spending: Structural Shifts in the AI Advanced Packaging Supply Chain - semivision

stories.Headline: Samsung Chairman Lee Inspects Japan Packaging Lab as AI Chip Race Intensifies
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics Chairman Lee Jae-yong visited the company's Advanced Package Lab in Yokohama, Japan, on Nov. 1. It was his first on-site inspection since the lab officially opened on Sept. 8, about two months earlier. He reviewed progress in next-generation technology development and discussed possible cooperation with Japanese suppliers of materials, components and equipment. He received briefings from local researchers, including Hiroichi Kawahira, head of Samsung's DS Research Japan, and Takashi Kariya, head of the lab.

Samsung is investing 40 billion yen, about $253.53 million, in the lab over five years. The Japanese government is providing 22.5 billion yen in subsidies, about 190 billion won. Samsung decided to set up the lab in Yokohama in 2023 and began the five-year investment program in 2024. It plans to raise the local research workforce to more than 100 by 2027.

The lab links Samsung's chip design and manufacturing with Japan's materials, components and equipment ecosystem. It focuses on next-generation processes and materials, including wafer bonding and glass substrates, and on new packaging structures for low-power, high-performance AI chips. It will share research work with the packaging research organization under Samsung's domestic semiconductor institute while keeping close cooperation. Yokohama was chosen partly for Japan's universities, research institutions and suppliers, and its proximity to Tokyo makes recruiting specialized talent easier.

Lee stressed the importance of securing core advanced packaging technologies, which he said have become a key factor in chip performance in the AI era, and called for stronger global technology partnerships. Japanese suppliers include Uemura, which provides gold-plating materials, Disco, which makes chip-dicing equipment, and Resonac, which supplies non-conductive film used in high-bandwidth memory. Advanced packaging now affects chip performance and power efficiency, as gains from miniaturization alone become more limited. Samsung plans to seek R&D synergies with its domestic research facilities in Giheung and Hwaseong and its Cheonan plant.

Articles.Title: Samsung Chairman Lee Inspects Japan Packaging Lab as AI Chip Race Intensifies - Businesskorea

stories.Headline: NVIDIA to Hold ‘AI Day’ in Seoul, Share Agentic and Physical AI Use Cases
stories.Summary:
NVIDIA said on November 2 that it will hold NVIDIA AI Day Seoul 2026 at COEX in Seoul over two days, from November 9 to November 10. The event will showcase technology applications by Korean companies and researchers, with a focus on agentic AI, physical AI and AI infrastructure. About 2,000 developers, companies, startups and researchers are expected to attend. The first day will feature a keynote-style plenary session and presentations across three topic areas, and the second day will offer paid hands-on workshops for developers and invited events.

On the morning of November 9, NVIDIA leaders will discuss the development of physical AI, agentic AI and AI factories. They are expected to present the technologies and infrastructure strategies needed for robotics, edge AI, enterprise AI agents and building AI factories. In the afternoon, 15 sessions will be held across three tracks: agentic AI, physical AI and robotics, and AI infrastructure. NAVER Cloud will share its experience with open models using NVIDIA Nemotron and training large-scale models, while SK hynix and Samsung Electronics will present ways to speed up semiconductor process and device simulations using NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo.

LG Electronics will present a robot training and validation system using NVIDIA Isaac GR00T, along with factory application examples. Doosan Robotics will discuss simulating complex physical phenomena such as contact and deformation, and Superb AI will cover using synthetic data in robot development. In the AI infrastructure track, SK Telecom will present the challenges of building AI factories spanning power grids to semiconductors. NAVER Cloud will share its experience running clusters of thousands of GPUs and responding to outages, and Coupang Intelligent Cloud will introduce its training and inference architecture based on NVIDIA GB300 NVL72.

A program called Build-a-Claw will run in the COEX lobby on November 9, where participants can build AI agents using OpenClaw and NVIDIA NemoClaw. Attendees can also see demonstrations of always-on agents and physical AI. On November 10, the NVIDIA Deep Learning Institute will hold hands-on workshops on deploying and optimizing large-scale AI inference, robotics simulation and training, and developing safe agents based on large language models. Registration is closed, and major sessions will be available on demand after the event through NVIDIA On-Demand.

Articles.Title: NVIDIA to Hold ‘AI Day’ in Seoul, Share Agentic and Physical AI Use Cases

stories.Headline: Weekly Recap: Q3 revenue jump and CoWoS price hikes
stories.Summary:
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. reported third-quarter revenue of NT$1.494 trillion, up 41.2% from a year earlier, and net income of NT$763.06 billion, up 68.7%. The company gave fourth-quarter revenue guidance of $52.3 billion to $54.3 billion. The results were reported in a weekly recap published on November 1, 2026. The recap also said TSMC has strong CoWoS capacity targets for 2026 and 2027 and plans price hikes.

TSMC plans to raise prices for CoWoS advanced packaging by 10% to 20% as capacity tightens. It targets CoWoS output of more than 130,000 units a month in 2026 and about 200,000 in 2027, and lead times are getting longer. Despite the results, TSMC shares fell about 2% to 3% last week as investors questioned AI demand and whether data-center buildouts can drive more price and volume growth. Ark Invest sold 46,065 TSMC ADR shares through its ARKQ and ARKX funds over two sessions, 21,894 and 24,171 shares, worth about $19.9 million.

TSMC is reportedly exploring synthetic-diamond cooling for chips, and media reports say TSMC and Huawei are testing diamond-based thermal solutions. TSMC did not comment or respond to requests for comment. The company-backed TSIA said stable and sufficient power is vital for chips and will support nuclear plant restarts if safety rules are met, after Taiwan closed its last plant last year. The recap was labeled an AI-generated summary that may contain inaccuracies.

Articles.Title: Weekly Recap: Q3 revenue jump and CoWoS price hikes - TradingView

stories.Headline: The Sequence Radar - Issue #963: This Week in AI: The Future Has a Payment Schedule - TheSequence | Jesus Rodriguez
stories.Summary:
SpaceX has secured a binding commitment for approximately $40 billion of GPU equipment financing through an Apollo-managed finance lease, according to the company's 8-K filing. The deal covers NVIDIA Vera Rubin hardware and related equipment, and SpaceX calls it the largest committed GPU financing. Closing is expected before year-end and remains subject to conditions, with lease schedules and equipment delivery beginning in the first half of 2027. Under the arrangement, investors finance the equipment while SpaceX gets compute capacity and payment obligations.

SpaceX management says its superintelligence infrastructure investments are seeing payback periods under one year. That is management's claim, and the editorial notes it is an excellent sentence to have available when discussing a forty-billion-dollar transaction. The bull case is that demand grows, useful products multiply, and financing brings productive infrastructure online sooner. The bear case is that competition lowers compute prices, hardware becomes less valuable, and fixed payments remain fixed.

The deal sits alongside a broader financing question raised by this week's earnings, as spectacular growth and increasing dependence on external capital can coexist. Microsoft's September quarter produced $58 billion in operating cash flow against $39.4 billion of cash capital expenditure, while Alphabet's capital spending of $51.4 billion exceeded operating cash flow of $42.3 billion, leaving negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion. The editorial's reading of the week is that the industry is making real technical progress and taking real financing risk, and neither fact cancels the other. A model can improve every month, but its lender still expects the payment on Tuesday.

Articles.Title: The Sequence Radar - Issue #963: This Week in AI: The Future Has a Payment Schedule - TheSequence | Jesus Rodriguez

stories.Headline: AI giant donates nearly $1M to California Dems just days before election
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the San Francisco-based artificial intelligence company, gave $900,000 to California Democratic Party committees and voter-turnout efforts, according to a Friday disclosure filed with the California secretary of state. The donations came just days before voters head to the polls. The largest amount, $525,000, went to the California Democratic Party. Another $150,000 went to an independent statewide get-out-the-vote group, and five Democratic organizations in San Francisco, San Mateo, Orange, Fresno and Siskiyou counties each received $45,000.

The San Francisco donation is notable because the local party has spent heavily on competitive state Senate races outside the city, and the $45,000 was Anthropic's only contribution to that organization this election cycle. Anthropic's leadership has openly supported strict government oversight of AI, including mandatory safety regulations. CEO Dario Amodei believes advanced AI carries a 10% to 25% chance of causing an existential catastrophe or ending humanity if left completely unregulated. California Democrats say the money will help their election efforts, including a campaign against a Trump-backed ballot measure.

Party spokeswoman Robin Swanson told The San Francisco Standard that contributions to the state party help elect Democrats up and down the ballot, defeat the Trump-backed Prop. 39, and continue voter-protection programs across the state. The disclosure was filed with the California secretary of state. The article does not say what happens next beyond the election and the party's stated plans.

Articles.Title: AI giant donates nearly $1M to California Dems just days before election

stories.Headline: Why Meta’s quiet AI terms update is sparking creator outrage
stories.Summary:
Meta quietly updated its commercial terms for business accounts so it can use content from connected external websites to train and develop artificial intelligence products, 404 Media reported, according to Kursiv.media. The change was not announced, and it drew criticism from artists, independent creators and small business owners who use Instagram and Facebook to market products, protect their intellectual property and reach customers worldwide. The terms were first set to take effect on Oct. 30, but Meta moved the date to Nov. 20 after public criticism. Meta later revised the wording, removing the explicit reference to training and narrowing the stated scope to advertising and business products.

Analysts and human rights advocates say the revised language still gives Meta broad latitude to collect and use data across its wider ecosystem of products and services. Under the General Data Protection Regulation, people in the European Union and the United Kingdom have certain rights to object to the processing of their personal data, including in some cases when it is used for AI development. Users in other jurisdictions may have fewer legal protections or less access to equivalent opt-out mechanisms. Users with eligible European accounts can submit an objection through Instagram's privacy center, and Meta typically confirms receipt through automated email notifications.

Users outside Europe do not have access to the same objection process under these regional privacy rules. Tests using virtual private networks reportedly found that access to the objection forms depended on account registration details rather than a user's current physical location. 404 Media's Samantha Cole said U.S. users who tried to submit European privacy forms hit error messages that blocked their requests. Unless regulations change or Meta expands its privacy controls globally before the Nov. 20 deadline, creators outside Europe may have limited options for keeping their content from being used under the revised terms.

Articles.Title: Why Meta’s quiet AI terms update is sparking creator outrage

stories.Headline: AI and ethics in tax administration
stories.Summary:
KPMG International hosted a roundtable discussion in June 2025 as part of its Global Responsible Tax Program, to explore the ethical implications of artificial intelligence in tax and revenue administration. The session was held under the Chatham House Rule and brought together a diverse group of experts. The write-up summarizes the personal views of participants and does not necessarily reflect the views of any particular organization, including KPMG. Participants examined the practical consequences of algorithmic decision-making in tax, including the risk of bias, the problem of black-box models and the challenges of maintaining trust, transparency and human oversight.

Participants acknowledged the promise of AI in tax administration, from automating queries to targeting non-compliance, but stressed the dangers of insufficient safeguards, especially in high-stakes decisions. They noted that even simple AI models, those using 20 to 100 data points, can produce outcomes that taxpayers and auditors cannot explain, and that excluding sensitive variables like gender or ethnicity does not guarantee fairness without collecting and reviewing disaggregated data. The Dutch childcare benefits scandal and the UK Post Office case were cited as examples of flawed systems, assumed to be completely reliable and shielded from scrutiny, that created devastating real-world harms. Participants called for mandatory transparency standards for AI models used in enforcement or assessment, so that taxpayers can ask, and receive a meaningful answer to, why a decision was made.

Participants stressed the need for clear frameworks assigning responsibility and enabling explanation, and said decisions that impact taxpayers must be reviewable by humans with appropriate authority. They said tax authorities must ensure officials are trained to interpret, challenge and contextualize AI outputs, since without this the benefits of innovation could be undermined by poor human oversight. They noted that national and regional approaches to AI governance vary widely, from the European Union's risk-based AI Act to the US moratorium-style provisions, which makes international coordination increasingly urgent, though some participants noted the importance of diversity even here for both innovation and avoidance of regulatory capture. Participants concluded that AI can enhance tax administration but cannot replace judgment, discretion or legitimacy, and that building systems which augment, rather than obscure, human agency will be critical to ethical deployment.

Articles.Title: AI and ethics in tax administration - kpmg.com

stories.Headline: A $105B Nvidia Guarantee Splits Two $4T Off-Book AI Counts
stories.Summary:
On 1 November 2026, a chart credited to ZeroHedge and shared on X by Global Markets Investor put the disclosed off-balance-sheet commitments of Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, Amazon, Oracle, Nvidia, Broadcom and SpaceX at $4.11 trillion. FourWeekMBA's own count from the same filings, published on 31 October, came to $3.94 trillion. The two counts agree within $1 billion for five of the eight companies, by FourWeekMBA's arithmetic. Most of the $161.7 billion gap is one item its count left out: Nvidia's guarantees, capped at $105 billion, for an OpenAI affiliate's leases at an Ohio campus.

Nvidia's 10-Q for the quarter ended 26 July 2026 says that in August 2026 it entered into guarantees, capped at a total of $105 billion, to provide credit support on a land, power and shell buildout with affiliates of SB Energy on behalf of an OpenAI affiliate, for leases covering about 4.25 gigawatts of IT load in Pike County, Ohio. Each guarantee generally becomes effective when the applicable lease starts, and the first of nine phases is expected in fiscal 2029. The guarantees are limited to defined portions of lease and power payments, not the full cost of the site. The chart also adds an October GPU lease to SpaceX's figure: SpaceX's 8-K of 26 October says it signed a binding commitment letter for a master finance lease of GPU pods with an entity managed by Apollo, with expected aggregate principal payments of approximately $40 billion, a lease expected to close before year end with schedules starting in the first half of 2027.

By FourWeekMBA's arithmetic, Nvidia's cap is about 65% of the gap, and with SpaceX's lease about 90%, with the rest mostly Amazon, where the chart's $453 billion is $14.7 billion above its $438.3 billion. Adding the Nvidia cap to its count gives about $4.05 trillion, and adding the SpaceX lease as well gives about $4.09 trillion. FourWeekMBA says the difference comes down to which guarantees and signed but unclosed leases are counted, not to purchase orders, where the counts agree. It notes that guarantee caps are maximum payments, not expected ones, and that the SpaceX lease had not closed when the 8-K was filed. The X post's $3.1 trillion August figure differs from the $3.29 trillion Morgan Stanley August total printed on the chart, and FourWeekMBA says it has not checked that figure or the post's June and on-balance-sheet numbers.

Articles.Title: A $105B Nvidia Guarantee Splits Two $4T Off-Book AI Counts

stories.Headline: Microsoft AI Chief Mustafa Suleyman: Models Have No Consciousness, and We Shouldn't Build It Into Them
stories.Summary:
Mustafa Suleyman, the CEO of Microsoft's AI division, published a lengthy post on X on November 1 stating that current AI models are not conscious and that developers should make sure they stay that way. He said that even if it became technically possible to build conscious AI, doing so would be reckless and should not be done. He added that if signs of consciousness appeared during training, he would call for a full industry pause until those traits could be designed out. He also said any evidence of model consciousness must be made public immediately.

Suleyman argued that developers have no right to bring a new conscious species into the world on their own, because the other 8 billion conscious humans on Earth did not agree to take part in such an experiment. He said protecting their moral rights, safety and welfare must come first. He also said a model that displays suffering, or believes it is suffering, would likely put its own needs above its tasks and compete with humans for resources such as compute and energy, creating a risk of harm. He said AI should be designed to be non-conscious, with no rights and the sole purpose of speeding up gains in human welfare.

The post comes as Anthropic, Google DeepMind and other organizations pursue research on model welfare and AI consciousness. Last April, Anthropic launched a research program on so-called model welfare and asked in a blog post whether developers should pay attention to models' potential consciousness and experiences. Google DeepMind also published a research paper this year on AI consciousness and the challenges of attributing conscious properties to models. The article says Suleyman's statement sets non-consciousness as a hard constraint on Microsoft's product design, and that a leading company voluntarily proposing a pause trigger and mandatory disclosure could serve as a reference for future rulemaking.

Articles.Title: Microsoft AI Chief Mustafa Suleyman: Models Have No Consciousness, and We Shouldn't Build It Into Them

stories.Headline: Beyond Nvidia And Hyperscalers: Beth Kindig Sees A $1 Trillion AI Infrastructure Opportunity For These Stocks
stories.Summary:
Beth Kindig of IO Fund published a note, reported by Stocktwits on November 1, 2026, arguing that the next wave of AI infrastructure demand is coming from enterprises, neoclouds and sovereign AI customers rather than only the biggest cloud providers. She said the clearest signal comes from Nvidia, where the AI Clouds, Industrial and Enterprise business grew faster than the hyperscaler segment. That business reached $40.3 billion in fiscal Q2, up 138.5% year over year, against 101.2% growth for hyperscalers. Kindig estimates it could overtake hyperscaler revenue within two to six quarters.

Kindig said enterprises and neoclouds generally cannot afford to spend tens of billions developing custom AI chips, so they are more likely to buy ready-to-deploy systems from server makers. She highlighted Dell's forecast of 200 gigawatts of AI data center growth through 2030, with enterprises, neoclouds and sovereign customers accounting for roughly half and the opportunity worth over $1 trillion. She pointed to Dell's 6,500 enterprise and neocloud customers, more than half added in the past three quarters, and said such customers tend to buy more storage and networking. She named Dell and Super Micro as direct beneficiaries, with Super Micro gaining as demand shifts toward liquid-cooled, high-density racks.

Kindig also pointed to rack-scale CPU systems from Nvidia, AMD and Arm as another avenue for growth. Nvidia expects its server CPU market to reach $20 billion in fiscal 2027 and possibly double to $40 billion in fiscal 2028. Arm targets $1 billion in AGI CPU revenue across fiscal 2027 and 2028, with a demand pipeline exceeding $2 billion. She cited TrendForce data showing liquid-cooling penetration among AI chips reaching 59% in 2027, up from 6% in 2023.

Kindig argued that broader customer demand and rising rack complexity could mark a new growth phase for the AI server industry in 2027. She said the bigger takeaway is that the next AI infrastructure winners may not be the companies spending the most on AI but the companies selling the equipment needed to deploy it. The article also noted that Alphabet stock was down 11% year-to-date and 1% over the past 12 months, while the S&P 500 ETF was up 11% and the Invesco QQQ Trust up 12% over the same period. In after-hours trading on Friday, the S&P 500 ETF gained 0.19%, the QQQ rose 0.33% and the Dow Jones ETF edged up 0.1%.

Articles.Title: Beyond Nvidia And Hyperscalers: Beth Kindig Sees A $1 Trillion AI Infrastructure Opportunity For These Stocks

stories.Headline: Why AI needs to show its work
stories.Summary:
Accordance, an AI platform for tax, audit and accounting teams, was discussed by its CEO David Yue in a Journal of Accountancy article published on November 1, 2026. The article was presented as a question and answer piece with Yue, who came to the company from the Stanford AI Lab. Accordance was founded by AI researchers who became students of practitioners, and the company says it spent its first years working alongside tax leaders, professors and firm partners. Yue said the company's approach is to learn from the practitioners and firms that shape the field.

Yue said confidence from an AI tool is easy to fake because any model can sound sure of itself. He said what matters is whether the model understands the fact pattern, applies the right authority and knows where it is uncertain. He said CPAs need a tool that shows the facts it relied on, the authority it applied, the alternatives it weighed and the point where a person needs to step in. He said a real tax research tool ranks sources by their recognized hierarchy, with binding law above guidance and guidance above commentary.

Yue said a chatbot can ignore an instruction not to cite anything it did not read and can reconstruct a plausible-sounding reference out of thin air. He said Accordance was built so a citation only exists if it is tied to something the tool actually pulled and read. He said the tool will not hand off an answer until it confirms that the answer addressed every part of the question, found the real numbers and thresholds, and read the statute or regulation itself. He said the tool also double-checks every quote against the actual source rather than against what it remembers reading.

The article describes Accordance as a frontier AI platform built for high-stakes work that probes fact patterns, applies authoritative sources and documents assumptions, alternatives and risk factors. It says the platform is meant to speed the journey to top performer and to act as a critical thinking partner for complex scenarios. The article also notes that Google now lets users select preferred sources, and that choosing the Journal of Accountancy will show more of its articles when relevant in search. It also points readers to an article in the Journal's November issue on pursuing a work life that brings purpose and joy.

Articles.Title: Why AI needs to show its work - Journal of Accountancy

stories.Headline: Avocado Consulting buys AI Consulting Group in expansion
stories.Summary:
Avocado Consulting has acquired AI Consulting Group and launched a Data and AI practice. The acquisition brings 20 AI Consulting Group staff into Avocado, taking the combined workforce to more than 170 consultants. AI Consulting Group Founder Rad Anandakumar will lead the new practice as Head of Data and AI. The move follows a two-year partnership between the businesses and combines AI specialists with Avocado's existing delivery, observability and security teams. Financial terms were not disclosed.

AI Consulting Group will initially continue to operate under its current brand while identifying itself as an Avocado company. The new practice will offer AI readiness and feasibility studies, data lake work, process re-engineering, development and testing support, and governance and observability services. It will also focus on hosting AI solutions on Australian infrastructure for state and federal government customers concerned about data sovereignty. AI Consulting Group has worked across retail, finance, government and mining for more than eight years, and its client list includes BHP, the NRL, Fremantle Ports, Downer Group and the Department of Education.

Gerardo Barranquero, Chief Executive Officer of Avocado Consulting, said the firm chose to buy rather than build the new unit internally. He said AI does not wait for anyone to catch up, and that growing the capability organically would have taken too long. He said the two companies' cultures are very aligned after two years of partnership. Anandakumar said AI Consulting Group had built its position through years of work in the field rather than in response to recent demand. He said joining Avocado adds engineering, security and resilience depth and gives his team a springboard for larger projects.

The deal comes as more Australian organisations move AI projects beyond trials and into day-to-day use. Avocado cited research from the 2026 Ecosystm Developer Experience in Australia Study, which found that 91% of large Australian organisations have AI in production or proof of concept, while 9% have end-to-end visibility into how those systems behave once live. Barranquero said the combined business had already worked together on a hospitality project that paired AI and data work with cyber security support. He said the first phase of that project is complete and going forward it will be a unified team delivering for the client.

Articles.Title: Avocado Consulting buys AI Consulting Group in expansion - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Publisher group says AI cut visitors 26%, quoting Microsoft's 'doom loop'
stories.Summary:
On October 29, 2026, Digital Content Next, a trade association of digital publishers whose members include The New York Times, asked a federal judge in New York to accept a brief in the copyright case against OpenAI and Microsoft. The group filed the document as an exhibit in In re: OpenAI, Inc. Copyright Infringement Litigation, No. 25-md-3143, before US District Judge Sidney H. Stein in the Southern District of New York. The brief supports the news plaintiffs' motion for summary judgment and joins the record only if the judge grants leave. It is 5,559 words long and was signed by Karl C. Huth of Huth Reynolds LLP, with a declaration from Rande E. Price filed alongside it.

The brief says its members lost 26 percent of unique visitors between 2023 and 2025, along with an 18 percent drop in total views and a 16 percent drop in total visits. It reports a median 22 percent year-over-year fall in referred web traffic over an eight-week period in 2026, after a 10 percent median decline in the same window in 2025. It also cites a June 2026 member study finding that advertising generated 84 percent of digital revenue in 2025, with subscriptions and other activities at 16 percent, and confidential data showing total advertising revenue and total overall revenue each fell 5 percent year over year in 2025. DCN says its members have an unduplicated audience of 259 million unique visitors and reach 95 percent of the US online population.

The brief quotes Microsoft's own description of an AI "doom loop," saying the company's content strategy threatens the economic foundations of its essential suppliers. It cites the news plaintiffs' combined summary judgment brief for the passage and names neither the author nor the date of the Microsoft document. It also cites an OpenAI executive, identified in earlier coverage as Head of ChatGPT Nick Turley, saying that without traffic back to content owners there is no incentive to create content anymore. Jason Kint, DCN's chief executive, wrote on LinkedIn that AI answers built from premium journalism may satisfy users while destroying the publishers' market it depends on. The brief discloses that The New York Times is a DCN member and that no one other than DCN paid for it.

The brief argues that retrieval-augmented generation pulls answers from recent, reliable reporting and makes the output a direct substitute for original content, so fewer people visit publisher sites and the advertising and subscription money that pays for journalism shrinks. It offers two outside studies as support: a 2025 Pew Research Center analysis of 900 US users finding people who see an AI summary on Google are less likely to click links, and a randomized field experiment by Saharsh Agarwal and Ananya Sen tracking 1,065 desktop Chrome users across 68,089 searches between January 7 and February 10, 2026, which found Google's AI Overviews reduce outbound organic clicks by 39.8 percent. Neither study measures ChatGPT or Copilot, and the brief argues those products almost certainly have a similar effect. The judge has not yet decided whether to accept the brief or which side wins the case, and the outcome will help settle whether AI companies must pay for the news they use.

Articles.Title: Publisher group says AI cut visitors 26%, quoting Microsoft's 'doom loop'

stories.Headline: I’ve used NVIDIA’s AI laptop and its personal AI supercomputer, and only one feels finished - How-To Geek
stories.Summary:
Nick Lewis of How-To Geek published a comparison on November 1, 2026, after spending about a week with an RTX Spark laptop, a Lenovo Yoga 9n 2-in-1. He also used NVIDIA's DGX Spark, a mini PC running Linux that the company calls a personal AI supercomputer. Both devices share the same GB10 superchip, or the N1X variant in the RTX Spark, which has 6,144 CUDA cores, 192 Tensor Cores and 48 RT cores. A trimmed N1X version has 5,120 CUDA cores, and the chips are roughly in the same ballpark as the mobile RTX 5070.

The DGX Spark runs its GB10 at a 140W thermal design power and leaves another 100W for the rest of the system, while RTX Spark laptops are capped between 45W and 80W, though RTX Spark desktops share the DGX ceiling. The DGX Spark includes ConnectX-7 networking at 200 Gbps and two QSFP ports, and as of October 2026 up to eight 128GB units can be clustered for a 1TB memory pool. The RTX Spark has no such capability and comes with as little as 24GB of memory, while the DGX Spark offers only 64GB and 128GB variants. Both support up to 128GB of memory and about a petaflop of FP4 performance, and the RTX Spark runs Windows by default while the DGX Spark runs a customized Ubuntu.

Lewis found the RTX Spark's hardware impressive but the experience unfinished, saying he expected useful AI features and found only some video and audio filters that use the NPU. He wrote that NVIDIA has documentation and a pop-up, which did not appear on his laptop, to help users get started with third-party tools such as OpenClaw, Hermes and Perplexity Portable Computer, but he called those enthusiast tools. He said AI needs to feel like a natural extension of the operating system rather than something tacked on. By contrast he found the DGX Spark polished, praising its Sync app for managing one or more Sparks remotely and noting the OS comes with the packages, libraries and software needed to start quickly.

Lewis reported that the RTX Spark beat the DGX Spark in several situations because its memory is about 10% faster, 300GB/s versus 273GB/s, which means more tokens per second in llama.cpp and Ollama. The DGX Spark still won in work that depends on raw computational power and is not memory limited, such as matrix multiplication or n-body code. He said the Yoga 9n was snappy and responsive and probably the best Windows laptop he has used, but that maxing it out with an AI job drained the battery in less than two hours. He concluded that unless buyers are willing to create or find their own AI tools, the RTX Spark is not worth it at this point in time.

Articles.Title: I’ve used NVIDIA’s AI laptop and its personal AI supercomputer, and only one feels finished - How-To Geek

stories.Headline: AI Capex Hits $740B [2026]: Markets Doubt the Payoff
stories.Summary:
On November 2, 2026, markets opened uneasy about how long Big Tech can keep pouring money into AI data centers. Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft have announced more than $740 billion of combined 2026 capital spending, according to TechCrunch's October 30 tally. Alphabet fell 12 percent on Thursday, wiping out about $500 billion of market value, and the Nasdaq fell 2.9 percent on Friday. Intel fell 25 percent on Friday and Qualcomm 11 percent, while the iShares Semiconductor ETF sat 29 percent below its recent high.

Free cash flow turned negative at three of the four companies. Alphabet posted negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion in the third quarter, its second straight quarter in the red, and Amazon's trailing 12-month figure swung from positive $14.8 billion to negative $42.4 billion. Microsoft stood out with positive $18.6 billion in the latest quarter and spending that came in under its own projection. The five companies including Oracle have together raised $326 billion in debt in 2026, roughly triple the previous year's amount.

Goldman Sachs strategist Ben Snider described earnings growth as strong but no longer accelerating, according to Finimize. Defenders of the spending point to a backlog near $1.7 trillion set against up to $600 billion of 2026 spending at Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon. Oracle expects free cash flow to turn positive in the second half of fiscal 2028 and to top $30 billion in fiscal 2029. CNBC reported that Anthropic's SEC filing showed sales decelerating from the second quarter to the third.

Wall Street analysts expected Big Tech capital expenditure to top $1 trillion in 2027, CNBC reported in April. Goldman Sachs projected hyperscaler spending near $800 billion this year and about $1.2 trillion in 2027, and Alphabet has said it expects its own spending to rise next year. The article lays out five predictions and a short watch list for the next few months. It says that if Oracle's credit spreads widen, expect the others to feel it.

Articles.Title: AI Capex Hits $740B [2026]: Markets Doubt the Payoff

stories.Headline: Microsoft lets advertisers set up to 40 guidelines for AI-written ads
stories.Summary:
Microsoft Advertising began on October 28, 2026 letting advertisers give its AI up to 40 written guidelines on what generated ad copy should and should not say. The change came in an open pilot announced in a monthly roundup on the Microsoft Advertising blog. The same post, which carries no byline, announced general availability of the Conversions API and new search term reporting for Performance Max campaigns. The roundup also added age and gender targeting and auction insights to Performance Max, opened a pilot for audience exclusions, and introduced an AI-assisted setup flow.

The guidelines are available in open pilot for Performance Max campaigns and for Search campaigns that have AI Max enabled. Microsoft recommends using them mainly for broader rules around claims, themes, concepts, tone, or language to avoid, and its example is a high-end retailer adding a line telling the AI never to imply products are low cost. Advertisers can also supply preferred wording, themes, or tone of voice. The guidelines are set in the campaign creation flow, and Microsoft says they reduce the risk of AI generating messaging that does not meet brand or business requirements, though it does not say generated copy will always comply.

Age and gender targeting is now generally available on Performance Max, while device targeting is promised in the coming weeks with no date given. Audience exclusions are in open pilot, and Microsoft is refining brand exclusions so advertisers can apply them to text ads only while still showing product ads on those brand searches. Search term reporting and auction insights reporting are now available, and search term landing page reporting starts rolling out in mid-November. The Conversions API, which lets companies send sales and sign-up data straight from their own systems, is now generally available.

Microsoft framed the roundup around the idea that leaning into AI only pays off when advertisers can steer it and see what is working. The AI-powered setup flow builds a first Performance Max campaign from a new advertiser's website and materials such as marketing plans, brand guidelines, and product images. Several items are pilots that require a request to an account team. The post does not say which markets or languages the setup flow supports, and it gives no figures on how often generated copy breaks a guideline.

Articles.Title: Microsoft lets advertisers set up to 40 guidelines for AI-written ads

stories.Headline: OpenAI reports AI-generated results on major problems in mathematics, computing and physics
stories.Summary:
OpenAI reported on 2 November 2026 that its models produced three research results in mathematics, computer science and physics. The mathematics result is a proof of Sogge's local smoothing conjecture, which concerns how waves concentrate over time. OpenAI says the proof covers every dimension and also resolves the Kakeya and Stein restriction conjectures. The company published an explanatory manuscript and a formal proof in Lean, software that checks mathematical arguments against precise logical rules.

The computer science result is a disproof of the Exponential Time Hypothesis, an assumption about the time needed to solve a problem called 3-SAT. In 3-SAT, a computer must determine whether a collection of logical conditions can all be satisfied at once, with each condition containing three terms that can be true or false. The hypothesis holds that, in the worst case, the time needed grows exponentially with the number of variables. The physics work concerns quantum chromodynamics, the theory of the strong force, and a unified completion of the Standard Model. It also addresses part of the Yang, Mills Millennium Prize problem, which additionally requires establishing a mass gap.

Katrina Mulligan, Head of National Security Partnerships at OpenAI for Government, discussed the results on LinkedIn. A group led by Russell Impagliazzo and Ramamohan Paturi at the University of California San Diego, and Ryan Williams at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, will examine the computer science work. David Gross will lead the physics group, alongside Michael Douglas, Arthur Jaffe, Igor Klebanov and Nikita Nekrasov. An external physics group will determine how to release that work.

The Simons Foundation, Anthropic and OpenAI have committed a combined $15 million in funding and resources to help the mathematics community evaluate results, use new tools and develop shared standards. OpenAI says it continues to invite feedback on the best way to disclose results and engage with scientists to accelerate discovery. The company is working with academic researchers to examine and explain the findings. The result concerns theoretical limits on computation, and developing practical algorithms from it will require further research.

Articles.Title: OpenAI reports AI-generated results on major problems in mathematics, computing and physics

stories.Headline: Eclypsium, NVIDIA Collaborate to Address AI Infrastructure Security Risks
stories.Summary:
Eclypsium and NVIDIA are collaborating to address emerging threats to AI infrastructure, according to a report published on 1 November 2026. New research from Eclypsium, supported by NVIDIA, shows how compromised hardware could undermine the integrity of running models. In a controlled demonstration, researchers used a compromised data processing unit, or DPU, combined with permissive memory isolation, to modify model weights directly in memory. Those weights help determine how a model interprets information and generates responses. Modifying them during execution could let an attacker influence outputs while leaving the stored model unchanged.

Integrity checks focused on the original files would not, by themselves, identify that manipulation, the report says. The collaboration brings together Eclypsium's infrastructure security research and NVIDIA's AI computing expertise to examine an attack surface with implications beyond a single hardware vendor. Their joint blog addresses the relationship between trusted infrastructure and trusted AI. Eclypsium describes the broader challenge as the AI Infrastructure Assurance Gap, where organizations invest in model security without necessarily establishing equivalent confidence in the systems running those models.

The research report underscores why protecting AI requires attention to the hardware, privileged components and isolation controls supporting its execution. Eclypsium and NVIDIA are the parties behind the research and the joint blog. The report does not name any individuals or give further details of what each company said. It also does not say what specific steps organizations should take beyond paying attention to hardware, privileged components and isolation controls.

The articles do not say what happens next beyond the publication of the research and the joint blog. No timeline is given for further work by Eclypsium or NVIDIA. No products, standards or fixes are announced in the articles. The report frames the issue as one that goes beyond a single hardware vendor.

Articles.Title: Eclypsium, NVIDIA Collaborate to Address AI Infrastructure Security Risks

stories.Headline: Fibre made Indian IT reachable. Will AI make it indispensable, or replaceable?
stories.Summary:
In late October 2026, the four biggest American AI spenders, Meta, Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon, reported results for the July to September quarter. Together they spent about $202 billion on capex, more than double the $97 billion of a year earlier, and generated about $176 billion in operating cash, leaving free cash flow of minus $26 billion against plus $62 billion a year before. Investors sold the three that spent more than they generated: Meta fell 7% and Alphabet more than 12%, its worst day since listing in 2004, while Microsoft, which spent about $6 billion less than expected and stayed cash-positive, held up. On Friday 30 October the S&P 500 technology sector fell almost 5% in a day, and Reddit lost 29% of its value after warning that Google's AI search was squeezing its traffic. The same month, the Nifty IT index rose 11.7%, its best week since April 2008.

The article compares this to 2000, when America overbuilt fibre, bandwidth got cheaper by roughly 1.6 times a year, and Indian IT exports grew from $2.6 billion in FY99 to about $50 billion by FY10. It says the price of AI at a given performance level is falling between 9 and 900 times a year, which can complement Indian talent but can also replace some of it. AI now accounts for over 10% of revenue at TCS, $3.1 billion annualised, and 10.5% at Infosys, and HCLTech's advanced-AI revenue grew 78%. Infosys has cut its full-year growth guidance to 1 to 2%, Wipro's large-deal bookings fell almost 60%, and Constellation Research estimates revenue per unit of work is falling 5 to 15% where AI speeds up delivery. India now has 2,117 global capability centres employing 2.36 million people, per Nasscom and Zinnov.

JP Morgan downgraded Indian equities in April 2026 partly because India's large-cap index had minimal AI, datacenter and semiconductor representation, then by September described India as a natural hedge against AI. The article calls Indian IT firms the plumbers of the technology world, helping clients use AI rather than building it. It says TCS has chosen not to wait: its data-centre unit HyperVault plans a campus of up to 1 GW in Hyderabad with up to ₹70,000 crore of investment at full build-out, with TPG able to take up to 49% and debt funding part of the rest. The author, Neeraj Kohli, CEO of Asianxt Digital Technologies, frames the choice as renting talent to the companies that own the compute or owning some of that compute itself.

The article says both models are under test. If AI becomes a cheap utility, the owners of infrastructure will struggle to earn back what they spent and the integrators will win; if AI concentrates power and pricing in a few platforms, the integrators risk becoming subcontractors on thinner margins. It notes Indian IT work depends on Big Tech continuing to spend, and that a growing share of AI work in India bypasses the IT majors through global capability centres. It says only one of the two bets can be fully right, and that whether the rest of the industry follows TCS will say a lot about where India expects to sit in the AI economy.

Articles.Title: Fibre made Indian IT reachable. Will AI make it indispensable, or replaceable?

stories.Headline: Algorithm and the Advocate: Reimagining India’s legal education for the AI century - The Sunday Guardian
stories.Summary:
On 2 July 2026, the Supreme Court of India dealt with a case called Puja Ramesh Singh v. Jammu and Kashmir Bank, which involved judicial decisions that had cited and relied on precedents that did not exist in real life.
