stories.Headline: SemiAnalysis launches GDPx, an agentic capability benchmark measuring 11 domains, including chip design, cybersecurity, and RSI; Opus 5.5 tops with a 12% score (SemiAnalysis)
stories.Summary:
SemiAnalysis launched GDPx on November 2, 2026, a benchmark for measuring how well frontier AI models handle agentic tasks across 11 domains. The domains are chip design, cybersecurity, biology, finance, legal, quant trading, recursive self-improvement, hardware design, materials science, alignment and software engineering. The benchmark was built by Max Kan, Andrew Megalaa and Dylan Patel with 14 specialized data partners, including Aria, Arcverex, Ergodex, Arithmetic, Latch Bio, Living Context, Chakra, Third Moment, Extrapolate, Beautiful Machines, ValenceForge, Emulated, Fleet and Datacurve. Opus 5.5 took the top overall score with just 12%, and SemiAnalysis says even the best model scores only 12%.

The benchmark gives each task a realistic environment rather than a single prompt. A finance example from Living Context is based on a real deal in which Bannock Capital buys about 62% of Haverly Snack Company for $880M plus an earnout, with Eakin Lowry as sell-side banker and Marbury Kline as accounting advisor, and the environment holds about 4,000 anonymized files. Cyber tasks are based on real zero days found by Arithmetic's engineers, materials science tasks run inside simulated laboratories, and hardware design tasks use live Siemens NX sessions tested on real AWS FPGA instances. SemiAnalysis says it forgoes industries such as government, real estate and insurance, and that finance and legal tasks are so hard that basically every model scores exactly 0.

SemiAnalysis says Opus 5.5 is the best all-around model and wins in quant trading, hardware design and chip design, while Gemini 4 Carbon is the best bio model and edges out the win in software engineering, and GPT-6 Astra wins convincingly for RSI and is best for materials science. It says Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra had overall scores lowered by their safety classifiers, and that excluding cyber, biology and alignment changes the results. It also says Muse Wonder Full is the best available cyber model by a meaningful margin. SemiAnalysis argues OpenAI's GDPval, released September 25, 2025, is inadequate for today's agents because its tasks are non-interactive and spoon-feed context, and it cites noisy rubric-based graders with 71% human expert agreement on the gold subset.

SemiAnalysis says it started by picking the domains it believes AI will most accelerate in the next one to two years, tied to a demand model projecting OpenAI and Anthropic revenue in 2027 and 2028, and it reached out to more than 30 RL environment companies. It says partners went through a rigorous QA process, and that for some domains multiple partners wanted exclusivity and it selected the one with the highest quality tasks. It thanks Fireworks for inference on open source models, Modal for sandbox infrastructure and Abhijay Rana for sourcing partners and early QA. It says it cannot make all the comparisons in one newsletter and points readers to the official website to explore the data.

Articles.Title: SemiAnalysis launches GDPx, an agentic capability benchmark measuring 11 domains, including chip design, cybersecurity, and RSI; Opus 5.5 tops with a 12% score (SemiAnalysis)

stories.Headline: Bites, whose AI tools deliver personalized training to frontline workers via WhatsApp, SMS, Slack, and other channels, raised a $40M Series A led by PeakSpan (Meir Orbach/CTech)
stories.Summary:
Bites, an AI platform that creates personalized training for employees who do not work at desks, raised $40 million in a Series A funding round, according to a report by Meir Orbach in Calcalistech. The round was led by PeakSpan Capital, with participation from existing investors Vertex Ventures, Horizon Capital, Rittenhouse Ventures, Lyra Ventures and others. The new funding brings the company's total raised to $55 million. PeakSpan's Phil Dur and Charlie Reinkemeyer will join the company's board.

Bites was founded in 2020 by CEO Eran Heffetz, COO Tal Nagler Almog and CIO Hagai Horovitz. The company employs 30 people across its development center in Tel Aviv and its headquarters in New York. Its customers include Unilever, Coca-Cola, Shake Shack, Wynn Resorts, The Venetian and Compass Group, as well as Israeli companies in hospitality and retail. The platform turns documents and standard operating procedures into branded training videos within minutes, delivered through channels employees already use, including WhatsApp, SMS, Microsoft Teams and Slack.

Heffetz said his route into technology began with a problem he encountered while managing restaurants and bars in Tel Aviv, where he repeatedly had to retrain staff as employees left and new workers joined. He said running restaurants taught him that business performance comes down to what people do on the floor every day, and whether they have the knowledge and support to do it well. He said the company initially faced a slow adoption process, although sales continued, primarily in the United States, and he described the past year as a turning point as the product evolved to serve large enterprises. He said AI has served as a significant catalyst, and that to create effective content that actually drives action, the process must be data-driven and supported by automated tools.

The company cites an estimate that approximately 80% of the global workforce, or about 2.8 billion people, do not work at a desk. Each lesson, known as a "Bite," lasts up to 90 seconds and combines a short video with a question, a summary and a discussion, and the platform supports more than 150 languages. Bites says its customers typically achieve engagement rates above 90% within three weeks, and it reports net revenue retention of 161%. The company plans to use the funding to accelerate its expansion in the United States, develop its AI platform, grow its sales and customer success teams, build partner and reseller channels, and expand into banking, insurance and businesses that rely on external workers.

Articles.Title: Bites, whose AI tools deliver personalized training to frontline workers via WhatsApp, SMS, Slack, and other channels, raised a $40M Series A led by PeakSpan (Meir Orbach/CTech)

stories.Headline: A profile of UCLA professor Terence Tao, who was once enthusiastic about AI's role in math but now warns of AI destroying the field's deliberative process (Rivka Galchen/New Yorker)
stories.Summary:
In early 2026, mathematicians and hobbyists using AI tools began solving some of the simpler unsolved Erdős problems, and in January GPT-5.2 Pro appeared to solve Erdős Problem #728 largely on its own, with Terence Tao and others verifying the proof. On May 20, OpenAI published a proof of Erdős Problem #90, the unit-distance problem, which top mathematicians had already worked on. On September 8, OpenAI announced it had solved the Navier-Stokes existence-and-smoothness problem, one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems announced by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000, each carrying a million-dollar award. Tao, a UCLA professor who won a Fields Medal at age thirty-one and founded the Foundation for Science and AI Research in 2025, gave a talk at Caltech three days later.

Tao said solutions were being published with little explanation or detail, relying on mathematicians to verify and explain them for free. AI-generated submissions were overwhelming journals and databases, and the volunteer system of referees was collapsing under the weight of what the article calls slop. He said sometimes even the person submitting a paper did not understand it, and that answers matter less than the insights gained while working toward them. He said the field has to slow down and called the pace insane. Asked where new problems would come from, he said they emerge from the slow, deliberative process of working toward a solution, and that this is what is being destroyed.

Tao was once enthusiastic about AI in math, when many peers dismissed it as a toy that makes many mistakes. AI labs such as Google DeepMind, OpenAI and Anthropic use math problems as benchmarks because proofs can be digitized and objectively verified. AI tools scored at the silver-medal level at the International Mathematical Olympiad in 2024 and at the gold level in 2025. Tao said AI solves problems in ways orthogonal to how humans do, devoting pages to what would be obvious to an undergraduate and only a few lines to what is a large, cloudy move for a human. The article does not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: A profile of UCLA professor Terence Tao, who was once enthusiastic about AI's role in math but now warns of AI destroying the field's deliberative process (Rivka Galchen/New Yorker)

stories.Headline: Dartmouth official resigns over AI use
stories.Summary:
Dartmouth Provost Santiago Schnell resigned after a faculty committee found he used artificial intelligence to shape his writing, the university announced on Wednesday. The investigation began in September after the student newspaper The Dartmouth and the outlet Semafor raised questions about his work. Semafor ran guest columns from major newspapers through an AI filter and found that Schnell's August Washington Post column, titled "Universities are fighting AI cheating. But there's a deeper problem," was entirely written by AI. The Dartmouth then ran other publications by Schnell through an AI detector and found high rates of AI use in his recent writing, while writing that predated ChatGPT's 2022 public release was found to be human-written.

The faculty committee concluded that Schnell used AI to meaningfully alter his writing in violation of at least one publication's AI use or disclosure requirement. It found he failed to disclose his AI use in clear violation of a national newspaper's stated policy, was not forthcoming about his AI use, and fell short of the standards set by Dartmouth's Code of Ethical Conduct, the Academic Honor Principle, and Geisel's Policy on Expectations for Professionalism. Schnell had said his use of AI was limited to language refinement, copy editing, improving clarity and organization, and making writing processes more efficient. He also told The Dartmouth he developed the substance and wrote a draft of an email, then used an AI tool to assist with language and clarity, and the paper found that statement was AI-written.

Dartmouth President Sian Leah Beilock said Schnell's departure was his decision and that the school wishes him well. She wrote that keeping Dartmouth at the forefront of AI means leading through an environment that is fluid and fast-changing, and that leaders must model the transparency and human judgment expected from students and scholars. Schnell, a Venezuelan-born mathematical biologist, previously taught and held leadership roles at the University of Notre Dame, the University of Michigan and Indiana University. He referred questions to his attorneys, who did not immediately respond to an email from The Associated Press seeking comment.

Matthew Delmont, a professor of history, will take over Schnell's position and become interim provost until June 2028. The announcement comes as colleges across the country grapple with how to transform teaching as more assignments can be completed with AI tools. Dartmouth touts itself as the birthplace of AI, saying the field got its start at the school in Hanover, New Hampshire, in 1956. A conference commemorating the 70th anniversary, titled "What Must Remain Human?", began Thursday.

Articles.Title: Dartmouth official resigns over AI use

stories.Headline: CrowdStrike’s SafeMind pits AI attackers against AI defenders
stories.Summary:
CrowdStrike has built a system called SafeMind that sets offensive AI models against emulated company networks and uses the traces of their attacks to train defensive models that can lock those networks down on their own. The work is led by CrowdStrike's Cyber Superintelligence Lab, which grew out of chief executive George Kurtz's ambition for the company to be the only pure-play cyber security firm doing frontier-style AI research. CrowdStrike unveiled SafeMind at its Fal.Con conference in Las Vegas in September. Bartley Richardson, CrowdStrike's chief AI and autonomous systems officer, described it as an "AI security factory" that turns out models, the harnesses that put them to work and the benchmarks used to evaluate them, with other parts to come online later.

The defensive models are trained by pitting them against offensive ones, an idea in machine learning that goes back to generative adversarial networks. The effort rests on 15 years of human-annotated adversary data collected by CrowdStrike and a harness that spins up emulated enterprise networks on real virtual machines, with 40,000 to 60,000 running at a time. CrowdStrike calls its offensive models Red Tempest and its defensive models Blue Solano. The red models are based on Nvidia's Nemotron family and open-weight models from Chinese developers including Zhipu AI's GLM, Moonshot AI's Kimi and Alibaba's Qwen, while the blue models rely largely on Nemotron, including its Ultra, Super and Nano versions. Nvidia is CrowdStrike's AI design partner on the project.

Richardson said the real goal of SafeMind from the beginning was to create the best defensive capabilities and tilt the advantage back to the defender, and that to create the best defence you must learn from the best possible offence. He said enough rounds of the loop make an attack intractable, and the aim is a defender model that understands the state of a network, including how misconfigurations compound, and acts as autonomously as possible. He said the company has a better understanding of the supply chain behind the Nemotron models and can run them in customer environments more easily. He also said the level of autonomy SafeMind gets in a customer's environment is up to that customer's risk appetite, so CrowdStrike keeps it tunable.

CrowdStrike is rolling out SafeMind in phases, starting with defensive models that will drive parts of its Falcon platform, with the first to be announced at Fal.Con Europe in Barcelona this week. More sophisticated customers will get direct access through Project QuiltWorks, which CrowdStrike launched in April as an industry coalition and is now shaping into its version of trusted-access programmes. The last phase is to make the emulation environment a product, with customers pumping Falcon telemetry into an emulated version of their network and getting detection content built for how that network is configured, without needing cloud access so long as they have enough compute. CrowdStrike is also training smaller models, including classifiers and small language models, to generate detection content and is looking into AI-powered honeypots, which Richardson said is in its early stages.

Articles.Title: CrowdStrike’s SafeMind pits AI attackers against AI defenders

stories.Headline: Türkiye launches antitrust probe into Google over AI search features
stories.Summary:
Türkiye's Competition Authority opened an investigation into Google's AI-powered search features and ordered interim measures over suspected unfair practices affecting news publishers. The probe targets AI Overviews and AI Mode and will examine whether the features violate competition law, according to a statement on the regulator's website. The board said evidence of potentially discriminatory and exploitative practices had reached the level of strong suspicion, which prompted the interim measures. Google introduced both features in Türkiye in February 2026.

The interim measures require Google to set conditions that prevent discrimination among publishers and reflect the economic value of content used in its AI services. Google must also let publishers decide whether their material appears in AI Overviews and AI Mode independently of their visibility and indexing across other Google services. This is meant to stop publishers having to choose between appearing in AI-generated responses and keeping their visibility in conventional search results. The measures do not ban the AI features. The investigation also looks at whether Google's content-use agreements with publishers contain unfair terms and whether the features have exclusionary effects on publishers and AI chatbot providers.

The board is responsible for the probe and issued the interim measures through its statement. It said the evidence of practices affecting news publishers had reached the level of strong suspicion. The regulator's concerns center on how Google uses publishers' content and the possible impact on competition. Google has not commented in the articles.

AI Overviews shows AI-generated summaries at the top of search results, drawing on websites and linking to sources. AI Mode offers a conversational search experience for more complex questions and follow-up queries. Both are available in Türkiye, and their use of material from across the web has raised concerns about traffic reaching original publishers. Publishers that rely on visits for advertising and subscribers could see income affected if referral traffic falls.

Articles.Title: Türkiye launches antitrust probe into Google over AI search features

stories.Headline: Hybridizing expert descriptors and learned embeddings yields transferable Mat2Vec-* element representations
stories.Summary:
Researchers reported a method for combining handcrafted chemical descriptors with learned element embeddings to produce reusable element representations called Mat2Vec-*. The work was published in Communications Chemistry on November 1, 2026, with a listed author group including Qiong Feng, Haotian Chen, Yuhang Wang and Tao Yang. The team trained controlled models on eight structure-based MatBench regression tasks, running 2,240 models across representation mixtures and latent dimensions. They used two crystal-graph backbones, CGCNN and MEGNet, and distilled the top-performing models into rotation-invariant cosine-distance relations. The distilled tables come in three forms, Mat2Vec-S from the hybrid, plus single-channel variants Mat2Vec-H and Mat2Vec-L. In the composition-only CrabNet model, the tables replaced or augmented corpus-derived Mat2Vec, and most configurations improved performance across all four MatBench composition tasks.

On the Matbench Discovery WBM benchmark, Mat2Vec-* features reduced errors for several modern structure-based predictors through lightweight residual correction. The authors describe the result as a compact, transferable supervised chemical prior for materials prediction. The authors said handcrafted and supervised representations encode complementary chemical information, and that supervised element geometry can be distilled into reusable tables. They noted that the additive fusion operation alone is not their contribution, and that fusion instead exposes a stable element-element relational geometry. They reported that hybrid inputs outperformed single-source endpoints across the controlled grid and that the learned and descriptor-derived channels stayed weakly entangled.

They used CGCNN and MEGNet as controlled testbeds rather than state-of-the-art predictors, and they evaluated the tables in two transfer regimes not used for distillation to avoid data leakage. The work frames element representations as a shared but often under-examined part of materials machine learning, sitting between discrete element identities and continuous vectors. The authors said the three usual approaches, handcrafted descriptors, corpus-derived embeddings and supervised embeddings, are typically treated as separate choices rather than complementary sources. They asked whether stable element relations from supervised prediction can be reused beyond the models that produced them. The article does not say what happens next beyond describing the transfer tests and the released table family.

Articles.Title: Hybridizing expert descriptors and learned embeddings yields transferable Mat2Vec-* element representations

stories.Headline: Empowering Breast Cancer Precision Diagnosis with Advanced Ultrasound: From Radiomics to Radio-multiomics
stories.Summary:
A review article on advanced ultrasound for breast cancer diagnosis was published on November 1, 2026, according to the DOI listing. The authors are Mo Li, Letian Jin, Ge Xue, Jiye Chen, Mohamed Aimene Benariba, Vicky Yang Wang, Gaojun Teng and Dong Xu. They are affiliated with institutions in Hangzhou, Quzhou, Taizhou and Wenling in Zhejiang, China, and with Southeast University in Nanjing, Jiangsu, China. The corresponding author is Dong Xu, listed with the Department of Diagnostic Ultrasound Imaging and Interventional Therapy at Zhejiang Cancer Hospital and the Hangzhou Institute of Medicine, Chinese Academy of Sciences. The article appears on the SciOpen platform, and a note says the content was generated by AMiner AI, with SciOpen taking no responsibility for it.

The review covers multi-modal ultrasound imaging, including microvascular and super-resolution imaging with contrast enhancement, elastography and viscoelastic imaging. It also covers quantitative analysis through radiofrequency signal analysis, radiomics and artificial intelligence-based image analysis. The authors describe uses in telling benign from malignant tumors, characterizing molecular subtypes and assessing lymph node metastasis. They trace a path from radiomics alone through radiogenomics to radio-multiomics, which combines ultrasound radiomics with genomic, transcriptomic and other multi-omics data. The article states that most radio-multiomics approaches remain at a preclinical or proof-of-concept stage.

The authors say breast cancer has substantial biological and molecular heterogeneity that conventional imaging and biopsy cannot fully capture, since biopsy is limited by sampling error and invasiveness. They write that ultrasound has moved from morphological imaging only to multi-dimensional functional imaging with quantitative analysis, improving diagnostic accessibility and efficiency. They describe radio-multiomics as a promising strategy for non-invasive molecular phenotyping, though its clinical application is still at its infancy. They also say such approaches still require validation in large-scale paired cohorts.

The review lists standardization, reproducibility, interpretability and data heterogeneity as issues that remain to be resolved. It discusses current challenges that should be addressed before ultrasound-based radio-multi-omics can be translated into a viable clinical tool. The article is open access under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International license. No abstract is available for the article, and the page offers a button to view the PDF directly.

Articles.Title: Empowering Breast Cancer Precision Diagnosis with Advanced Ultrasound: From Radiomics to Radio-multiomics

stories.Headline: Can SpaceX Overcome the AI Trade Sell-Off?
stories.Summary:
SpaceX held its initial public offering in June, and its shares have stayed below the $150 opening price since then, trading at about $134.72 in the most recent session, down roughly 5% from that opening price. In the third quarter, which ended September 30, the company's AI revenue jumped 830% to $7.6 billion and made up 52% of total revenue. That AI segment includes the Grok bot and the rental of AI cloud capacity to customers. Even so, shareholders stayed skeptical and the stock has remained under its IPO price for months.

The wider AI sell-off has hit many tech stocks as investors question whether huge data center spending will pay off. Microsoft reported that Azure cloud revenue for its first fiscal quarter, ended September 30, rose 48% to $33.1 billion, and it said Azure revenue will grow by up to 50% this quarter. Alphabet's stock fell about 10% the day after its third-quarter results, when capital expenditures reached $51.3 billion and the company missed analysts' estimates for sales and earnings. SpaceX's own capital expenditures rose 185% to $19.6 billion in the quarter, with 83% of that going to AI, and the company says capex will reach up to $40 billion this year.

SpaceX is not entirely dependent on AI, since Starlink sales rose 69% to $5.2 billion with 13.6 million subscribers and the business is profitable. Its launch business grew too, with 12 launches in the quarter and a 6% revenue increase to $1.8 billion. Chris Neiger of The Motley Fool wrote that it is reasonable for shareholders and potential investors to be skeptical about the spending right now. He added that the pessimism about so much capex could hamper the stock for a while and that it is unlikely SpaceX will overcome the AI trade sell-off at the moment.

The article says investors are watching closely to see whether SpaceX can keep its AI sales accelerating as spending rises. Neiger wrote that the stock could struggle to gain ground if investors continue to doubt tech companies' AI investments. The Motley Fool's Stock Advisor team did not include SpaceX among its 10 best stocks to buy now. The article gives no further details on what happens next for the company.

Articles.Title: Can SpaceX Overcome the AI Trade Sell-Off?

stories.Headline: CoS-VQ: Coordinated Shared-Scale Vector Quantization for Large Language Models
stories.Summary:
Zukang Xu, Zhixiong Zhao, Xing Hu, Zhe Jiang, Xin Si and Dawei Yang posted a paper titled CoS-VQ: Coordinated Shared-Scale Vector Quantization for Large Language Models to arXiv on November 1, 2026. The paper proposes a method for low-bit weight quantization of large language models, which need substantial memory. The authors say existing vector quantization methods often improve accuracy by increasing the effective coding dimension, which can complicate independent lookup and local codeword updates. CoS-VQ instead keeps low-dimensional codewords while jointly optimizing hard indices and their shared scale across positions. The method addresses what the authors call scale-induced coupling, where the best scale depends on the whole codeword combination and in turn changes candidate rankings across positions.

CoS-VQ collects candidates at multiple probe scales and builds a tangent separable upper bound for the residual-aware quadratic objective. By reducing candidate comparisons to lower envelopes of lines over positive scales, it finds finitely many representative intervals for joint index and scale updates without listing every codeword combination. On Qwen3.8-27B, the authors report that CoS-VQ outperforms QTIP and LLVQ on the evaluated language modeling, coding and reasoning benchmarks. The authors say ablations from the same initialization show larger gains from joint updates than from scale-only refinement. They present joint selection as an alternative to increasing codeword dimensionality.

The paper lists six authors, and the abstract says the code is available at a URL given there. The posting appears on arXiv under identifier 2610.37336. The abstract does not say what happens next beyond the release of the paper and the code. It gives no further plans for the work.

Articles.Title: CoS-VQ: Coordinated Shared-Scale Vector Quantization for Large Language Models

stories.Headline: ADTGuard: Adaptive Depth-Time Safeguard for Streaming Inference in Large Language Models
stories.Summary:
Chuming Wei, Churui Yang, Zihan Zhang, Ruien Li, Wusheng Zhang, Yan Zhang and Guangwen Yang posted a paper on arXiv on 1 November 2026 describing a safeguard for streaming inference in large language models. The paper says large language models can produce fluent answers to many user requests, but streaming can expose users to harmful content before generation finishes. It says existing guardrails have two weaknesses in this setting. One is that moderation at response or chunk boundaries comes too late, so harmful material may be seen before it is checked.

The paper introduces ADTGuard, which checks each token before it is released, refines token-level training targets step by step, and adapts layer selection to the current prefix. It models risk across depth and time through Depth-Time Safety Dynamics, which combines safety evidence across layers at each token and uses it to guide risk accumulation over successive tokens. A Causal Depth Router adapts the choice of observation layers to the current prefix. With only response-level labels available, Risk-Onset Target Refinement progressively builds token-level training targets for both components. The authors report experiments across multiple safety benchmarks in which ADTGuard matched or surpassed state-of-the-art safeguards while requiring only 16M trainable parameters and keeping competitive per-token latency.

The authors are responsible for the work, and the paper presents their findings in its own words. They say existing post-hoc moderation delays intervention and risks harmful exposure when content is released before verification. They also say coarse response-level supervision does not specify when harmful content begins, and fixed-layer readouts may miss relevant safety signals at other depths. They describe their experiments as extensive and say the method consistently achieves strong streaming detection performance.

The paper is listed on arXiv with the identifier 2610.36574 and is dated 1 November 2026. It appears under the title ADTGuard: Adaptive Depth-Time Safeguard for Streaming Inference in Large Language Models, with a PDF and other formats offered. The listing also includes standard arXivLabs text about collaborators and shared values. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the paper's publication.

Articles.Title: ADTGuard: Adaptive Depth-Time Safeguard for Streaming Inference in Large Language Models

stories.Headline: Meta Models: Models that Model Learning
stories.Summary:
Peihang Li and Ziming Liu posted a paper on arXiv on November 1, 2026, titled Meta Models: Models that Model Learning. The paper studies meta-models, which are models that predict how other models will learn. The authors say every neural-network training run produces a model and also evidence about how models learn. They ask whether accumulated experiments can let people predict and compare new training runs before those runs are executed.

The paper treats final-performance prediction, learning-curve prediction and hyperparameter selection as different queries to the same training response function. The authors take what they call a first, humble empirical step by treating real language-model training records as native numeric data. They find that an off-the-shelf tabular in-context learner, TabPFN, can match or outperform a fine-tuned LLM meta-model in multiple evaluated settings. Recent work fine-tunes LLMs on tokenized configurations at a cost of tens to hundreds of GPU-hours, while TabPFN needs seconds of fit-and-predict time without task-specific weight updates. Adding Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks, or KANs, to TabPFN further improves accuracy on selected prediction tasks.

The authors argue that meta-modeling is better treated as its own numeric modality rather than as a text task for LLMs. They pre-registered a forecast of the Marin Hero Run, a 535B-parameter public training run. The ground truth of that run is revealed point by point as training progresses, which puts meta-model predictions to the test against outcomes not yet observed at the time of forecasting. The paper is by Peihang Li and one other author, Ziming Liu.

The posting appears on arXiv, which describes arXivLabs as a framework that lets collaborators develop and share features on its website. arXiv says both individuals and organizations working with arXivLabs have accepted its values of openness, community, excellence and user data privacy. arXiv states that it is committed to these values and works only with partners that adhere to them. The page also invites ideas for projects that would add value for the arXiv community.

Articles.Title: Meta Models: Models that Model Learning

stories.Headline: VideoLVR: Latent Visual Reasoning over Grounded Video Evidence
stories.Summary:
Shilong Li, Xingyuan Bu, Hao Shi, Yun Xing, Weixin Feng, Qiangpeng Yang and Shilei Wen posted a paper titled VideoLVR: Latent Visual Reasoning over Grounded Video Evidence to the arXiv repository on 1 November 2026. The work addresses a problem in video understanding by multimodal large language models, where language-based reasoning traces do not give the model a reliable way to revisit relevant visual evidence. This leads to visual forgetting and weakens the model's ability to reason over video content. The authors list the paper under Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition and Artificial Intelligence.

The paper says existing methods keep visual grounding during reasoning in two main ways. One way refers to evidence using textual coordinates, which give symbolic locations rather than the visual content itself. The other reinserts cropped regions or frames into the multimodal context, which keeps visual details but expands the context substantially. VideoLVR instead builds latent visual evidence from local regions at relevant video moments, giving visual support for intermediate reasoning steps. The authors add a visual token prediction objective that treats visual token reconstruction as prediction over a vocabulary derived from the input video, so visual evidence reconstruction and text generation share one token prediction framework.

The authors say this shared framework lets the models reason over interleaved text tokens and latent visual states while integrating evidence from different moments. They also extend VideoLVR to reinforcement learning by treating sampled visual tokens as actions alongside text tokens and jointly optimizing the policy using final-answer rewards. According to the abstract, VideoLVR improves video understanding without substantially expanding the multimodal context by efficiently revisiting task-relevant visual information during reasoning. The authors report experiments on multiple video benchmarks showing the method is effective, especially on tasks that require fine-grained visual evidence.

The paper is listed under Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition and Artificial Intelligence, and the arXiv page offers a PDF, experimental HTML and TeX source. The page also describes arXivLabs, a framework that lets collaborators develop and share features directly on the arXiv website. It says individuals and organizations working with arXivLabs have accepted values of openness, community, excellence and user data privacy, and that arXiv works only with partners who adhere to them. The page invites ideas for projects that would add value for the arXiv community.

Articles.Title: VideoLVR: Latent Visual Reasoning over Grounded Video Evidence

stories.Headline: Wall Street Veteran Dumps Most of His NVIDIA Stake, Warns of AI Spending Slowdown
stories.Summary:
Steve Weiss, founder and managing partner of Short Hills Capital Partners, said he sold most of his NVIDIA holdings, according to a CNBC interview on Friday reported by Benzinga on Nov. 2, 2026. He said he was concerned that AI infrastructure spending may be nearing a peak. He warned of significant over-ordering of memory chips, semiconductors and data-center capacity, and he compared the situation with earlier technology investment cycles. NVIDIA stock rose nearly 2% in Monday's premarket trading as technology stocks gained ground.

Weiss said AI investment is far from over, but he expects capital-spending growth to slow as companies assess their returns. He questioned whether hyperscalers can keep up their current pace of AI investment even though major technology companies continue to report strong growth. NVIDIA was set to report earnings on Nov. 17, with analysts expecting $2.48 per share on revenue of $109.17 billion, compared with $1.30 per share and $57.01 billion a year earlier. The stock carried a consensus Buy rating, with an average analyst price forecast of $342.08 across 50 analysts.

The article said NVIDIA traded 6.1% below its 20-day simple moving average of $221.46 and 6.2% below its 50-day SMA of $221.75, signaling near-term weakness. It sat 3.1% below its 100-day SMA of $214.52 but remained 1.7% above its 200-day SMA of $204.38, suggesting the longer-term trend remained intact. The MACD indicator stayed below its signal line, pointing to weakening momentum, with resistance near $235 and support around $190. NVIDIA shares gained 1.64% to $207.99 in Monday's premarket trading, according to Benzinga Pro data.

Articles.Title: Wall Street Veteran Dumps Most of His NVIDIA Stake, Warns of AI Spending Slowdown

stories.Headline: Machine Learning Hamiltonians with Polarizations for Heterogeneous Systems
stories.Summary:
A paper posted on arXiv on November 1, 2026 describes a machine learning model for predicting Hamiltonians in heterogeneous systems. The work is by Jia-Yu Zhou, Wentao Zhang, Mouyi Weng, Zhao-Yi Yan and Lin-Wang Wang. Machine learning Hamiltonians normally use local atomic structures to determine local Hamiltonian matrix elements without self-consistent calculations. The authors say that in heterogeneous systems the electron electrostatic potential energy is often set by faraway features, such as interface or surface dipoles, or even an applied voltage in a nanodevice, so local atomic structures alone cannot determine it.

The proposed model is called DeepH-Polar. It explicitly predicts intrinsic atomic dipoles and polarizability tensors and uses them to solve the electron electrostatic potential energy self-consistently. The authors note that intrinsic dipoles and polarizabilities are local properties, while the applied potential energy is a prescribed input. Benchmarks on polar GaN systems and crystalline-Si/amorphous-SiO2 interfaces show improved Hamiltonian accuracy, reproduction of thickness-dependent electrostatic variations, and spatially nonuniform field-induced screening that models without polarization fail to capture.

The model also allows the study of nanoscale electronic devices. By iteratively solving the Hamiltonian eigenproblem and self-consistently updating free-carrier occupations and the electrostatic potential, the authors simulate an 8,194-atom gated semiconductor device. The paper states that machine learning Hamiltonians have been used to study large systems and to carry out high-throughput screening for their electronic and optical properties. The authors present DeepH-Polar as a physically informed model that addresses the limitation of local-only predictions in heterogeneous systems.

The article does not say what happens next beyond the benchmarks and the device simulation. It reports improved accuracy on the tested systems and the ability to model spatially nonuniform field-induced screening. It also reports the simulation of the gated device with 8,194 atoms. No further plans or follow-up work are given in the article.

Articles.Title: Machine Learning Hamiltonians with Polarizations for Heterogeneous Systems

stories.Headline: Robust LLM Data Selection via Content-Invariant Gradient Attribution
stories.Summary:
Jia Gu, Liang Pang and Huawei Shen posted a paper to arXiv on November 1, 2026, describing a new method for choosing instruction fine-tuning data for large language models. The paper is titled Robust LLM Data Selection via Content-Invariant Gradient Attribution and carries the identifier 2610.36755. The authors report that existing global gradient attribution methods suffer from what they call surface-form bias. Small changes to details that do not affect meaning, such as wording or formatting, can produce highly inconsistent attribution scores even when the underlying content stays the same. To address this, the authors propose Content-Invariant Gradient Attribution, or CIGA, a framework for instruction data selection.

CIGA first identifies layers whose gradients are both influential for attribution and stable under semantics-preserving surface-form perturbations, which reduces formatting noise in gradient features. It then dynamically fuses these attribution signals with semantic representations of the input, combining optimization-level influence with content-level information. The abstract reports extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks, and it says CIGA also reduces attribution cost. The authors say CIGA produces more stable rankings under surface-form perturbations while preserving downstream capabilities and improving average performance. They describe it as a robust and efficient approach to data selection for LLM instruction tuning.

The paper is attributed to Jia Gu, Liang Pang and Huawei Shen, listed as Jia Gu and two other authors. The posting page also includes standard arXivLabs text about openness, community, excellence and user data privacy, and a note inviting ideas for projects that would add value for the arXiv community. The articles do not say what happens next, such as whether the work will be published elsewhere or released as code. They give no numbers beyond the paper identifier and the posting date of November 1, 2026. No independent comment or response from other researchers is included.

Articles.Title: Robust LLM Data Selection via Content-Invariant Gradient Attribution

stories.Headline: Amazon vs. Home Depot: One Is Riding the AI Boom, While the Other Faces a Different Reality
stories.Summary:
Amazon reported third quarter 2026 revenue of $201.9 billion, up 12% from a year earlier, in results published around the end of October 2026. Its cloud unit, Amazon Web Services, grew 39% to $46 billion as demand for cloud computing and artificial intelligence infrastructure accelerated, and North American retail sales rose 6%. Home Depot reported second quarter fiscal 2026 revenue of $47.9 billion, up 5.7%, with comparable sales up 1.7% but customer transactions down 0.8%. The figures come from a Motley Fool comparison of the two retailers' last eight quarters, which also lists Amazon's revenue of $187.8 billion in the quarter ended Dec. 31, 2024, $155.7 billion in the quarter ended March 31, 2025, $167.7 billion in the quarter ended June 30, 2025, $180.2 billion in the quarter ended Sept. 30, 2025, $213.4 billion in the quarter ended Dec. 31, 2025, $181.5 billion in the quarter ended March 31, 2026, and $200.6 billion in the quarter ended June 30, 2026, and Home Depot's revenue of $39.7 billion in the quarter ended Feb. 2, 2025, $39.9 billion in the quarter ended May 4, 2025, $45.3 billion in the quarter ended Aug. 3, 2025, $41.4 billion in the quarter ended Nov. 2, 2025, $38.2 billion in the quarter ended Feb. 1, 2026, and $41.8 billion in the quarter ended May 3, 2026.

The article says Amazon draws revenue from global e-commerce, AWS, advertising and subscriptions, while Home Depot sells building materials, home improvement products and professional installation services to homeowners and contractors. Home Depot's management said consumers continued to favor smaller repair and maintenance projects as housing affordability pressures weighed on larger renovations. The article says higher spending per purchase, rather than more customer traffic, drove Home Depot's growth, and that elevated interest rates and housing affordability make sustained revenue growth harder for the company. It says AWS earns substantially higher operating margins than Amazon's retail business, so continued cloud growth could have an outsized effect on profitability.

The article is an investing analysis by RJ Fulton, published Nov. 2, 2026, and it draws no statements from Amazon itself beyond the reported figures. It says Home Depot remains a strong business with an established customer base and significant exposure to professional contractors, and that a recovery in housing activity could give its sales a meaningful boost, though the timing is uncertain. It calls Amazon the better buy for long-term investors, citing its multiple growth engines and expanding cloud business, and says Home Depot could benefit considerably from an eventual housing recovery. Home Depot had not yet reported results for the quarter ended Sept. 30, 2026, according to the article.

Articles.Title: Amazon vs. Home Depot: One Is Riding the AI Boom, While the Other Faces a Different Reality

stories.Headline: Dynamical coarse-graining of neural-network training
stories.Summary:
A paper titled Dynamical coarse-graining of neural-network training was posted on arXiv on November 1, 2026. Its authors are Lin-Juan Wang, Da Li, Huiling Duan and Jianxiang Wang. The work concerns neural-network training, which the abstract describes as something that can be predicted and controlled in a state space far smaller than the parameter space. The paper is listed under machine learning, soft condensed matter and neural and evolutionary computing.

The paper first defines a learning operator that follows the training law of neural networks. It then establishes a descent theorem for that operator, which is meant to determine whether the operator is sufficient to characterize the learning dynamics. After that it presents an exact closure theorem and a dynamic coarse-graining theorem in sequence. The authors say the three theorems together give a systematic framework for building and assessing dynamical coarse-grained models of neural-network training.

The authors demonstrate the applicability of the theorems with a finite-width nonlinear ReLU network. For a fixed pattern, its dynamic coarse-grained model is exactly derived and is composed of five independent moments. The authors say this model exactly predicts the training outputs and the evolving learning operator. They add that the framework may also guide the development of approximate coarse-grained models for more general neural networks when exact closure is unavailable.

The article does not name any individual as responsible beyond the four listed authors. It does not include any statements from them beyond the abstract. The abstract says the three theorems provide a systematic framework for constructing and assessing dynamical coarse-grained models. It also says the framework may guide approximate models for more general networks when exact closure is unavailable.

Articles.Title: Dynamical coarse-graining of neural-network training

stories.Headline: Let the Gate Decide: Per-Lookup Precision for Quantized Conditional Memory in LLMs
stories.Summary:
Tianqi Chen, Xunchao Li, Linchuan Xie, Guanghua Yu, Jianchen Zhu, Peisong Wang and Jian Cheng posted a paper to arXiv on November 1, 2026 about conditional memory layers in large language models. These layers, such as DeepSeek's Engram, attach large hashed n-gram tables to a model. The authors report that removing them from DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash costs 36.8 PopQA points. They also found that low-bit quantization loses long-tail facts first, and that the usual fix of giving more bits to frequently accessed rows does worse than refining rows at random.

The paper traces this to the gate that scales each retrieved row. A lookup's quantization error is weighted by its gate, which is small for frequent n-grams and large for the rare n-grams of long-tail entities, and the gate can be computed from a 1-bit code. Their method, GateRQ, stores each row as a ladder of 1-bit residual codes, keeps level 1 in GPU memory to compute the gate, and reads deeper levels only for the lookups the gate ranks highest. Without retraining, GateRQ cuts GPU table memory by 7.8x on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, which raises vLLM throughput by 11% to 31% over FP8 tables. It loses about 1 PopQA point at 1.50 bits read per lookup and 0.2 points at 2.10 bits across two models.

The authors are responsible for the work, and the abstract presents these results as their findings. The paper is listed on arXiv with the identifier 2610.35985. The posting also includes links to a PDF, experimental HTML and TeX source, and a note describing arXivLabs, a framework for collaborators to develop and share features on the site. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the paper's availability.

Articles.Title: Let the Gate Decide: Per-Lookup Precision for Quantized Conditional Memory in LLMs

stories.Headline: AI security for OT and industrial environments
stories.Summary:
AI is starting to appear in industrial settings for reasons such as analysing alarms, summarising maintenance notes, supporting predictive maintenance and speeding up engineering tasks, according to a Security Bloggers Network post from Clear Path Security Ltd published on 2 November 2026. In OT environments the security bar differs from a normal business application, because the main concerns are not only confidentiality and integrity but also availability, safety and controlled change. A model that gives a wrong answer in a back-office workflow may be inconvenient, but the same model can create operational disruption or safety issues if it influences a setpoint, a maintenance decision or an operator action. For UK SMEs running plants, utilities, warehouses or industrial services, the post says the right approach is to treat AI as part of the control environment rather than as a standalone IT feature.

The post says AI is being introduced into industrial operations in a few common ways, including large language models that help engineers with documentation, shift handover summaries or troubleshooting. Others connect AI to historians, SCADA data, maintenance systems or engineering workstations to detect anomalies or recommend actions, and in more advanced cases AI is linked to workflow tools that can create tickets, trigger maintenance tasks or suggest control changes. The problem is that industrial environments are built around predictable behaviour, with long asset lifecycles, vendor-specific protocols and strict change windows, while AI systems are more dynamic and may depend on cloud services, external APIs, changing prompts, retrained models or retrieval from live documents. The post says this introduces a wider attack surface and more uncertainty, and that availability and safety matter more because downtime can stop production and an incorrect recommendation can be acted on by a human or an automated workflow.

The post names data poisoning as one of the most important risks, because an attacker or careless insider can influence output by inserting misleading records, manipulated maintenance notes or false examples into the data set. It also describes model tampering, where a changed model artefact, configuration, prompt template or orchestration layer can alter thresholds, instructions or how alerts are prioritised. Prompt injection is relevant where AI reads documents, emails, tickets, manuals or web content and then acts on them, and indirect prompt injection is particularly important in retrieval workflows because a harmful instruction may be hidden inside a document that looks legitimate. Shadow AI and unmanaged integrations create a quieter risk, since staff may use public AI tools outside approved channels and sensitive operational data can leave the environment without review.

The post recommends starting with segmentation and identity, placing AI services in a constrained zone with tightly defined conduits rather than on the same flat network as control systems. It says prompts, retrieved documents, uploaded files and API responses should be treated as untrusted, and that tool-using systems should have allow-listed actions and parameters rather than broad command capability. Model output should not flow directly into control actions, scripts or privileged workflows, and sensitive actions should require a meaningful human approval step in which the operator or engineer sees the source data, the recommendation and the reason it was produced. Logging and monitoring should cover prompts, retrieved sources, tool calls, model responses, user identity and any downstream action, and the post says operational data needs a clear handling model defining which sources are approved, who can add new sources and how changes are reviewed.

Articles.Title: AI security for OT and industrial environments

stories.Headline: LLMs Can Tackle High Energy Theoretical Physics, yet Gaps Remain: Part I, Quantum Field Theory
stories.Summary:
Tong Liu, Bohan Li, Gongrui Cheng, Zixiong Yu, Yulan He and Volker Tresp posted a paper to arXiv on November 1, 2026, introducing QFT-Bench, a benchmark of 75 problems in quantum field theory. The problems range from graduate to research level and require extensive reasoning and derivation across core subareas of the field. Each question has a well-defined target and a closed-form reference answer. The team evaluated 39 proprietary and open-source models, combining symbolic verification with an LLM-based judge.

The results show that frontier models already handle nontrivial quantum field theory calculations, with the strongest models exceeding 95% accuracy. Gaps remain, however. Even strong models still make errors in calculations, conventions and instruction following, while weaker models often fail at the level of physical concepts or derivations. The authors also monitored the models' chains of thought and found nontrivial reasoning unfaithfulness, meaning models could reach correct answers even when their reasoning did not justify or logically support those answers.

The authors describe the work as a quantitative assessment of current LLM capabilities in quantum field theory and a first step toward broader evaluation in high-energy theoretical physics. They frame it as an effort to push LLMs into that area and to find where their abilities might break. The paper is listed under high-energy physics phenomenology, computation and language, and high-energy physics theory. It does not say what follow-up work is planned.

Articles.Title: LLMs Can Tackle High Energy Theoretical Physics, yet Gaps Remain: Part I, Quantum Field Theory

stories.Headline: AU SFB probes data leak, Vijay Sales admin access for sale
stories.Summary:
AU Small Finance Bank is investigating a potential data leak from a Salesforce-hosted platform that holds limited information on its vehicle loan customers. The probe follows claims by a hacker group called ScarlettGroup that it accessed sensitive customer and internal records. The Jaipur-based lender said its own systems were not affected and that banking services are running normally. The group claimed the data includes KYC records, PAN and Aadhaar details, credit reports, bank statements, loan applications and signed agreements. It also alleged access to customer relationship management data, employee information and audit logs.

Separately, a threat actor using the handle shinymontanna allegedly offered super administrator access to Vijay Sales systems for $25,000. The claim was shared by the X account DarkWeb Informer. The listing claims access to more than 3 million order records, details for 15,000 employees and billing records for about 1.4 lakh vendors. The actor also claims access to customer information, payment records, inventory, financial reports and internal applications, with permissions to view, modify and export data. Screenshots said to show administrative dashboards have circulated, but the claims are unverified.

A bank spokesperson told ThePrint that AU SFB is investigating a potential data leak from a Salesforce-managed software-as-a-service platform. The bank did not confirm whether that platform was the source of the data claimed by ScarlettGroup. It also did not disclose how many customers may be affected. Inc42 said it could not independently verify the claims, and there is no independent confirmation of the alleged extent of access or data extraction at Vijay Sales.

The reports follow other recent cybersecurity events. SBI flagged the exposure of 3,897 customer records on the dark web. Two critical vulnerabilities in PHP were also discovered, prompting emergency actions worldwide. Cybersecurity firm eMudhra announced plans to wind down its global SSL/TLS certificate business after a security incident involving private keys.

Articles.Title: AU SFB probes data leak, Vijay Sales admin access for sale

stories.Headline: Google's space AI data centre online, faces power challenge
stories.Summary:
Google's Project Suncatcher prototype satellite, launched on October 1, completed its first AI test in orbit. Engineers sent an AI prompt to the satellite, which processed it and sent the response back to Earth. Google CEO Sundar Pichai described this as a hello world milestone for the project on X, noting the satellite generated a haiku. The satellite carries four Google Tensor Processing Units, known as TPUs. The current power supply allows only one chip to operate at a time for about 20 minutes.

Google plans to launch two more satellites in 2027 with enhanced power generation capabilities and optical links for inter-satellite communication. The company is currently testing how its TPUs function under extreme temperatures and radiation in space. Radiation can cause bit flips that corrupt data without triggering normal monitoring systems, a factor Google aims to understand better in actual space conditions. Pichai, Google's CEO, called the test a hello world milestone for Project Suncatcher in his post on X. He noted that the satellite generated a haiku as part of the test. Google itself says it now needs to assess how its custom TPUs perform under extreme space conditions.

The company also says it aims to better understand radiation effects such as bit flips in real space conditions. The test showed the prototype can process a prompt in orbit and return a response to Earth. Google plans two more satellites in 2027 with better power generation and optical links between satellites. The company is still assessing how its chips hold up under space radiation and temperatures.

Articles.Title: Google's space AI data centre online, faces power challenge

stories.Headline: Prada goes anti-AI for their new Christmas campaign - and it's working
stories.Summary:
Prada has released a Christmas campaign called "Drawing Prada: Animated By Hand," which uses traditional hand-drawn illustration instead of AI-generated images. The campaign was developed under the creative direction of Miuccia Prada and Raf Simons, with Ferdinando Verderi overseeing campaign creative direction. Veteran animator John Pomeroy led a team of artists to create the animated characters and environments. The live-action scenes were photographed by Glen Luchford, and each frame was drawn by hand. The campaign combines live-action footage with hand-drawn characters and features celebrity ambassadors including Sadie Sink, Maya Hawke, Chen Haoyu, Luther Ford and Kelvin Harrison Jr. Pomeroy, best known for his work at Disney on films such as Winnie the Pooh and Tigger Too, The Rescuers and The Fox and the Hound, explained his commitment to traditional technique in a behind-the-scenes film.

He said he learned his craft with pencil and paper and that the team has remained faithful to that approach. He added that there is a distinct and purposeful reason to do hand-drawn animation, which is to show that handcrafted work is still alive today. A press release said that the sense of touch expresses a fundamental notion of humanity and a connection with craft that always lies at the heart of Prada's approach to creation. The article says the campaign feels like a direct response to those still using a technology that threatens human creativity and livelihoods. It notes that Coca-Cola's AI-generated Christmas advertisements faced criticism in both 2024 and 2025.

The article also says the "not-made-by-AI" approach has become a major selling point, and it reports online comments praising the campaign as a breath of fresh air with soul. The article says more people have grown wary of AI and that a growing backlash has led younger, digital-savvy generations to appreciate human creativity while older generations embrace traditional crafts. It says Prada's campaign has sparked enthusiasm online, with users saying they respect artists and that this is how an ad should be made. The article ends by addressing Coca-Cola, asking whether the company will pay real animators this year or produce another campaign based on artists' works used without permission.

Articles.Title: Prada goes anti-AI for their new Christmas campaign - and it's working

stories.Headline: North Korean hackers linked to crypto thefts
stories.Summary:
Blockchain investigation firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis have linked recent cryptocurrency thefts to a North Korean hacking group called TraderTraitor. The group was previously named in a 2022 joint warning from the FBI, CISA, and the US Treasury. That warning described how the hackers used malicious software and other techniques. Their targets included software developers and IT staff inside cryptocurrency companies. The attribution was reported on November 1, 2026.

Microsoft Threat Intelligence said in an October 29, 2026 blog post that North Korean threat actors are expanding their use of AI at different levels. Microsoft grouped the actors into four stages: emerging, expanding, accelerating, and operationalized. It rated Jade Sleet, Coral Sleet, and Jasper Sleet as operationalized, and Diamond Sleet, Onyx Sleet, Pearl Sleet, and Sapphire Sleet as accelerating. Emerald Sleet was placed at the expanding stage, and no North Korean actor was assessed as emerging. Microsoft said the actors use AI mainly to speed up existing tradecraft and operator productivity, and that the operations remain human-directed rather than fully autonomous.

Microsoft described several examples of AI-enabled activity. Between June 8 and June 12, 2026, Jade Sleet ran job-themed targeting against people at cybersecurity, AI, blockchain, and recruitment companies, posing as recruiters for a spoofed AI-powered blockchain intelligence company and using two more front companies in the same week. Onyx Sleet generated dozens of tailored lures in minutes, and Coral Sleet quickly built a capability to trojanize private source code repositories. Diamond Sleet used AI for persona development and front company creation, and since August 2026 it has returned to targeting the oil and gas sector for the first time since 2023. Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet are also using the open-source agentic AI penetration testing framework ARTEX.

Microsoft said North Korea operates under extensive international sanctions and uses cyber operations and other illicit means to evade them. It said the actors mainly seek revenue for the regime, strategic intelligence, and in some cases politically motivated disruption, and that they commonly target cryptocurrency and financial organizations, IT companies and software supply chains, government entities, and education-related organizations. Microsoft provided mitigation guidance and Defender detections to help organizations defend against these threats. The articles do not say what happens next beyond that guidance.

Articles.Title: North Korean hackers linked to crypto thefts

stories.Headline: Palantir AI tech unused or little used by 29 NHS trusts said to be benefiting from it
stories.Summary:
More than two dozen hospital trusts that NHS England publicly lists as "realising benefits" from Palantir's £330m federated data platform have told the Guardian they are not using all or most of the AI-powered technology. The 29 trusts said the system was either not live or they were not using any of its applications, according to more than 100 freedom of information requests obtained by the medical charity Medact. Epsom and St Helier said it was "not using FDP at the moment", Kent and Medway said the platform was "not currently live", Mersey Care said it had "not yet gone live", and University Hospitals of North Midlands said it did not intend to roll it out. NHS England says 137 trusts are "live" with the FDP, which began in 2024 and aims to connect scattered medical files, speed up hospital discharges and improve surgery scheduling.

NHS England has claimed that 117,539 more operations were carried out by trusts using the FDP in a year, but this summer it conceded it could not prove cause and effect, and the Office for Statistics Regulation ran an investigation. The OSR said it will now take the matter forward under its casework function. NHS England insisted nearly 140 trusts "have now reported benefits", and it has previously said its list includes trusts using the tools for back office data analysis and submission rather than patient care. A Palantir spokesperson said the software was helping deliver better care, citing 117,000 additional operations, a 14.3% reduction in discharge delays for long stay patients and a 5.6% improvement in people finding out whether they have cancer within 28 days.

A senior health official described the gap between the NHS claim and the trusts' understanding as "very misleading". Chi Onwurah, chair of the Commons science and technology committee, called on the government to activate the 2027 break clause in Palantir's contract and launch an open competition for a UK-owned supplier, and the Commons health select committee is also calling for ministers to pull the deal. Palantir's UK and Europe chief executive, Louis Mosley, said ending the contract would be "putting politics above patients", and the company last month hired Labour's former deputy leader Lord Tom Watson as a full-time senior lobbyist. Marc Farr, chair of the NHS Chief Data and Analytics Officers Network, said it was crucial for public support that benefits are reported accurately and transparently.

The health secretary, Yvette Cooper, faces calls from MPs and campaigners to axe the contract. Medact spokesperson Dr Rhiannon Mihranian Osborne asked whether ministers are being misled if they are using the claims to make their decision. Palantir has contracts to supply AI to the Israeli military and Donald Trump's homeland security crackdown, and its billionaire founder, Peter Thiel, has questioned democracy. Watson and Mosley have written to critical MPs in letters counting the times they have spoken out against the company, which Labour's Clive Lewis described as "very Big Brother".

Articles.Title: Palantir AI tech unused or little used by 29 NHS trusts said to be benefiting from it

stories.Headline: Citi raises AI revenue estimates on hyperscaler demand strength
stories.Summary:
Citi raised its AI service revenue estimates for calendar years 2026 through 2028 on November 2, 2026, citing continued strength in artificial intelligence demand and monetization at major cloud providers. The firm increased its AI service estimates by 9% for 2026, 7% for 2027, and 17% for 2028. Combined revenue for AWS, Meta, Google, and Microsoft accelerated to 25% year-over-year growth in the third quarter. Cloud revenue growth for the top three cloud service providers accelerated to 56% year-over-year in the third quarter versus 48% in the second quarter and 39% in the first quarter.

Amazon called for AWS growth above 40% in both fiscal years 2027 and 2028. Google Cloud Platform reported 2,600 customers consumed more than 100 billion tokens in the last twelve months versus 2,000 in the second quarter. Microsoft 365 Copilot customers using consumption-based billing grew more than 75% quarter-over-quarter, while Fortune 500 AWS spend increased nearly seven times year-over-year. Combined quarter-over-quarter backlog additions slowed to $128 billion versus $237 billion in the second quarter.

Hyperscaler backlogs grew 142% year-over-year, a nine-point deceleration versus the second quarter on a 14-point tougher comparison. Microsoft's commercial bookings declined 11% in constant currency, impacted by large Azure commitments in the prior year. Citi expects global AI capital expenditures of $1.68 trillion in calendar year 2027, up 64% versus 2026, with the top four hyperscalers accounting for approximately 64% of overall investment. SpaceX increased its year-end 2027 compute capacity target to approximately 13 gigawatts, up from its prior 5-10 gigawatt outlook, while targeting approximately 20 gigawatts of supporting power infrastructure.

Articles.Title: Citi raises AI revenue estimates on hyperscaler demand strength

stories.Headline: AFTERLIGHT uses open-weight AI to revive forgotten code
stories.Summary:
The AFTERLIGHT project uses open-weight artificial intelligence to reconstruct the history of forgotten or abandoned software, TechGig reported on November 1, 2026. It combines static analysis, Git history, evidence-based retrieval, and open-weight AI to help developers understand unfamiliar codebases. The system links its findings to source files, line numbers, and historical commits so developers can inspect the evidence behind them. It also reconstructs project history by presenting Git commits, timestamps, authors, and changed files.

AFTERLIGHT identifies potential issues such as undocumented functions, unused import candidates, outdated dependencies, and missing tests within repositories. Its AI Explorer component uses Gemma through Ollama for local inference, retrieving relevant source-code chunks and historical context to generate explanations. After investigation, the project organises possible improvements into a prioritised roadmap covering maintenance, dependencies, testing, documentation, and architecture. Open-weight AI allows local inference, which can help keep private source code private, and gives developers flexibility to adapt the system.

The article names no individual people and gives no direct statements from anyone involved in the project. It attributes the work to the AFTERLIGHT project as a whole rather than to a named developer or team. The reported details describe what the system does, not who is responsible for it or what they said about it. No further plans, timelines, or next steps are mentioned in the article.

Articles.Title: AFTERLIGHT uses open-weight AI to revive forgotten code

stories.Headline: GE HealthCare Unveils Allia Celeo to Advance AI-Assisted Cardiac Imaging
stories.Summary:
GE HealthCare introduced Allia Celeo, a ceiling-mounted imaging system that uses artificial intelligence, automated positioning and predictive maintenance to support cardiac and other minimally invasive procedures. The company unveiled the system on Sunday at the Transcatheter Cardiovascular Therapeutics conference in San Diego. The launch expands GE HealthCare's interventional imaging portfolio as hospitals look to improve procedural efficiency and manage operating costs. The system follows the company's 2025 launch of the floor-mounted Allia Moveo, which became commercially available earlier in 2026.

Allia Celeo features a wide-opening C-arm, an X-ray device that captures images from multiple angles around a patient. Its ceiling-mounted setup gives clinical teams more room for staff and equipment, and automated positioning aims to reduce workflow interruptions. AI-assisted software adjusts imaging settings to balance image quality and radiation exposure, and a digital representation of the equipment lets clinicians preview its position before making physical adjustments. The platform also supports GE HealthCare software for visualizing coronary stents, guiding heart valve procedures and assisting with cancer treatments, extending its uses beyond cardiac care.

For maintenance, Allia Celeo integrates with OnWatch Predict, GE HealthCare's remote monitoring and predictive analytics technology, which flags potential equipment issues before they lead to breakdowns. The articles do not name any individual who spoke about the launch or give any statements from the company. They also do not say who at GE HealthCare is responsible for the system. No further details on responsibility or comments are provided.

The articles give little context beyond the launch itself and the earlier Allia Moveo system. They do not say what happens next, such as when Allia Celeo will become commercially available or how much it will cost. No timeline for future rollout or regulatory steps is mentioned. The only stated next step in the coverage is the system's introduction at the conference.

Articles.Title: GE HealthCare Unveils Allia Celeo to Advance AI-Assisted Cardiac Imaging

stories.Headline: RepoSeance: open-source AI tool helps debug complex codebases
stories.Summary:
RepoSeance is an open-source, local-first AI tool that helps developers understand unfamiliar codebases, according to TechGig. It was covered by the outlet on November 1, 2026, in a report published at 04:55 AM IST. The tool combines source-code analysis, Git history investigation, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation. Developers can ask natural-language questions about a repository and get AI-generated answers backed by source-code and Git evidence.

RepoSeance offers repository archaeology for TypeScript and JavaScript projects, letting users discover structure and extract symbols. It also investigates Git history, including commit history and blame information, and answers questions using locally running open-weight models. Answers include references to source files and lines, and the tool works through an interactive terminal chat and a CLI without a web dashboard or cloud AI service. It is available as an npm package and requires Node.js 22 or higher, Git, and Ollama installed and running.

The technology stack includes TypeScript, Node.js, Commander.js, Ollama, Gemma open-weight language models, MiniSearch for local indexing, simple-git for history investigation, and the TypeScript Compiler API for code analysis. The AI works through repository discovery, code analysis, Git archaeology, local indexing, context retrieval, AI inference, and evidence validation. Its privacy-first architecture keeps repository analysis and AI inference local through Ollama. This approach avoids sending the entire repository to a large language model, focusing context and improving answer utility.

Articles.Title: RepoSeance: open-source AI tool helps debug complex codebases

stories.Headline: Google Play Store to evaluate foldable app performance next year
stories.Summary:
Google announced at the Android Dev Summit that its Play Store will start evaluating how apps and games perform on foldable screens next year. Apps that adapt cleanly to these flexible displays will earn prime promotional placement and enhanced visibility across the store, the company said. Detailed criteria for the evaluation process will arrive later this year. Google has not clarified whether poorly adapted apps will face outright search penalties or simply lose featured discovery slots.

The change ties Play Store discovery directly to foldable quality, which Google aims to use to break the chicken-and-egg dynamic that has kept foldable development stalled. Google also rolled out developer tools meant to help engineers modernise software without keeping separate codebases for every screen size. These include Compose adaptive skill, powered by AI coding agents, which audits compact mobile interfaces and scales them across foldables, tablets, Googlebooks, parked cars and XR headsets. Desktop-ready controls automatically add desktop-grade inputs such as custom pointer cursors, hover states, keyboard shortcuts and control tooltips. Tabletop refactoring automatically reorganises camera and media interfaces into dedicated tabletop modes when a device is partially bent.

According to a report by Android Authority, Google had largely relied on voluntary design guidelines until now. The report said the adoption curve for foldables is shifting fast. With Apple's entry via the iPhone Duo expanding the foldable audience, Google hopes broader hardware interest will encourage cross-platform optimisation. Google admits that some of its own apps have created friction by running stretched, unoptimised phone layouts on larger laptop displays.

Articles.Title: Google Play Store to evaluate foldable app performance next year

stories.Headline: Mistral releases the weights for Mistral Large 4, or Le Chonk, and says it rivals top open models such as GLM-5.3 on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index (Radhika Rajkumar/ZDNET)
stories.Summary:
Mistral AI released its Large 4 model to the public on Thursday, according to TechGig. The French startup designed the model to help organisations find and fix cybersecurity vulnerabilities. Unlike systems such as Google's Gemini, the model can be downloaded and run independently, which Mistral says reduces reliance on a third-party provider. The released version is an upgrade from one shown three weeks earlier, after testing with governments and corporate users that the company says improved performance.

Mistral's own blog says Large 4, nicknamed Le Chonk, is a 1-trillion-parameter multimodal model trained from scratch on European infrastructure. It entered public preview on Oct. 6, and three weeks of extra reinforcement learning took it to the lead on FrontierCode and Terminal-Bench, with a score of 19.7% on Cognition's FrontierCode 2.0. On the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index it scores 48%, effectively tied with GLM-5.3 while using 47% fewer tokens per task, and on Terminal-Bench 4.0 it rose 13 percentage points to 41%. It offers three reasoning modes, Low, Medium and High, and scores 51% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index with an average refusal rate of 96.6% on malicious cyber requests.

Pierre Stock, Mistral's Vice President of Science, said he is not comfortable living in a world without open weights. Brad Medairy, President National Cyber at Booz Allen Hamilton, said testing showed the model matched other frontier cyber models on vulnerability detection recall with a compelling cost curve. Amy Chang, Head of Cisco's AI Threat Intelligence and Security Research, said open-weight models let enterprises and governments host and customise AI under their own control. Hugues Foulon, CEO of Orange Cyberdefense, said the two companies are building European cyber AI operated under the control of their experts.

ZDNET reports that the release sets a new bar for Western open models, which are increasingly competitive with proprietary ones. Mistral's blog says the model was preferred over GLM-5.3, Kimi K3 and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash in Surge Code's blind evaluations, ranking behind only Claude Opus 5.5. Laura Heuvinck, Head of Communications of ENISA, said the agency is testing Mistral Large 4 to find vulnerabilities, audit code and analyse defensive logs. The articles do not say what Mistral plans to release next.

Articles.Title: Mistral AI launches Large 4 model for cybersecurity

stories.Headline: AI vs. Quantum Computing: Key Differences, How Each Works, and What Sets Them Apart
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is software that learns from patterns in data to make predictions and decisions, and it runs on ordinary computers using CPUs and GPUs. Quantum computing is hardware built on quantum physics, and it uses qubits that can hold a combination of 0 and 1 at once, a state called superposition. A well-designed quantum algorithm uses interference to raise the odds of the right answer and cancel out wrong ones, though this works only for problems with the right mathematical structure. The two technologies are distinct, but they could converge to solve intricate scientific problems in the future.

Quantum computers are still small and error-prone, but they are improving fast.
