Ben Swerdlow, co-founder and chief executive of the startup Freestyle Cloud, posted four short lines naming three AI leaders as vegetarians: Dario Amodei, Sam Altman and Sundar Pichai. The post ended with the phrase “Let that sink in,” a line Musk had used when he bought Twitter. Elon Musk replied the next morning with his breakfast order: steak, eggs and coffee every day, plus a flexed-arm emoji. The exchange was reported on 31 October 2026.

The claims about the three executives come from their own words. Altman told Fortune in a June interview that he has been vegetarian since childhood. Amodei said on The Builders podcast, with his sister and Anthropic co-founder Daniela Amodei, that she went vegetarian first and he followed about three years later. Pichai has said that because he is vegetarian he eats an omelette with toast for protein, so the one vegetarian whose breakfast is on record eats eggs.

By Saturday, Swerdlow’s post had close to two million views and roughly 9,600 likes. Musk’s reply, posted around 13 hours later, had about 1.9 million views and more than 99,000 likes, about ten times the approval for far fewer words. Most headlines about the exchange led with Musk. Altman, Pichai and Amodei had not responded publicly in the coverage so far.

Musk’s own breakfast claims have shifted before. In 2023 he replied to XPRIZE chief Peter Diamandis, who had posted that sugar is poison, by writing that he eats a donut every morning and is still alive. Insider noted at the time that he had told Joe Rogan he would rather eat tasty food and live a shorter life. The article says habits change, and that Musk tends to answer such subjects with a short, contrarian line casting him as the unfussy outlier. It adds that the next list of what AI’s leaders have in common will likely get the same treatment.

Articles.Title: Elon Musk Answers Vegetarian AI CEOs OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei With Steak and Eggs

stories.Headline: Speeding up planning decisions with AI
stories.Summary:
Google DeepMind announced on October 31, 2026, that its AI planning tool PlanAssist will be made available to an additional 12 local planning authorities across England. The tool was developed by Google DeepMind with the UK government, Google Cloud, and Faculty. It has been piloted since June across Barnet, Camden, and Dorset councils. In early pilot testing, PlanAssist cut the average time a planning officer spent on householder assessment tasks by up to 58%.

PlanAssist handles routine householder applications, which account for up to 70% of planning officers' workloads. It validates application documents and architectural drawings, checks applications against heritage constraints such as tree preservation orders, and checks local and national planning policies and any previous objections. It then drafts fully cited reports that officers can edit before a final decision. More than 70% of the reports it generated were approved by officers with no edits required.

Planning officers retain the final say on every application, and the tool is designed to support human judgement. The announcement said planning bottlenecks have real costs, slowing progress toward the UK government's goal of building 1.5 million new homes by 2029 and leaving families waiting months for approvals like loft conversions, conservatories, or extensions. The announcement described providing access to these new councils as the natural next step. It also said the company looks forward to continuing to support the UK government as it seeks to build more homes and unlock economic growth.

PlanAssist is now moving into a 12-month Beta phase using live applications, starting with a subset of councils. Twelve more councils will be onboarded in three cohorts, bringing the total involved to 15, including metropolitan and rural districts across the country. Subject to successful testing, the government plans for the tool to be made available to all councils in England in 2027. Every assessment will be reviewed and approved by a qualified planning officer before any decision is made.

Articles.Title: Speeding up planning decisions with AI

stories.Headline: Is this real, or is it AI? - The Mountain-Ear
stories.Summary:
The Mountain-Ear reported last week that the National Newspaper Association had passed along word from Meta. Meta had revised its proposed commercial terms, narrowing the provision to advertising and business products, for its collection of material from its platforms to train its products. The article says this implies Meta has so far been taking everything posted on its platforms to improve its AI. It adds that if you posted it on a Meta platform, the company can use it to train its AI programs with no acknowledgement or compensation.

The article names Meta's platforms as Instagram, Facebook, WhatsApp, Threads and Meta AI. It says AI has so far consumed most of the printed universe and that AI can lie, though it is more likely to produce untruths by accident. It notes that video used to be treated as a true record of an event, but with AI so dominant it is hard to know what is true online. It also says this election season is the most volatile and angry in the writer's lifetime, and that many AI-created campaign ads and posts are undoubtedly appearing.

The piece is by Lynn Hirshman, writing from Nederland, and was posted on Saturday, October 31, 2026 at 11:15 am. She writes that the news leaves journalism in a tenuous and awkward position. She asks how anyone can be sure what they publish is accurate unless they have seen it in person, and how readers can be sure what they see online or on TV is real. She offers no answers, only questions and deeply uneasy feelings.

The article gives no further steps by Meta or the National Newspaper Association. It does not say what happens next or when any change takes effect. The full item sits behind a subscriber wall at themtnear.com, which asks readers to confirm a subscription, log in or subscribe. The page also lists a phone number, 303-810-5409, and an email address for questions.

Articles.Title: Is this real, or is it AI? - The Mountain-Ear

stories.Headline: Anthropic's next big AI business is life sciences, from biotech research to drug discovery
stories.Summary:
Anthropic filed its S-1 ahead of an initial public offering planned for next month, and the document presents life sciences as a major part of its future business. The filing says AI could rapidly accelerate scientific innovation and bring cures for major diseases within reach. It also lists biological progress first among the ways the company hopes AI will improve lives. Anthropic declined to comment to Business Insider.

The filing says nine of the 10 largest pharmaceutical companies and eight of the 10 largest healthcare companies in the Fortune 500 spent at least $100,000 with Anthropic over a recent yearlong period. It states that annual global pharmaceutical spend is expected to exceed $2 trillion in 2026, with Claude used in drug discovery and development by customers, biotech partners and the company's own researchers. Anthropic's Claude Science product, in beta, came out in June. The company started a molecular biology lab in the Bay Area this year and spent $400 million in stock in April to buy the biotech startup Coefficient Bio. In August it announced a robotics standard that lets AI control lab equipment.

Vas Narasimhan, CEO of Novartis, joined Anthropic's board in April. CEO Dario Amodei, a former theoretical physicist, has repeatedly cited life sciences as a reason to advance AI, writing that biology is probably the area where scientific progress has the greatest potential to improve human life. He said he hopes AI-enabled research will help prevent and treat all infectious diseases, eliminate most cancers and double the human lifespan. Ben Mann, co-leader of Anthropic's Labs organization, said his team has shifted focus from standard software engineering toward what Amodei has described as curing all diseases.

The filing also says the drug company Lilly, valued at $1.3 trillion, has 50,000 employees with access to a Claude enterprise account, and that more than 85% of its staff actively use the tool. Anthropic's careers page shows hiring for life sciences roles across chemistry, experimental biology and research engineering, with two roles opened late this week offering $320,000 salaries to researchers who can design and manufacture antibodies. Anthropic published August survey results finding that 91% of its staff think AI will make a Nobel-level discovery by 2030, compared with 39% of US adults. The article notes that no AI-designed drugs have ever received FDA approval, and that OpenAI offers a competing product called Rosalind while Google spinoff Isomorphic Labs plans to use AI to create cancer drugs.

Articles.Title: Anthropic's next big AI business is life sciences, from biotech research to drug discovery

stories.Headline: Biopharma’s AI Fork in the Road
stories.Summary:
A guest post by Danny Sigurdson, founder and CEO of Courier Health, published on Drug Channels on November 2, 2026, describes how biopharma companies are approaching patient services, partner changes and artificial intelligence in 2027. He writes that over the past decade manufacturers have brought more of the patient journey in-house to gain control. Courier Health's annual research shows 75% of Patient Services teams are now internal or hybrid, up from 60% a year earlier, and Field Access teams are 83% majority internal. He told commercial leaders at the third annual Patient Innovators Summit that biopharma has reached a fork in the road, and every manufacturer will pick a path in 2027 whether it decides to or not.

Two forces are speeding this up, according to the article. Hub and services providers are consolidating, and some of the largest are exiting the market, which leaves manufacturers with patients to migrate, workflows to rebuild and data to recover. At the same time, commercial leaders face pressure to automate, but a Harris Poll found 72% of AI decision-makers trace failed initiatives to a poor data foundation. Courier Health's own research found nearly 60% of biopharma companies call their data fragmented or inactionable, and fewer than 10% have the data maturity to use AI meaningfully. MIT's State of AI in Business 2025 found 95% of enterprise generative AI pilots fail to deliver value, while the 5% that succeed embed AI in high-value workflows and work with specialized partners, an approach MIT found succeeds about twice as often.

Sigurdson argues that manufacturers should own a connected data foundation so patient records do not live with a vendor, and that purpose-built AI can flag at-risk patients and route tasks to a person or agent. He says manufacturers excel at developing therapies and building relationships, but building software for frontline access teams is not on that list. He describes standing still as a choice that ensures a harder path, and says the next few quarters decide which path each manufacturer takes. The post promotes Courier Health's whitepaper on the 2026 Summit, where leaders from more than 75 companies representing 35 million patients shared their views.

Articles.Title: Biopharma’s AI Fork in the Road

stories.Headline: Claude Smart Reports 2026: What Your AI Spend Really Buys
stories.Summary:
Anthropic launched three tools for Claude Enterprise customers on October 28, 2026. The main tool is Claude smart reports, which shows managers what their teams do with Claude and what it costs. The other two tools are in-app surveys and pooled group budgets. The launch came two days after Anthropic filed to go public on October 26.

Smart reports let a manager pick a team, a date range of up to the last 28 days, and which Claude products to include, such as chat, Claude Code or Claude Cowork. Claude then reviews a sample of the team's transcripts and groups the work into workstreams, showing spend, output and problems like a missing connector or a failed tool call. Each report ends with a list of recommendations, and managers can ask custom questions and save them as templates. Pooled budgets give a whole team one shared monthly budget, with individual limits as a backstop, and billing admins get email alerts at 50%, 75%, 95% and 100% of the budget. Organisations get up to 10 free smart reports a month, then pay extra fees.

Anthropic says smart reports are not for evaluating individual performance or making employment decisions. John Jannone, an AI enablement lead at DoorDash, said in the announcement that the reports still surfaced things he did not know. Anthropic also said admins with billing permission can raise a spend limit straight from a report if it is holding someone back. The article notes that Claude is grading Claude, since the analysis runs on Anthropic's own model reviewing work done with its own product.

Jellyfish, which tracks AI use across more than 1,300 companies and 294,000 engineers, found the median AI spend per engineer grew 3.8 times between the first and third quarters of 2026, while headcount stayed at 98% of first-quarter levels. Anthropic's filing reported about 900% net revenue retention and about 250 customers spending $10 million or more a year, and it warned that a big drop in spending by its largest customers could hurt the business. OpenAI launched usage analytics and spend controls on June 18, 2026, and Anthropic added spend alerts and cost dashboards on July 2, 2026. The reports measure activity and cost, not revenue, so the article says proving a return still takes a company's own numbers.

Articles.Title: Claude Smart Reports 2026: What Your AI Spend Really Buys

stories.Headline: Forward-Deployed Engineers vs. Consultants: Key Distinctions for Tech Leaders
stories.Summary:
Forward-Deployed Engineers are gaining attention as a distinct way to implement technology, especially in fast-moving AI ecosystems, according to TechGig. They differ from traditional implementation consultants in speed, focus on new technology and team structure. The FDE concept began at Palantir in 2006 and was popularised recently by AI vendors such as OpenAI and Anthropic, which use FDE teams to help clients implement their products. FDEs can work directly for technology providers or as independent consultants with deep expertise in specific vendor offerings.

FDE teams follow a structured workflow that starts with an extensive discovery phase to identify precise customer needs, which often differ from what clients first think. They then assess data readiness and evaluate user needs and capabilities so the solution fits end users. FDEs build only what is necessary to fill functional gaps and integrate new functions to enhance rather than disrupt client operations. After implementation they carry out knowledge transfer and ownership so clients can run the solutions independently.

The main difference from traditional consultants is velocity, with FDEs aiming to create value within weeks by delivering production-ready products and then building on them iteratively, while traditional consulting can take months or years. FDEs also lean into new technology, often preferring cutting-edge options for innovation-focused enterprises, whereas traditional consultants may favour tried-and-true solutions for risk-averse clients. FDE teams are typically smaller, often no more than a half-dozen experts who stay with clients throughout the entire implementation journey. TechGig says engineering leaders must understand these distinctions to select the optimal implementation partner.

Articles.Title: forward deployed engineers vs consultants key distinctions for tech leaders

stories.Headline: As the AI model race heats up, who will come out on top?
stories.Summary:
Meta's Muse app passed 10 million downloads in the US and Canada, a milestone CEO Mark Zuckerberg announced on the company's earnings call last week. ChatGPT's app took about three times as long to reach the same number, according to Sensor Tower data. Anthropic's Claude Cowork triggered a sell-off in software stocks in February as investors worried AI could undermine traditional software business models. Anthropic filed its S-1 registration earlier this week and revealed an operating loss of $693 million in the first half of 2026.

Goldman Sachs estimates the largest US AI hyperscalers are on track to spend $800 billion in capital expenditure in 2026, with consensus forecasts pointing to $1.1 trillion in 2027. The bank says hyperscalers will need to generate roughly $300 billion in annual AI revenue over the next few years to break even. A Bloomberg report citing The Epoch Capabilities Index said the top spot among AI models changed 20 times since 2024, and a model has stayed at the frontier for only about seven weeks. In September, OpenAI added GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna and cut API prices by 50% compared with GPT-5.6 promotional pricing, while Anthropic introduced Claude Opus 5.5 at around 40% less to run than Opus 5.

Alexander Lis, chief investment officer at SDV, told Invezz it will take massive additional revenues, from $5 trillion to $8 trillion in incremental sales, to justify current aggregate CapEx levels of about $1.4 trillion a year. He warned that a problem could emerge when investors begin to doubt whether such sales are achievable, and that massive CapEx would become a problem if AI adoption decelerates. Ilman Shazhaev, founder and CEO of Dizzaract, said the core misconception behind 2026 capital spending of roughly $765 billion is mistaking high use for high value. He estimated that AI accelerators could become obsolete within three to five years while new chip generations arrive about every 12 months, and that the gap between accounting depreciation and economic reality could reach $176 billion between 2026 and 2028.

A Bloomberg News analysis found that Moonshot's Kimi K3 could build the same e-commerce website as Anthropic's Claude Fable 5 for one-fourth of the cost. OpenRouter said the five most popular models on its platform were Chinese, suggesting affordability and accessibility can influence adoption alongside technical performance. Lis said large technology incumbents are in a stronger position to fund the race because of their access to public markets. Shazhaev argued that as raw intelligence becomes commoditized, proprietary behavioral data and distribution matter far more than capital or hardware.

Articles.Title: As the AI model race heats up, who will come out on top?

stories.Headline: US Midterms 2026: Affordability, Artificial Intelligence And Iran War Top Voters’ Concerns Ahead Of November Poll; Other Key Issues Shaping How Americans Will Vote - The Sunday Guardian
stories.Summary:
Americans vote in the midterms on November 3, and they are judging the election mainly on affordability, with the war with Iran and the rapid growth of artificial intelligence also shaping their choices. A Gallup survey of 1,200 adults, conducted by telephone between 1 and 19 October, found that half of registered voters called the economy and healthcare extremely important to their vote for Congress. Iran came next at 47 per cent, and Gallup included the Iran conflict and the construction of artificial intelligence data centres in its midterm list for the first time. Gallup also found that Democrats place greater urgency on most issues than Republicans, and that no issue among the 11 tested was rated extremely important by a majority of Republicans. Crime was the clearest exception, with 43 per cent of Republicans rating it extremely important compared with 32 per cent of Democrats.

An Economist/YouGov poll in October found a plurality of respondents named inflation as the issue that mattered most to them, and the rise in the price of petrol, home heating oil and diesel linked to the conflict with Iran has added to those pressures. A Reuters/Ipsos poll in mid-October found that 34 per cent of respondents approved of the US strikes on Iran, while 54 per cent said the war had not been worth fighting. A Fox News poll found that nearly nine in ten voters expect AI to change how they live in the next few years, with 53 per cent saying the change would be significant, and eight in ten said they were extremely or very concerned that AI was eroding trust in what people see and hear in the news and on social media. A Bloomberg US report published last week described American voters as deeply dissatisfied with the country's direction and listed inflation, healthcare costs, data centres, immigration and government corruption among the leading concerns.

A 30-year-old machine operator from Bogalusa, Louisiana, who voted for Trump in 2024, told The Guardian the war was an evil war against Iran which must end, reflecting wider unease within parts of the Republican coalition about foreign military action. A 23-year-old business school graduate in Houston linked the affordability crisis to the administration's trade policy, describing Trump's idiotic tariff scheme. The Council on Foreign Relations has argued that foreign policy is feeding directly into household budgets, with the Iran war and trade policy reshaping how voters see the economy. Independents, whose votes often decide close races, rank the economy, healthcare and Iran highest, according to the Gallup survey.

How far the Iran conflict and concerns about AI translate into votes will depend on turnout, the performance of candidates in swing districts and the outcome on election night. Many of those who spoke to the newspaper expressed frustration rather than enthusiasm for either party, and some said they were still undecided while others said a single issue would determine their vote. Worries about data centres, electricity bills and employment are also surfacing, particularly in states where new facilities are planned, and Gallup's decision to include data centres on its list reflects how politically significant the subject has become, although the economic effects remain a matter of debate. For candidates, the message is that prices and healthcare remain powerful themes, but that foreign policy and technology are now competing for the same voters' attention.

Articles.Title: US Midterms 2026: Affordability, Artificial Intelligence And Iran War Top Voters’ Concerns Ahead Of November Poll; Other Key Issues Shaping How Americans Will Vote - The Sunday Guardian

stories.Headline: ongc chairman urges tech focus funds energy startups
stories.Summary:
ONGC Chairman and CEO Arun Kumar Singh spoke at the MC+ IGNITE Mumbai City Connect event at IIT Bombay, where he called for greater focus on technology and innovation to strengthen India's energy security and reduce import dependence. He said India needs to do things in a fundamentally different way to meet its energy needs. He pointed to artificial intelligence as a key technology that can improve production efficiency, cut wastage, and optimise assets and processes. He also noted AI's potential in areas such as enhanced oil recovery and exploration. The event was organised by ONGC with MC+ Ignite, an initiative under the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, to find and fund startups working in the core energy sector.

MC+ IGNITE plans to support up to 30 high-potential early-stage startups with a 30 crore grant pooled from public sector oil and gas companies, plus up to 2 crore in milestone-linked convertible funding. ONGC will work with the programme on themes such as AI-driven Subsurface Intelligence. A tripartite MoU was signed between MC+ Foundation, IIT Bombay, and IIT Bombay's Society for Innovation and Entrepreneurship (SINE). Singh committed ONGC's support and funding for startups in the core energy sector.

He stressed that a focused approach to innovation and efficient use of resources is essential for energy security. The MoU is meant to build industry, academia and startup collaboration, giving startups access to research and development facilities, mentorship, funding and pilot projects. ONGC joined the MC+ ecosystem as a partner public sector undertaking. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the plans and the MoU.

Articles.Title: ongc chairman urges tech focus funds energy startups

stories.Headline: why most enterprise ai pilots fail to scale in conversation with pavan nanjundaiah
stories.Summary:
Pavan Nanjundaiah, senior vice president and head of AI innovations at Tredence, spoke on an ET TechGig podcast hosted by Khushi Mudgal about why enterprise AI pilots often fail to reach production. The episode was published on May 21, 2026. He said many companies can build proofs of concept easily but then struggle to run them at scale, a problem he called the demo-to-durability gap. Weak data foundations, fragmented ownership, rigid architecture and limited workforce readiness were among the barriers he named.

Nanjundaiah said a pilot should have someone from the business involved in running it, because otherwise it may not last. He argued that success should be measured by business outcomes such as revenue growth or reduced churn, not only by model accuracy or an LLM evaluation. On data, he said that if data is not fixed, poor input will keep producing poor output, and he called for stronger governance, robust data models and scalable architectures. He also pointed to data products, semantic layers, ontologies and taxonomies as ways to standardize business logic.

On architecture, he warned against depending on a single large language model and said customers should use the best model for each use case, with smaller models often handling simpler tasks at lower latency and cost. He said governance should be built into engineering platforms rather than handled by separate committees, with security, monitoring, compliance checks and guardrails embedded in development workflows. He also said governance should be tiered by how sensitive a use case is. On people, he said buying tools alone does not make a workforce AI-ready, and he described Tredence's internal AI Forge initiative, which trains employees in AI engineering, governance and production deployment.

He gave the example of a North American consumer packaged goods company that built a flexible multi-cloud AI platform and put marketing teams into the development process from the start. That effort reportedly improved return on ad spend. He said companies need strong data foundations, modular architecture, integrated governance, business-aligned metrics and continuous workforce transformation to move from isolated pilots to durable systems. He also warned that firms risk losing top talent if they are not AI-ready.

Articles.Title: why most enterprise ai pilots fail to scale in conversation with pavan nanjundaiah

stories.Headline: Britain: Meta accused of using news site content to develop artificial intelligence
stories.Summary:
Britain’s Competition and Markets Authority opened a formal investigation into Meta, the parent company of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, the UK regulator announced. The investigation concerns new trading terms that could let Meta collect content from news sites and media organizations and use it to develop its services and products, including artificial intelligence technologies. The CMA said this could happen without giving content owners the right to choose how their material is used. The move follows widespread objections from media organizations, publishers and digital content companies.

Meta had planned to amend its terms of service on October 30, then postponed the implementation to November 20 before announcing a suspension of the changes pending consultations with relevant institutions and stakeholders. The CMA said the investigation will examine whether the company holds a dominant position in any relevant market within the UK. It will also investigate whether the proposed terms constitute an abuse of this position or impose unfair commercial conditions on publishers and advertisers. The UK’s media watchdog emphasized that the investigation does not yet constitute proof of wrongdoing by the company.

Meta rejected the justifications for opening the investigation, asserting that there were no grounds for taking competitive action against it. It pointed out that it had committed to not changing its terms without consulting publishers and other stakeholders. It also stated that it welcomed the opportunity to clarify its position to regulatory authorities. The CMA stated that it will gather evidence and information from Meta and affected parties before reaching any final decision.

The case raises broader concerns about the rights of news organizations in the digital age, especially given the increasing reliance of technology companies on online content to develop artificial intelligence models. This raises questions about intellectual property rights, financial compensation and consent mechanisms. The investigation opens a new chapter in the ongoing confrontation between media organizations and major technology companies. The dispute centers on the ownership of journalistic content and the limits of its use in developing artificial intelligence, amid growing calls for regulations that protect publishers’ rights and strike a balance between technological innovation and the sustainability of the journalism industry.

Articles.Title: Britain: Meta accused of using news site content to develop artificial intelligence

stories.Headline: University of Bologna and United Nations University: an agreement to strengthen the collaboration on artificial intelligence
stories.Summary:
The University of Bologna and the United Nations University signed a new framework cooperation agreement on 31 October 2026. Rector Giovanni Molari signed for Bologna and Professor Tshilidzi Marwala, Rector of the United Nations University, signed for the UN body, which is an autonomous organ of the UN General Assembly. The signing took place in the Rector's office. An event titled "Education, Research and Global Collaboration" was held for the occasion, and the two Rectors and Francesco Umbertini, President of Cineca, gave speeches.

The agreement aims to develop joint initiatives in areas of common interest and names artificial intelligence as one of the main fields for collaboration. This comes ahead of the imminent launch of the United Nations University Institute for Artificial Intelligence (UNU-AI). The activities may cover research and innovation, higher education and capacity development, with the goal of contributing to research and policies on AI governance. Possible activities include joint education and capacity development programmes, research mobility, seminars, Summer Schools, e-learning and innovation initiatives. The collaboration will also create activities for public decisionmakers, policymakers and other stakeholders, allow joint participation in UN system activities and initiatives, and include sharing of research results.

Particular attention will go to education, and the two institutions have launched work on an integrated master's degree programme focused on global governance and the societal implications of AI and digital technologies. The agreement will also facilitate further collaborations through second cycle degrees, PhDs and Professional Masters programmes. It covers mobility and joint-degree opportunities for doctorates, including mobility for visiting professors and scholars. Molari said the event reminds the academic community of its responsibility for the changes under way, including their accessibility and sustainability, their social and ethical implications, and the preparation of future generations of experts and of society as a whole. He described the consequences of this revolution as uncertain and difficult to predict.

Articles.Title: University of Bologna and United Nations University: an agreement to strengthen the collaboration on artificial intelligence

stories.Headline: Artificial intelligence answers: what is the expected result of the derby of anger?
stories.Summary:
An artificial intelligence tool was asked by Kooora to predict the result of the Milan versus Inter match in the tenth round of the Italian league. The answer was published by Goal.com on October 31, 2026, in an article by Hussein Hamdy. The AI said the Derby of Anger kicks off on the evening of Saturday, October 31, 2026, at the San Siro stadium. It predicted a 1-1 draw or a narrow 2-1 win for Inter Milan.

The AI gave four reasons for its prediction. It said derby matches are marked by caution and intense rivalry, and the scales often tip towards a draw when the sides are at similar levels. It said Inter sit top of the table but have influential absences, most notably their top scorer and captain Lautaro Martinez, who has a muscle injury, along with some defensive absences. It said Milan should benefit from the return of key starters such as Luka Modric and Christian Pulisic, who were rested in the previous match, giving them solidity in midfield against Inter's midfield led by Calhanoglu and Barella. It also said the San Siro is home to both teams, so crowd pressure is split evenly and the away advantage is reduced.

The article states that all answers, including any linguistic or informational errors, were reproduced exactly as stated by the artificial intelligence, without editorial intervention. It notes that machines carry no emotions or feelings, which is why Kooora put a number of contentious questions to the AI. The piece lists Inter's next match in the Champions League on November 3, 2026, at 14:00, and a Europa League match on November 5, 2026, at 11:45. It does not say what happens after the derby beyond those fixtures.

Articles.Title: Artificial intelligence answers: what is the expected result of the derby of anger?

stories.Headline: Deepfake porn: the violence against women created by Artificial intelligence_8427_102
stories.Summary:
Deepfake porn is a form of digital violence in which artificial intelligence is used to create fake sexual images or videos of real people. It works by taking a real photo, such as a person's face or body, and using AI to alter the body, location or movements so the person appears in an intimate situation that never happened. The practice emerged in June of this year, when around 50 adolescents from two pre-university schools in CABA exchanged and sold AI-generated pornographic images and videos in a WhatsApp group. The images featured adolescents whose photos had been stolen and altered, and the case quickly went viral and opened a debate about what measures should be taken against those responsible.

According to the State of Deepfakes report, pornographic videos created with artificial intelligence rose by 464% between 2022 and 2023, from 3,725 to 21,019 videos, and 99% of the people who appear in them are women. In Seville, three men were sentenced to nine months in prison each for using AI to manipulate photographs of three former schoolmates and simulate that they were naked, the first conviction in the city for this type of act. They took the images from the young women's public Instagram profiles, modified them with an AI application on Telegram, and shared them in WhatsApp and Discord groups. The judge banned them from using Telegram, WhatsApp, Instagram and Discord for three years and nine months and ordered them to complete a sexual education program, applying the gender aggravating circumstance.

Cristina Pujol, a professor at the UOC, said deepfakes are not new and began with celebrities whose faces were cut out and embedded in pornographic scenes uploaded to adult websites. Rocío Pina, also a professor at the UOC, said sexual deepfakes can be considered violence against women because fake images are used to manipulate and damage a person's reputation, and victims can suffer personal, social and emotional problems even when the video is fake. Eduard Blasi, a law professor and privacy expert at the UOC, said the content can violate rights such as privacy, honor and one's own image because a person's real face or voice is used without permission. Pedro Sánchez argued that artificial intelligence should not remain under the control of tech companies and that public regulation and supervision are needed, saying it is a mistake to put the fox in charge of the henhouse.

The European Union is taking new measures to combat sexual deepfakes, including a prohibition on AI tools that let people create fake sexual images or videos of real people without consent, which also covers applications that use a person's photograph to create an image in which they appear naked. The EU wants tech companies to be more responsible for the tools they create, so action can be taken not only against the person who uses the applications to cause harm but also against companies that allow their systems to be used for this content, and companies will have to include security measures to prevent such uses. The new rules consider it a crime to create or share child sexual abuse material using AI or deepfakes. The articles also ask what happens when the social media ban ends and what guarantees victims have that they will not suffer a similar situation again.

Articles.Title: Deepfake porn: the violence against women created by Artificial Intelligence

stories.Headline: Companies that had been pouring huge amounts of money into artificial intelligence (AI) investments
stories.Summary:
OpenAI recently lowered its funding target from $30 billion to $20 billion, and its corporate valuation fell from $1.4 trillion a month earlier to $1.25 trillion, according to the Financial Times on the 30th. Some investors reduced the size of their investment agreements as AI-related stocks kept selling, and the first deadline was reported to fall short of the lowered target. OpenAI had raised $122 billion in March and is seeking more money to develop AI models and expand computing infrastructure. Competitor Anthropic is preparing to list on Nasdaq in the middle of this month with a target of at least $1.5 trillion in corporate value, and the two companies are competing for funds over overlapping institutional investors.

Blackstone recently told investors that Anthropic is likely to remain in the upper speculative grade, BB, without receiving an investment grade after its IPO, though it had been expected to get one by the end of this year. Anthropic's listing application laid out plans to invest more than $800 billion in AI computing infrastructure by 2045, and a failure to get an investment grade would limit pension funds and insurers and raise borrowing rates. In a $63 billion financing transaction to lease Google AI chips, Broadcom guaranteed more than $42 billion in senior loans, and Blackstone acquired $9 billion of subordinated debt on condition of an annual return of more than 10%. Fitch, Moody's and Standard & Poor's have not yet released Anthropic's official credit ratings.

S&P Global Ratings downgraded Meta's credit outlook to negative from stable on the 30th of last month while keeping its AA- rating, citing a surge in AI facility investment and worsening free cash flow. Meta plans to invest between $135 billion and $145 billion in AI infrastructure this year, and its free cash flow turned into a deficit of $2.12 billion in the third quarter. S&P predicted the deficit will rise to $71 billion in 2027 and reach $39 billion in 2028, reversing its earlier forecast of a surplus in 2028, and said Meta's ability to monetize AI investments is more limited than competitors. Meta spokesperson Kamran Mumtaz said the company respectfully disagrees with S&P's claims about AI monetization and that it has significant product and business opportunities ahead to support very solid creditworthiness.

Meta is also pushing to issue up to $95 billion in shares, the largest in its history, with $35 billion offered immediately and $60 billion issued at market price after non-voting stocks are listed in the first quarter of next year. Investment bank William Blair predicted investors will keep questioning the financing method and the possibility of further capital increases. Naveen Sarma, a general manager at S&P Global Ratings, said creditworthiness will keep weakening and cash flows will be negative if facility investment stays high and grows faster than expected. On the 30th of last month Apple overtook Nvidia to regain the top spot in global market capitalization for the first time in about three months, closing at $5.30 trillion as Nvidia fell 4.2% to $4.93 trillion, and Apple shares are up 27% this year, the highest gain among the Magnificent 7.

stories.Headline: Wahoo CEO talks finances, artificial intelligence and the company's 'next big opportunity'
stories.Summary:
Wahoo Fitness has returned to year on year growth following its recapitalisation in 2023, CEO Gareth Joyce told Cyclingnews in an interview published on 31 October 2026. Joyce joined Wahoo as CEO in 2024, and he had never worked in the bike industry before. He is an engineer and a keen cyclist and runner, and he admits he was not an obvious candidate for the role. He said his recent experience of talking a company through Chapter 11 bankruptcy made him well suited to Wahoo at a time of financial turbulence.

Joyce said the company has a busy product roadmap, with seven or eight launches planned for 2027 after a year spent reorganising development. He explained why it took so long to update the Kickr Core even as the Kickr reached its sixth iteration, and he discussed the launch of a treadmill and a partnership with Coros. He said cycling remains at the centre of the business, but running is taking on increasing importance. He also said 2038 is going to be a very busy year for the company.

Joyce sees his role as bringing corporate structure to a startup business. He said Wahoo's foundations were built on innovation, but its scale no longer supports that way of working. He said it is no longer just a startup, and that the company has a large customer base it has a responsibility to. Asked whether the changes since the recapitalisation are working, he gave an answer the article describes as pretty conclusive.

Articles.Title: Wahoo CEO talks finances, artificial intelligence and the company's 'next big opportunity'

stories.Headline: EXCLUSIVE: Elon Musk's AI Odyssey Film Slammed as 'Trash' by Movie Fans
stories.Summary:
Elon Musk released the first seven-minute installment of his Grok Imagine project on X on November 1, 2026, according to AOL. The production is an AI-generated adaptation of Homer's Odyssey, made with Wonder Studios and director Dev Walker. Musk, 55, had promised a feature-length version three months earlier. Viewers responded with heavy criticism, calling the work trash and questioning whether AI can replace human filmmakers.

The film begins with Odysseus preparing to leave for Troy while Penelope gives him a wooden horse for their infant son. It then shows Greek soldiers preparing for battle, scenes from the Trojan War and Telemachus growing up. The characters have airbrushed appearances and speak English rather than ancient Greek. Musk announced the project in July, shortly after Christopher Nolan's adaptation opened, and said it would be historically accurate and true to Homer. He had attacked Nolan's casting of Lupita Nyong'o as Helen of Troy and Elliot Page as Sinon, accusing Nolan of desecrating Homer to satisfy what he called woke rules required to win an Oscar.

One X user said the film was pure garbage and that Musk has no taste. Another wrote that if this is what the richest man on the planet can produce, AI movies will not replace actual movies soon. A third said the film shows how little AI understands art or humans. Others complained that the computer-generated characters moved unnaturally, with one asking why everything seemed to be moving underwater, and another compared the figures to characters from Game of Thrones.

Nolan's adaptation stars Matt Damon as Odysseus, Anne Hathaway as Penelope and Tom Holland as Telemachus, with Robert Pattinson, Zendaya, Samantha Morton and Charlize Theron also in the cast. It opened in July and has grossed more than $1.7 billion worldwide, including $264.1 million in its opening weekend, becoming Universal Pictures' highest-grossing release ahead of Jurassic World. Nolan dismissed pre-release arguments about historical accuracy as irrelevant because no one having them knows what the film is yet. He also compared AI to a Trojan horse that everyone knows the Greeks are inside, a transparent horse made of glass.

Articles.Title: EXCLUSIVE: Elon Musk's AI Odyssey Film Slammed as 'Trash' by Movie Fans

stories.Headline: Creeps Are Using AI to Undress Celebrities in Paparazzi Shots for Clicks
stories.Summary:
Accounts on X, formerly Twitter, have been using AI to undress celebrity men in paparazzi photos and republishing the altered images as if they were real, according to a report published on October 31, 2026. The writer Sarah Hagi flagged the practice earlier that week. Posters take existing paparazzi shots and change them so the men appear shirtless and, most often, extremely muscular. One frequent target is the British actor Callum Turner, the husband of the pop star Dua Lipa, and an account called UKViewTIme has posted several altered photos of the couple on the streets of New York City. In the edited images, Lipa is fully clothed in pants and long jackets while Turner walks shirtless, though the original paparazzi photos show he was clothed in real life.

Another post from an account called BiTheWay shows the Stranger Things star Noah Schnapp walking with the actor Sheridan Townsley, with both young men pictured shirtless even though the originals show them wearing shirts and jackets. The people behind the images go to great lengths to keep them looking authentic, including keeping the pop singer Harry Styles' famous tattoos intact in manipulated topless photos, which UKViewTime also posted. Other repeat targets include Knox Jolie-Pitt, the son of Angelina Jolie and Brad Pitt, and Pitt himself, who was shown in a black tank top with artificially muscular arms instead of the yellow suit he wore in the original photos. The report attributes the images to engagement-seeking accounts on X, naming UKViewTime and BiTheWay as posters, and says the undressing is more than likely nonconsensual. It describes the scheme as gross and says the deepfakes can be hard to spot because most of each image is largely real.

It offers a simple tell for readers, noting that if Dua Lipa is dressed in an ankle-sweeping coat while her husband is out without a shirt, the answer is likely that the image has been skewed by AI. The articles do not say what platform rules or consequences, if any, the accounts face, and they give no next steps beyond the report itself. They also link the practice to wider coverage of AI deepfakes, including a separate piece saying liberals are falling for extremely obvious AI fakes. No statement from X, the named accounts, or any of the celebrities is included.

Articles.Title: Creeps Are Using AI to Undress Celebrities in Paparazzi Shots for Clicks

stories.Headline: Amid a series of test irregularities using artificial intelligence (AI) smart glasses, a study found..
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Martin Luther Halle-Wittenberg University in Germany presented a study at the 17th International Conference on Computer Support Education, known as CSEDU 2025, on the problem-solving ability of AI models on U.S. college entrance exam questions. The experiment used 720 SAT questions released in the past, including 396 reading and 324 mathematics questions. Instead of connecting actual smart glasses to AI, the researchers reproduced image distortions that can appear when looking at a test paper through smart glasses. They applied a perspective distortion of about 75 degrees, a blur effect of 3 pixels and 5 percent noise to simulate viewing the paper from a distance. Google's Gemini 1.5 Pro-002 answered 82.78 percent of the processed questions correctly, with 87.96 percent of math and 78.54 percent of reading questions right.

OpenAI's GPT-4o answered 75.69 percent overall, with 74.69 percent in math and 76.52 percent in reading. When clean problems without image distortion were given, GPT-4o recorded 87.22 percent and Gemini 84.58 percent. The researchers concluded that commercial AI models can solve test problems with high accuracy even in poor image quality, and that smart glasses can threaten the fairness of face-to-face tests. The researchers said smart glasses may be used as an input means to deliver test questions to AI, and that glasses without a screen display function are virtually difficult to distinguish from ordinary glasses to unfamiliar people. They noted that smart glasses can be used to pass problems to AI models without students having to cooperate separately.

However, they did not make actual working AI cheating glasses and verify them at a test site. The test questions were also processed so that only one question was visible on a page, so the difficulty of a real test situation, where AI would have to find a full question among several, was not sufficiently reflected. In Korea, cheating with smart glasses has already occurred. Last month, test-takers who wore general glasses before the test and then switched to smart glasses after it began were caught in the essay examination at Yonsei University and University of Seoul.

The national qualification test has confirmed five cases of cheating using smart glasses this year. The Ministry of Education plans to deploy one person per test site to check for smart glasses at this year's College Scholastic Ability Test. Taking the test in smart glasses will invalidate the test and suspend qualifications for the next year's exam, and simply having them will nullify the test. The ministry will also take criminal measures such as requesting an investigation, and will push to increase the suspension period for cheaters from the current one year to three years.

Articles.Title: Amid a series of test irregularities using artificial intelligence (AI) smart glasses, a study found..

stories.Headline: Antropic, which developed the artificial intelligence (AI) service "Claude," is seeking to list on t..
stories.Summary:
Antropic, the company behind the Claude artificial intelligence service, has filed to list on the U.S. stock market. It submitted a securities report, known as an S-1, to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on the 26th, local time. The company plans to list on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the stock code ANT. It is aiming for an enterprise value of up to $2 trillion, with foreign media mentioning a possible listing next month. The number of shares and the price range have not yet been decided.

The filing shows rapid growth and heavy costs. Antropic recorded sales of $16.3 billion in the first half of this year, nearly 14 times the $1.2 billion in the same period last year. Its net loss in the first half was $80.74 billion, reflecting about $72.4 billion in non-cash expenses tied to changes in the value of convertible bonds and derivatives. Excluding those one-time losses, adjusted operating profit was $1.618 billion, the first half-year operating surplus since the company was founded. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are the main organizers, and 22 financial companies are listed as underwriters, with no domestic Korean brokerage among them.

Antropic was co-founded in 2021 by seven people who left OpenAI, including CEO Dario Amodei and President Daniela Amodei. The seven co-founders together hold 50.1% of the company, a structure that lets them keep management control focused on long-term technology development and safety, though it may limit the influence of ordinary shareholders. The company warned in its filing that highly developed AI, if misused, replicated, weaponized or run with a high level of autonomy, could pose a catastrophic threat to humanity. The market sees the listing as a key test of whether growth expectations for generative AI companies turn into actual investment demand.

The listing comes as some infrastructure companies delay going public over concerns about interest rates, market volatility and the sustainability of AI investment, according to Reuters. For Korean investors, direct subscription is unlikely, since no domestic brokerage participated as an underwriter, and Mirae Asset Securities, which pushed for SpaceX shares in May, was not allocated supplies in the end. No domestic securities company has filed a report with the Financial Supervisory Service about acquiring Antropic IPO shares. Realistic routes for Korean investors are limited to exchange-traded funds, indirect investment in unlisted shares or listed companies holding old shares, and buying directly on the first day of trading.

Articles.Title: Antropic, which developed the artificial intelligence (AI) service "Claude," is seeking to list on t..

stories.Headline: Italian researchers use artificial intelligence to map how Taurasi wine ages
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the Institute of Food Sciences of Italy’s National Research Council in Avellino said on Friday, October 30, 2026, that they had used laboratory analysis and artificial intelligence to study how Taurasi wine changes as it ages. The study examined four Taurasi DOCG vintages, from 2015, 2018, 2021 and 2022. The team measured main chemical components, including polyphenols, anthocyanins and aromatic compounds, then applied machine-learning algorithms to find patterns across the samples. The institute said this produced what it described as a chemical map of the wine’s evolution over time.

Daniela Evangelista is listed as first author, and the work was carried out by a research group at the Avellino institute. The findings were published in the scientific journal Metabolites as part of the Agritech project, which is funded through Italy’s National Recovery and Resilience Plan, known as the PNRR. The institute said the study focuses on Taurasi DOCG, one of the best known red wines from the Irpinia area of Campania, and uses it as a case study for broader questions about how wines develop during aging. The research combines classical chemical testing with data analysis systems that can process complex sets of measurements.

The institute presented the study as an early step toward wider applications of artificial intelligence in the analysis of wine quality, characterization and authenticity. It did not present AI as a replacement for traditional enological analysis, and the announcement described the work as a first step, suggesting it remains exploratory. The models depend on the quality of the chemical data collected from the wines rather than operating as a stand-alone shortcut. The institute said the value of the project lies in showing that the aging of a wine such as Taurasi can be tracked through an integrated reading of chemistry and data analysis.

The work adds to a wider trend in agricultural and food science, where AI is increasingly being tested on tasks such as product classification, traceability and fraud detection. Taurasi holds DOCG status, Italy’s highest protected designation for wine origin and production standards, which the article says makes it a suitable subject for research into chemical markers and classification methods. The article says the method would need broader validation on more wines, more vintages and additional production contexts before it could become a standard tool. If similar methods prove reliable at larger scale, the article says they could give wineries, laboratories and regulators another way to monitor how products evolve over time and to strengthen analytical checks tied to origin and authenticity.

Articles.Title: Italian researchers use artificial intelligence to map how Taurasi wine ages

stories.Headline: Workshop demystifies artificial intelligence - Eagle-Tribune
stories.Summary:
Mark Glisson, assistant director of the Hooksett Library, will present an introduction to artificial intelligence on Monday, Nov. 2 at 6 p.m. The session is described as a plain-language guide designed for curious beginners or casual users of AI. It aims to demystify the fast-moving technology. The workshop is listed in the Eagle-Tribune calendar for that Monday.

The event runs from 6 to 7 p.m. at the Leach Library, 276 Mammoth Road in Londonderry. People can register by calling 603-432-1132 or visiting www.londonderrynh.gov. The calendar lists the program under the heading AI Intro with Mark Glisson. It appears among other Monday library events in the same listing.

Glisson is named as the presenter, and the library is named as the host and registration contact. The listing describes the session as designed for curious beginners or casual users of AI. No further remarks from organizers are given in the article. The item gives no cost for the workshop.

The article presents the workshop as a way to learn more about AI in plain language. It does not say what happens after the session or whether more workshops will follow. The only date given is Monday, Nov. 2, and the only time is 6 to 7 p.m. Registration details are provided through the library.

stories.Headline: AI Revolutionizes Engineering: Teams, Skills, and Ethics for 2026
stories.Summary:
A 2026 InfoQ Culture and Methods Trends Report, discussed by a panel of QCon speakers and InfoQ contributors and covered by TechGig on August 8, 2026, says artificial intelligence is reshaping engineering team dynamics, roles and the human side of software development. The panel called for a balanced approach to AI adoption that manages risks and keeps human-centred values. Vanessa Formicola, an engineering leader, said teams tend to take an all-or-nothing approach and should match AI integration to software risk and their own circumstances. Philip Mortimer, a machine learning engineer, cited GitHub's projection of a 14x rise in pull requests by 2026, from one billion to 14 billion, and said the resulting cognitive load demands new development processes.

The report says engineer roles are shifting from pure coding toward becoming custodians who build platforms and guardrails for AI agents. Yinka Omole, a software engineer, said this blurs the lines between product, design and engineering and could lead to smaller, one-person teams. Vanessa Formicola said labels such as architect, developer and manager are becoming obsolete, and that success will depend on broad cross-functional skills and accountability for what is delivered rather than the volume of code shipped. Rafiq Gemmail, a senior director at MarTech, said AI is a massive force multiplier for experienced seniors but juniors may lack the judgment to spot scalable or maintainable AI-generated code.

Ben Linders stressed that psychological safety and transparency are crucial as collaboration patterns change, and he noted a dip in psychological safety after COVID and with recent global developments. Shane Hastie quoted Jim Highsmith's warning that organisations which failed at agile will fail catastrophically at AI. Craig Smith, a delivery lead, said the gap is widening between organisations that have embraced AI and those still struggling with basic agile practices, and he warned that adoption is outpacing practices for people and technology, producing code slop and weaker collaboration. On ethics, Formicola questioned who is accountable for AI-generated code that could cause data leaks or societal damage, while Shawna Martell raised AI's electricity and water use and Omole cited studies showing AI intensifies work and anxiety.

Looking ahead, the panelists asked for greater mindfulness in using AI, with respect for people, the environment and business growth. Linders called for checking on colleagues to protect psychological safety, and Mortimer urged a renewed focus on quality and testing. Martell said the industry should not lose sight of enduring leadership qualities such as vision, judgment and fostering talent as the tools evolve. Gemmail pointed to initiatives such as Neuralwatt, which bases pricing on power consumption, as a possible model for greater environmental awareness.

stories.Headline: Investor Says We're Rapidly Approaching the Point At Which Economic Systems Collapse Under the Weight of AI
stories.Summary:
Investor Raoul Pal said in a post on X on October 31, 2026, that the world may have only about four years before it stops working as it does now. Pal, a crypto investor and finance media figure with 1.5 million followers, made the claim alongside a clip of his podcast and a link to buy his book, “The Everything Code.” He said wages have not kept up with the cost of living for years and that governments must keep debasing currency to fund everything. He said the part that is new is how fast exponential technologies such as AI, robotics, energy and crypto are moving.

Pal said the systems built for the old world cannot keep up with those technologies. In his view, the average person will eventually be unable to trust what they see or hear, and even the idea of running a business will stop meaning what it means today. He called that moment the “Economic Singularity.” The article describes his post as openly self-promotional.

The article pushes back on Pal’s claims, saying they rest on vague observations treated as fact. It notes that persistent inflation is not a new phenomenon and that economist Richard Wolff observed in 2022 that inflationary pressure is a longstanding feature of capitalism, not a sign of end times. It also says severe economic crises in the past, such as 2004 versus 2008 and 2016 versus 2020, changed things dramatically for working class people but the structures of capitalism survived. The article says Pal is one of many doomsayers appearing at a time of severe financial hardship, and calls him an oracle for people in need of order among economic chaos.

The article also mentions other warnings about AI and the economy. It cites financial commentator Harris Kupperman, who warned that the math on data center investments is unsustainable, and economist Michael Roberts, who called AI the biggest economic bet in US history. It says the International Monetary Fund has begun worrying that the world economy is on a knife’s edge. It adds that the wealthy and powerful keep putting money into AI and related industries anyway.

Articles.Title: Investor Says We're Rapidly Approaching the Point At Which Economic Systems Collapse Under the Weight of AI

stories.Headline: EM update on AI data center development at federal sites
stories.Summary:
Robert Seifert, the Department of Energy’s Environmental Management director of infrastructure disposition and regulatory policy, spoke Wednesday at the Energy Technology and Environmental Business Association’s annual conference in Knoxville, Tennessee. He said the office is embracing artificial intelligence data centers on remediated land at federal nuclear sites. The effort is a priority under President Donald Trump’s administration, and Assistant Secretary for Environmental Management Tim Walsh has pushed for a heavy focus on AI in nuclear cleanup and future land reindustrialization. DOE issued a request for information last year that identified 16 nuclear complex sites as candidate sites for data centers.

In July 2025, DOE selected four sites: Idaho National Laboratory, the Oak Ridge Site in Tennessee, the Paducah Site in Kentucky and the Savannah River Site in South Carolina. Seifert said Idaho, Paducah and Savannah River are under development and moving forward in the leasing process, while DOE is looking to take a different approach at Oak Ridge. With Tennessee’s selection under DOE’s nuclear campus program, he said DOE will consider working with various nuclear developers in the Oak Ridge area and see where the data center fits in the potential campus setup. DOE is also developing a data center and energy project at its Portsmouth Site in Ohio.

Seifert said DOE makes efforts to bring on companies capable of providing energy without significantly increasing customers’ electricity rates, since data centers need ample power generation. The Trump administration released the Ratepayer Protection Pledge in March to build out data center infrastructure and meet growing demands without raising electricity bills. He said that if a company or entity wants to bring data center compute to department lands or facilities, it must bring the associated power as well. He added that EM cleanup dollars do not go to these efforts and are appropriated to affect the cleanup and advance that mission, and he said the office is fully committed to ensuring that continues.

Connecticut’s expanded privacy framework took effect October 1 under Public Act 26-64, as amended by Public Act 26-100, and covered data brokers must begin registering with the Connecticut Department of Consumer Protection on January 1, 2027. The state’s Public Act 26-15 adds AI requirements staggered between 2026 and 2027, with principal developer and deployer notice obligations applying to qualifying technology deployed on or after October 1, 2027. On September 9, Governor Gavin Newsom signed AB 1405 and SB 813, which require the Government Operations Agency to establish an AI Auditor Registry by January 1, 2029, and standards for independent verification organizations by January 1, 2028. European regulators finalized guidance on the Digital Services Act and the General Data Protection Regulation, and regulators in Australia, South Korea and Hong Kong continued to develop privacy rules for automated and increasingly autonomous AI systems.

stories.Headline: Chelan considers rules for AI use, public records and data privacy
stories.Summary:
Chelan’s HR and Communications Director, Chad Coltman, presented a draft policy on city use of artificial intelligence to the City Council on Oct. 27, 2026. The proposal would let city employees use AI to draft reports, research projects and streamline daily work. It would also require them to verify AI-generated information, protect confidential records and disclose when publicly distributed images or videos were made with the technology. The policy would apply to city employees, elected officials, volunteers, contractors and others authorized to access city information, including when they do city business on personal devices.

Under the draft, the city’s preferred platform would be Microsoft Copilot, which integrates with Outlook, Word and Excel. Employees could use the free version of Copilot for research, brainstorming and drafting based on publicly available information, and licensed enterprise versions could be used with authorized city business information. For more complex tasks, including technical analysis and extensive document preparation, the city would favor an enterprise version of Claude. Personal accounts on services such as ChatGPT and Google’s Gemini would generally not be permitted for official city work without prior authorization.

The policy would bar employees from entering confidential city information into unauthorized AI systems. Sensitive personal information, including Social Security numbers, financial account details and medical records, would be restricted to approved enterprise systems with safeguards. Attorney-client communications, executive session materials and certain law-enforcement-sensitive information would need specific authorization from the city attorney. AI could assist with research and reports but could not be the sole basis for permitting, enforcement or other government decisions affecting residents, and the same restriction would apply to hiring, discipline, promotion and termination decisions.

Prompts, conversations and documents generated through AI tools may qualify as public records when they relate to city business, and employees would have to retain qualifying records in approved city systems. Public-facing AI-generated or AI-assisted images, audio and video would require clear labeling. Coltman said the goal is not to discourage AI use but to set consistent expectations and keep employees responsible for the results, and he said the disclosure requirement is meant to prevent confusion about whether an image or recording is real. Council took no action Oct. 27, and the policy is expected to return for additional review before members consider adoption.

Articles.Title: Chelan considers rules for AI use, public records and data privacy - Lake Chelan Mirror

stories.Headline: AI writes 75% of Google's new code; developer distrust rises
stories.Summary:
Google reported that artificial intelligence generated 75 per cent of its new code by spring 2026, up from over 30 per cent by spring 2025, according to TechGig on 2 November 2026. The rise came alongside growing developer distrust in AI output, which reached 46 per cent in 2025. GitClear analysed 623 million changed lines of code and found an 81 per cent increase in duplicated code blocks since 2023, reaching 73 per million. Code churn, meaning lines reverted or substantially rewritten within two weeks, doubled from 3.3 per cent to 7.1 per cent.

The Stack Overflow 2025 developer survey found favourable views of AI tools fell from over 70 per cent in 2023 and 2024 to about 60 per cent in 2025. The same survey found developer distrust in the accuracy of AI output grew from 31 per cent to 46 per cent in a single year. The report says AI is mainly replacing undifferentiated code such as boilerplate and CRUD endpoints, where requirements are clear and the cost of errors is low. It adds that the maintenance numbers suggest value for engineers is shifting downstream to review, integration, understanding errors and deciding whether code should exist.

The report states that the role of engineers is consolidating around judgment rather than volume-based productivity metrics like lines per day. It says strong teams now focus on writing precise specifications, reviewing generated code effectively, owning outcomes and exercising judgment on what code not to generate. Google stated the figures on how much of its new code came from AI. The article does not say what Google or other companies plan to do next.

Articles.Title: AI writes 75% of Google's new code; developer distrust rises

stories.Headline: Utsav Planner uses GenAI for Indian event planning, code for calculations
stories.Summary:
Utsav Planner, a GenAI tool for Indian weddings, birthdays and community festivals, was published by TechGig on 2 November 2026. The tool lets AI models interpret natural language requests, such as budget changes or guest count adjustments, while all financial and date-related calculations are handled by tested code. Users must approve every proposed change after reviewing a preview that details each modification. The app was built using AI coding agents, including Google Stitch for mockups, Google Antigravity for implementation planning and Claude Code as the primary coding agent.

The app gives an instant budget split, timeline and vendor checklist even before AI personalisation. It suggests ideas based on city and season and offers ways to save when the budget is exceeded. Developers used 63 test cases to find and correct bloopers in AI model behaviour, such as misinterpreting dates or producing incorrect sums. Essential budget lines like food and venue cannot be removed, only adjusted. Groq's gpt-oss-120b and two Gemini Flash-Lite models power the in-app AI, chosen based on test results.

The separation of AI interpretation from code-based calculations is the developers' safety net against AI models' unreliability at precise arithmetic, which they observed in testing. The app includes a fallback mechanism, so if all AI models are unavailable it still works by showing standard, non-AI suggestions. Plans are tied to the browser, with no accounts, sharing, booking or payment features. The design uses colours from Kalamkari fabric and a Phulkari band under the header, supports light and dark themes, and was checked automatically for contrast, keyboard use and screen-reader labels.

Articles.Title: Utsav Planner uses GenAI for Indian event planning, code for calculations

stories.Headline: Google, Amazon and Intel stumble as investors begin to question the price of the AI boom - CTech
stories.Summary:
Google, Amazon and Intel each reported financial results in late October 2026 that disappointed investors, and the reaction hit the Nasdaq on Friday, October 30, 2026. The tech-heavy index fell 2.86% that day and ended the month nearly 8% below the peak it reached in early October, its sharpest decline in a year and a half. The S&P 500 fell 1.8% on the day and remained 3% below its own peak from earlier in the month. Investors grew concerned that an AI bubble was inflating and could be close to bursting.

At Amazon, the company narrowly missed forecasts, and a second consecutive quarter of negative operating cash flow added to concerns. Google's shares plunged 12%, wiping roughly half a trillion dollars off its market capitalization in one session, and the decline continued on Friday, capping its worst week since it went public about two decades ago. Intel's shares plunged 28%, its second-worst trading day since 1974, and its weak forecast pulled the semiconductor sector down, with Nvidia falling 4% and the semiconductor index dropping 7%. Nvidia, valued at less than $5 trillion, also lost its place as the world's most valuable company to Apple. Amazon and Google both signaled they would keep ramping up spending on AI infrastructure.

The article says Wall Street's central question is now about cost, meaning how much more capital the market can provide to finance AI infrastructure. It describes a circular financial ecosystem in which Nvidia invests in companies across the sector so they can keep buying its GPUs, and in which Amazon, Microsoft, Google and SpaceX commit hundreds of billions of dollars to cloud capacity, while neo-cloud operators such as Nebius and CoreWeave rely on debt to build data centers. The article says Anthropic's full prospectus, published the week before, suggested its costs and revenues are beginning to converge, and that an offering at a valuation of around $2 trillion toward the end of November could become a catalyst for a year-end rally, depending on broader conditions including whether the United States avoids deep involvement in a renewed conflict with Iran. It also notes that after the selloff, Nvidia trades at roughly 25 times expected earnings, Amazon at 19 times and Google at 14 times, comparable to the S&P 500's historical average and below the Nasdaq's average.

Articles.Title: Google, Amazon and Intel stumble as investors begin to question the price of the AI boom - CTech
